div.head: ' TRAINING OF BOYS.
div.p: ' TRAINING OF BOYS.
Chief Scout and Character Development.

Speaking at Tunbridge Wells on Saturday on "Schools and the Scout Movement," Sir Robert Baden Powell, the Chief Scout, said he had had to deal with many boys on their entering the Army, and he found they were well up in reading, writing and arithmetic, but they had no "character." That was because teachers were bound up, and not allowed to impart their indivi- duality to their pupils. He was glad that they were now altering that by developing their own character, and forcing the education authorities to recognise the matter. It was bound to improve the character of boys. During his tour of the world he had been impressed by the fact that overseas they were endeavouring to intro- duce" character into the training of the boys as much as academic knowledge. However, in America the system seemed good until one looked for the results outside the schools. It was then that one noticed in the big cities of America the great amount of poverty and unemployment. There had of late been a good many meddlers like himself in the question of character. The Boy Scout movement was formed to give the boys character. That was its first great aim ; the other two were to encourage boys to learn a trade and to do some- body a good turn every day.

div.head: "FAR FROM A CHRISTIAN THING." THE MAYOR OF SOUTHPORT AND LANDOWNERS.
div.p: "FAR FROM A CHRISTIAN THING." THE MAYOR OF SOUTHPORT AND LANDOWNERS.

Speaking at a reception in connection with the Southport Free Church Council on Monday the Mnyor (Mr F T Reynolds) said that in Southport they had a large number of people earning less than twenty shillings a week. On that miserable wage they bad to bring up their wives and families and pay rents altogether out of proportion to their total earnings. They wanted to work for a time when they would be able to get land on such terms that they could build houses which would not bs hovels. Owners of land in places like Southport should realise that it was far from being a Christian thing that they should deny children places in which to play.

div.head: AFTER THE WAR.
div.p: AFTER THE WAR.
LORD NEWTON AND THE DIVISION
OF THE SPOILS.

Lord Newton presided at the quarterly meeting of the Newton Division Conservative Association held at Warrington on Saturday and devoted much of his speech to the war in the Balkans. He said the first thing which struck anybody who reflected upon the situation was the absurd and ridiculous position pre- sented by the so-called Great Powers. Their notes and diplomatic overtures to the Balkan States had been about as effective as the grumblings and mumblings of some old women who were endeavouring to stop a prize light. If it had been intended to stop the war it could have been done, and could only have been done by making it perfectly clear that the Powers would use force to stop it. Lord Newton expressed the opinion that Turkey would inevitably get the worst of the war, his reasons being that the Turks wei e fighting in a hostile country, so that it was certain that their communications would be cut and their reinforcement prevented; and,secondly that the Turkish fighting man was not so intelligent as his opponent. He then discussed what would follow the wan The position would be serious between this country and the other great Powers when the question of the division of the spoils arose. The Balkan States had been told by the Powers that they would not be allowed to take what they conquered. It would be a very difficult task to dislodge them from the territory they occupied, and it was certain that there would then come a crisis, because Austria, and perhaps Russia as well, would put forward pretensions, and it was quite conceivable that they would take upon themselves to order the Balkan people out of that territory. Looking at the matter simply and solely from the point of view of this country, it seemed to him that if the Tirrks were really going to be driven out of Europe, and he did not believe that even if the Turks were successful they would be permitted to retain their European provinces, the best thing would be that their territory should fall to the small Balkan Powers rather than that it should pass into the possession of one, or both, of the great military empires of the Continent.

div.head: COMMON-SENSE RULE
div.p: A COMMON-SENSE RULE
WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
A PLEA FOR ITS INCLUSION IN THE REFORM BILL.
Speeches by Mrs. Corbett Ashby. and Miss Crosfield.
"That this meeting demands the enfranchisement, o women and urges the 11ou3e of Commons to secure thia in 1912 by adopting an nmendmeht to the Government lieform

'fhis was the resolution passed at a public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, Sanisey-streett4 on Wednesday evening, under the auspices of the %%erring- ton brancu of the brational Union of Women's Suffrage societies. Miss Lucy Broadbent presided over ahatt, atteudance and the principal speakers were Mra Ashby arid Mies Truda Croslleld. Miss BROADBENT declared that women's suffrage was amoral and religious question. They would achieve victory, but whether it came soon or Bite, depended upon the energy and zeal they put into the work now. They were inspired by the teller that the granticg. of women s suffrage would help the cause of purity. They were not asking for an untried experiment; as th 3 enfranchisement of women had been attended with good results in several couuti its, including two of .eur own Colonies. The movement had reached a critical stage because the Reform Bill would soon be intro- duced and it was importaut that they should press for tne inclusion of women in its provisions. (Applause.) Mrs CORBETT As/By, in Moving the above resolution, said they were actually within sight of ,rrictury and they wanted every ounce of energy they oeuld expend oil tte cause. The better work a wr..man did in Ler own sphere —the home—the More right the tact to be consulted as to all that domestic legislation which web occupying so mum] time in earliament. Tuey were not es'aiug for the vote for the sake of having the vote, but, simply because they believed it would enable women to take a larger share in national affairs. Tuey believed there was an immense wealth of practical sympathy and experience which women could coutriuute to the solution of social questions. Last nstek n most impor- tant meeting was ueld an INarringto4 on the question of the

NVHITE SLAVE 7RAFFIC. _ . That was a sui.ject on which women felt very keenly and strongly.. Tney realized what an awful coat it weal to the nation that thousands of lives should be ruined 1 annually. They also appreciated the dangers. 'edict difficulties. No one knew better than they that they could not make a bad person goon by Act of Perlisrnent. There would always be some men end women who were vicious and degraded. '.I hey could, titr';.ev,-r,l be severely punished and prevented from sacritlekng innocent. victims. (Applause.) N inety-ftve out, of (fiery 100 girls in that itwtul traffic bad been innocently trapped into it. Those were the girls who must be saved. (Applame.) The National Vigilance Eoeiey had been working for years to bring a Bill befOre Pailiament. The best men—those woo awaited must keenly what that indamous traffia meant to the n ton were, as always, on their sine. The Bill-would, ere 3, have gone through in its present shape miles ~:to.' women had found in it their chief argirlleaLn.ar practical interference in the affairs of State. Kikpgri- ence taught them, continued Mrs Ashby, that vviiene'ver they had trusted women with fresh advantages, aust; as education or participation in local Government; riet bad risen -LI, it‘e height of their responsibilitydnp nothing but good had come of it. What was se itt some quarters. about the suffragists to-day was-said about Florence Nightingale when silo tried to,etart her great crusewe in tue Crimea. There was an outcry in the Press against a woman who was so shameless and brazen that she would actually go out and nur!.e. 0 ! common soldier in the war. Touching upon the question of • ,

INFANTILE MORTALITY, the speaker pointed out that twice as many children oied in the .dg overcrowded centres in the first year of their life, as died in the ga, den cities. The greater number of those deaths in the industrial centres might be prevented if the conditions into which the chifdren were born were really healthy. They were morally responsible for Jhose deaths. It was no use women saying "1 don't know about these affairs. Politics are men's business." It was their business that those babies were dying. The question of a pure milk supply had an important hearing on the question and if women had had votes they would have said to Parliament "You must talk one week less about Home Rule and pass the Pure Milk Bill in that week." (Applause). She could not believe that the Empire or the country would have been any the worse for it. Women had not the faintest idea of setting themselves against men. They said that If it was good for the family that men and women should work together in the home, it was also good that in the larger family of the nation men and women should co-operate. (Applause). Now they had a

• RLIORIII BILL which would give the vote to every man who fulfilled the simplest qualification of six months' residence or occupation, and, once granted, the man would never lose it. Because practically all men would have votes, the Government would feel that if it had consulted the men, it had consulted the whole of the nation. The wider the franchise given to ' the men, the more they differentiated against women by leaving them out. They were perfecting their mechinery and the people who had no place in it were ! rendered weaker and voiceless. The word " male " person in the first clause of the Bill was a gratuitous insult to women. It had never been inserted in any previous Franchise Bill for, according to a decision ,in the Law Courts, "person "in a Franchise Act meant a man and therefore the insertion of the qualification " male " was unnecessary. What it meant was that as long as that word remained in the measure, it was impossible to include women in the Reform Bill. Dealing wiih amendments which she considered had a good chance of passing, Mrs Ashby said the one favoured on the Conservative side would give the Parliamentary vote only to those women who already had a vote in municipal elections. That would mean that, against 13,000,000 men voters they would only ' have 1,250,000 women electors. Another amendment I which found considerable support on the Liberal and Labour benches would also cunfer the vote on married women over 25 years of age who were the wives of occupiers. That uould place 7,000,000 women on the register. She appealed to supporters of the movement to urge that women should be included in one of those forms. (Applause). Miss TRUDA CROSFIELD, in seconding the resolution, emphasised the economic side of the question. The Government had never restricted the way in which' Men might earn their living, hut on several ' occasions it had tried to restrict •the work of women. Miss Cusfleld alluded to the attempts to prohibit the employment of pit brow girls to the number of G,OOO and of barmaids to the number of 100,000 and to the regulations of the sale of flowers in the streets, to the great disadvantage of the girls as compared with the boys. A paternal Government attempted to take away from women their mean e of livelihood, by a stroke of the pen, but in no single instance did it provide an alternative means of earning their living. Many people talked as if it were wrong ' for women to earn their own living, but surely it was the right and duty of everybody, to work. Why was it chivalrous to give the protection of the vote to men and deny it to women who were weaker physically? She often felt indignant when people talked about chivalry. The anti-suffragists said : " Women are so worshipped in England ; there is such chivalry towards them. You would take away that chivalry by flinging them into the dust and mire of politics." It was all very fine on the surface, but bow was it that all those chivalrous people had forgotten that the drudgery, the worst paid, the heaviest, dirtiest work was often left to women, without a word being said about it ? An argument which amused her immensely was that women ought not to have the vote because they could not fight. (Laughter.) Nowadays it was not personal bravery but training which determined whether men should fight or not and, as only an average of one men in ten had been trained in the army, navy or Territorials, the logical outcome of the argu- ment was that the other nine ought to be disfranchised. (Laughter.) Another absurdity was that the great majority of the actual fighters—the soldiers and sailors —were not allowed to vote. The granting of the vote to married women had worked exceedingly well in Norway. A great many people, however, thought it would mean

DISSENSION IN THE HOME. It seemed to her that if a woman was enlightened enough to care about i prditics, there was much more likelihood of dissension, f sbe held different political views from her husband, as long as she was disfran- chised. If they both possessed votes they had the satisfaction of knowing that one would nullify the other and that no harm would be done. (Laughter.) Did they suppose that some of the finest men on both sides of the House—the Labour party was solid for it—would have worked for women's suffrage if they thought it would be harmful to the interests of men ? Miss Crosfield also quoted the views of leading scientists in support of the movement. Having argued that there should be no taxation without representation and shown that £25,000,000 annually went from the pockets of women into the Treasury, Miss Crosfleld concluded by endorsing Mr. Ellis Griffith's view that woman should be man's partner in the State. The welfare of the State was just as much her concern as the man's and the ideal thing was for them to work side by side to reduce the sum of human misery, and produce happiness in the country. (Applause). The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried. Mrs ASHBY then moved a second resolution in support of Mr Philip Snowden's amendment to give women the right to vote for THE IRISH PARLIAMENT which the Home Role Bill proposed to set up, She pointed out that such a provision would establish an important precedent and if Home Rule .was afterwards given to the other parts of the I.lipted Kingdom, women would be in the strong position of being able to point to the good results which they knew would accrue from consulting Irish women on Irish affairs Mr Boner Law and Sir Edward Carson, although so strongly opposed to Home Rule, had promised to

div.head: BOWLS FOR CHILDREN ?
div.p: BOWLS FOR CHILDREN ?
INTERESTING SUGGESTION AT THE 'WORKS BOWLING ASSOCIATION
Annual Prize Distributien.

A logical and feasible question " Why serSuld our' children not indulge iLI the game of bowls? " was raised at the annual presentation of prizes in connec- tion with the Warrington Works Bowling Association at the Horse end Jockey Hotel, on Saturday evening The season which closed some weeks ago has been one of the most successful in the annals of the associa- tion and it is such success,and the great benefit which workingmen derive from this wholesome, healthy and enjoyable recreation provided by. the Works Associa- tion that makes the realisation of Captain Crostield's soggestion in regard to bowls for children, possible. The progress if the association was reviewed from the commencement and one could appreciate the sacrifices the committee had made and the energy they have expended in bringing the organisation to such a high position. The function was held in the club-room and t! e-Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) occurpied the chair. There were also present : Captain George R. Cros- field (president of the association), Mr J W illet (chair- man), Mr T O'Brien (vice-chairman), Mr J A Bush. worth (hon. treasurer', Comv..iillor Jenkins, Mr W Webster, Mr H Hope and Mr W Patrick (hon. secre- tary). Letters -of apolopy for non-attendance had been received by the secretary from Mr A U Crosfield, Mr Murray, Mr Peter Bate, Sir Gilbeit Greenall Bart C.V.0., Hr W P ilylands, and Mr Harold Smith M.P., The president was congratulated upon his promotion to the rank of major in the Territorial Army and the Mayor was congratulated upon his re-election as Mayor for the third time.

div.head: NAZIM PASHA,
div.p: NAZIM PASHA,
the Commander-in-Chief of the Turkish Army, whose forces have sustained such a crushing defeat by the Balkan Allies this week.

During the evening an excellent musical and vocal programie was submitted by the following artistes in a capable manner which evoked the warm appreciation of all. Messrs N Cook, W Farrington (humorist), J Houghton, (whose rendering of "Thora " called forth an encore), and Mr Howarth, clarinet soloist. Mr W Pemberton was an efficient accompanist.

The loyal toast having been honoured on the proposition of the president, Mr W Webster proposed Our President " and in doing so said he was pleased to hear of Captain Crosfield's promotion in the Territorial ranks. Ile knew he was echoing the senti- ments of all present when be said that they heartily :congratulaied him on such promotion and they hoped and trusted further promotion would follow for their president was certainly a deserv- ing officer. (Applause.) They must not forget also, the high honour which had been conferred upon him some time ago, that of honorary captain in the standing army. (Hear, hear.) Captain Crosfield was a man who did a great deal of good work but he hid the light of his charity under a bu4ael. He had been president of their association for 10 years and he had made a most ardent and enthusiastic one. (Hear, hear.) He had worked hard and given time and money irimaking the association as successful as they saw it now. The Bowling Association had made rapid progress and there was no telling towhat dimensions the mains would reach It struck him that would have to play bowls both in summer and winter. (Laughter.) They had at the head of affairs a staunch supporter of all sports and of every- thing that was for the betterment of his fellow men. (Applause.) et.ptain CROSFIELD, in reply, said he was pleased to be president of such a flue energetic set of men and to give any assistance he could to such a worthy cause. They had an excellent set of officials who worked hard in the interests of the association. They were going on steadily year by year, and in the past season they had no fewer than 63 teams entering in the competition, representing 37 works and 602 entries against 483 for the previous year. It must be intensely gratifying to them and to those who started the associa- tion to see that great organisation growing so steadily, and to feel that more and more they were providing facilities for men to enjoy the game of bowls. The association did not go smoothly at the beginning, but now they were prospering from strength to strength, and he did not see why they should stop at any limit. (Hear, hear.) He had said on a previous occasion, and he would repeat again that whereas work must always be the first essential in a man's life, play was never- theless necessary for everybody. (Hear, hear.) It was the old story of the balance of life. It was no good doing one thing to the exclusion of everything else -, they must have a balanced life to grew up happy and healthy individuals. "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy, and all play and no work makes Jack an empty boy.' (Hear, hear.) He thought it was very sad to go round our big cities and see children having no place to play in except the streets. (Hear, bear.) For the children, play was absolutely necessary and essential. If they looked round nature, they found all in the animal kingdom played. It was a fine work Mrs Humphry Ward was doing in trying to get play- grounds for the children in our cities. Why should they not have bowls for children? They might be able to arrange for the children of Warrington to start playing bowls with small woods, during the hours the men did not occupy the greens. The idea had occurred to him the other evening and perhaps they would think it over and see if it were practicable. He wished them great success in the coming year. (Applause). The MAYOR, in presenting the prizes, said he had been associated with working men all his life and he had a very great respect for them. He took a great interest in their welfare and happiness and, looking at it from that point of view, he could not help contrast- ing the opportunities the working man had for healthy enjoyment now, as compared with 35 years ago. The cause of that rested in great measure with the magnificent efforts of workingmen and the good feeling of one man towards another, as shown in their worthy president. It was such men as he who had done much to bring that great change about. (Hear, bear.) With regard to the game ot bowls, which he had watched, he could quite understand the men taking an interest in such a healthy and skilful pastime. It was a game of skill which fitted the participators physically and mentally for their work. To engage in a game of skill made them better workmen. If they were skilful bowlers the tech- nical exercise of the hands and rankles made them better w orkraan if they were engaged in manual labour. He was sorry to say they could not do anything in regard to a playground for the children in the centre of the town. Ile bad expressed his regret to the Local Government Board Inspector—who bad been bolding an inquiry at the Town Hall recently with reference to the Town Planning Bill—that they could not do it. The errors of the past, so far as the outlying districts were concerned,would not be repeated.He was sorry they could not improve, to the extent they would like, the condi- tions of the poorest classes of people who lived in the heart of the town. At the same time there were public-spirited men in Warrington who would do much in that direction. There would be no errors in the future. He did not want to call our grandfathers who might have acted as they thought best at the time being. It was quite easy to pick holes in other people's policies, but very likely if we had

been in their shoes we might have done the same or possibly worse. (Laughter.) In regard to children playing bowls, he thought it was quite feasible. It was a most excellent idea and he would be very glad to support it as far as he could. (Applause.) In con- clusion he would say that any association which had officials like the Warrington Works Bowling Association was bound to be a success. (Applause.) His Worship then presented the first eight prizes to the following gentlemen, the remaining prizes having been handed over to the winners by Mr Patrick : Messrs W Gibbons. Spilsbury, E Clare, T Hardmau, J Broadhurst, H Langley, .1 Bibby, and 11 Slather. Sir dIBBONS, the cup-winner in the annual main briefly replied, and the MAYOR said he had two more interesting presentations to make. One was that of a cheque value £4 5s 2d to Councillor Jenkius on behalf of the Childrens' Summer Camp and the other was £6 to Mr Hope on behalf of the Nursing Association.l (Applause). Councillor JENKINS in returning thanks, said they bad been able to send 518 children to the camp in 1912,1 as against 483 for the previous year, and the cheque I would be extremely useful because their balance at the bank-was the wrong way about. With a little persever- ance they would char that difficulty away. (Hear, hear and applause). Mr HOPE said it was not rrany weeks since he received £7 as a result of the match in connection with the Caledonian Association and the Works Association. He was glad to see that they appreciated the services of the nurses in the town. So long as the workpeople supported them there would he no need to ealk of any Parliamentary measures affecting them. Mr W PATRICK, in proposieg a vote of thanks to the donors of prizes said that when he took over the position of secretary to the Association six years ago, the amount of subscriptions received amounted to the magnificent sum of £ll 15s subscribed by eight individuals. From one individual alone they received £8 of that amount and that would show that they had not a great Dumber of subscribers. Once saddled with the burden, he intended to get rid of it. Instead of having eight subscribers to-day they had 59 and the possibilities were they would have a few more in a week or so. (Applause.) He had not finished yet. To-day they bad £66 from those 59 subscriters as against £ll 15s from the few at the beginning. There ,were only five works out of the 37 competing who did not contribute to the Association in cssh and those were conoerns like the Corporation and the Winwick Asylum He was, however, hoping in the future to be able to obtain something from them. (Hear, bear.) They wanted the works to assist them, as they provided their workmen with recreation outside their working hours. Mr T O'BRIEN (vice-chairman) seconded and said if it had not been for Mr Patrick they might not have had a Works Bowling Association to-day. (Hear, hear.) He suggested a presentation to Mr Patrick for the services he had rendered the association. The toast" Our Association " was honoured on the proposition of Mr H Hope who said the Association had been of no mushroom growth. Whereas 10 years ago they had 2a teams with 200 players, this season they had had 60 teams with 2,500 players and a handicap just finished with 600 players. To his mind their associa- tion was about the strongest in England. Mr J WILLETT (chairman), in reply said he was onel of the founders of the association and they had fought the battle through. They had a great deal of opposi- tion at the commencement but the more opposition there was, the more they had flourished. They were working the association for the benefit of the working men. They provided the facilities whereby men who had toiled hard in the workshops during the week could have healthy recreation at the week-end and by that they were being made healthier and better MPII and more fit for their employment at the commencement of the week. The employers reaped a benefit from the association, for the men were better and more efficient workmen and entered into their various occupations with a zest and zeal which was cultivated in a large degree on the bowling green. (Hear, hear.) Ihe further success of the association depended upon the support of the workingmen of the town. With that patronage the success of the association would increase each years (Applause). Mr. A. E. B URDETT proposed a hearty vote of thank to the Mayor and Captain Crosfielet, and Mr list.Fortu having seconded, the resolution was carried with musical hononrs. Captain CROS FIELD, in responding, said he was quite sure the association would be doing the right thing in making a presentation to Mr. Patrick. The Secretary had done much hard work, and it would be an apprecia- tion of his valuable services to give him a present next year. ((Applause). On the proposition of Mr. Councillor ARCHER, seconded by Mr. JONATHAN WOODS, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the treasurer, secretary and a r tiges.

div.p: BOWLING.
LANCASHIRE COUNTY AMATEUR ASSOCIATION. WARRINGTON PRIZE WINNERS.

There was a representative gathering of delegates from all parts of the county to the headquarters of this association, at the Albion Hotel, Nianchester. on Saturday. The Lancashire President,Mr J G Coombs, occupied the chair. The association hon secretary (Mr C W Smith) read the report of the Finance Committee, which showed that a sum of £lOO had been set aside for prizes won during the 1912 season. In connection with the county championship .C. 40 had been set aside, whilst for the individual merit a sum of .E2O was allotted to the" all sections," £lO to the Manchester section, I:10 to the Liverpool section, and £8 each to Warrington and Blackpool sections. The President read a list,compiled by the association secretary, of county players who were awarded gold medals for the county championship of the British Crown Green Amateur Bowling Association, won by Lancashire this year. They included :—J W Gleave, A Gleave, and T Humphreys, of Warrington. The Liverpool and District Bowling League applied and were accepted as members of the County Association. A resolution moved by J Southern (Leigl3),'?" That all players taking part in county matches be paid travelling expenses by the County Association," was defeated by 32 votes to 21. The Wigan delegate, F Bullen, moved a resolution. "That the entrance fee for the second teams champion- ship ba increased from lOs 83 to 155," which was defeated. The County President presented the following with prizes won during the 1912 season : County Individual Championship (All Sections).—G W Corner, Urmston, 1 ; Joseph Gleave, Warrington, 2 ; W Mawdsley, Liverpool, 3; J W Jolley, Warrington 4. div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" The Queen of the Redskins."

The wild and picturesque life of the West presents an inexhaustible theme for the dramatist, and Mr Travis Green's play "The Queen of the Redskins " is a vivid and exciting story in which Indians,Cowboys, as well as repreeentatives of the more conventional and artificial world, have their part. Some of the incidents are far-fetched but the play, as a whole, has a fair semblance of reality, and it undoubtedly keeps a firm grip on the audience. At the head of a strong com- pany is Mr Jerrold Heather, who impersonates the dashing, fearless Broncho Bill as to the manner born. The honours are shared by Miss Hilda Shirley, as Queen of the Reaskins, her natural and touching por- trayal creating a great impression. Mr Horace Booth does justice to the thankless part cf George Lyndhurst, the villain of the piece, and he has a thorough-going accomplice in Miss Amy Maitland as Olive Lyndhurst. Another successful impersonation is that of Mr Arthur C Russell as the unsuspecting but duped William Lyndhurst. Little Christine Murray, as Queenie, is a great favourite ana some bright comedy is introduced by Mr Frank Cox as Samba and :Jibs Jessie Campbell as Julia. The other parts are in capable hands and the play is elaborately mounted. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Next week the sensational American drama" The Slave Girl," a story of America's fight for freedom, will be presented.

div.head: JUNIOR LIBERAL "TOWN COUNCIL."
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERAL "TOWN COUNCIL."

In order to familiarise its members with municipal " questions, the Warrington Junior Liberal Association has formed a " Town Council " and debates will beh conducted in conformity with the procedure of that, authority. At the opening meeting, held in the Association's rooms in Horsernarket-street, there a good attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. E. Lloyd Jone,-,, whit' has been elected " Mayor " of the Council. During the course of his address he emphasised the necessiti. , for a greater interest in the municipal work of the town. He said the work of a Town Council vas becoming more important every year, and the increase was bound to be greater in the future than in the past' A deep and well rooted knowledge of Imperial affairs was impossible unless a person was well jO touch with municipal matters. The Town Council would have a great deal to do with the working of the Insurance Act. Thus it behoved every one to studl and debate those questions, and it was for such reasons as this that the Junior Liberal Town Council ha°l been inaugurated. With a view to giving the members a closer insight into the working of Town Councila generally, it was decided to invite leading Alder men and Councillors from the Warrington To°l3 Council, including Alderman Bennett and Councill°r Henry Roberts, to deliver short addresses to the Junior Liberals on "The present day outlook and work of Town Councils," and particulars of these addresses will be published later. The Chairman thought that the young men in connection with the Junior Liberaldl were quite capable of running a Town Council, a° , perhaps, he said, it would be an incentive for some them to take up municipal work, and in the near future he hoped to see some Junior Liberal taking his stand for municipal honours. Members were then elected as Councillors for the various wards.

div.head: NOTES BY " MUST."
div.p: NOTES BY " MUST."

Warrington have their first taste of cup tie football to-day, and quit el possibly it will he their last until the great competition comes round next March. The team xvhicla is available for the match at St. llelens in Round tr' of the Lancashire Cup Competition is by no means a formidable one, and does not inspire much confidPnce. In fact, were it not a cup-tie I should place Warrington's chances at practically nil, but in cup-tie warfare the Wirepullers have always to be taken seriously. Therefore they must be considered to have a chance even at St. Helens and with a weakened team.

It was no secret that Warrington's new Welshmen •were not available for this Competitiou, but it was not anticipated that Renwick would also be an absentee. The skipper has got a damaged shoulder and requires another week's rest before donning the jersey again, so that the team will be short of Renwick, R Thomas, Cm and Nicholas. These

changes reveal the paucity of the reserves,particularly forward. The" A "team scrummagers are none of them of the requisite physique for League football, and very few of them will improve to any notable extent. This is one of the departments where the club still requires new men.

--- The team selected to do anty at St Helens is : Jolley, full back; Brooks, Dickenson, Tranter and Woodburn, threequarters ; Rushton and Douglas, half backs; Thomas, Cheaters, Fearnley, Skelhorne, -Naylor and Bevan forwards.

This is not a bad side when you consider than St. Ilelens have no reputation for .forward strength. Runcorn's triumph last Saturday showed ,up the weakness of the Saints' scrummagers and as Warring- ton beat the Runcorn forwards at Irwell-lane they

should be able to give their barks a chance or two to-dap. I am glad to see Douglas get a trial with the seniors. He is the only junior half-back we have with ideas of combination, and deserves encourage- ment. Brooks would be better on Tranter's wing right) in my opinion. The St. Helens committee have made many changes in their team for the match with Warrington. Flanagan Resin comes into the wing three-quarter position, and Barton, the former captain, who has been incapacitated for some time, is selected for the other wing, while Molyneux partners Richardson at half-back, Kelly being dropped. Heaton and Waddell came into the forwards, along with Manchester, who Played three-quarter last week. The full team is as follows: Turtill; Flanagan, Greenwood, Browning, T Barton; Molytieux, Richard- son ; Heaton, Shallcross, Mavitty, Waddell, Prescott, Manchester.

Last Saturday was reminiscent of the days when Stuntz was a regular performer in the Warrington ranks. He got a rare baptism of mud in an abnorm- ally wet winter and I have always regretted his non- return to see what he could do on drier days. We have not had a wing as dangerous on the attack since be returned " down under." This by the way. The downpour last Saturday made football almost impossi- ble but the clubs got through the appointed programme. Warrington had a sorry experience at Widnes where the ground was partly under water and where the match was stopped by the referee ten minutes from time, with Warrington in arrears by 8 points to 2.

Warrington had a chance—perhaps only a slight one—of pulling the match out of the mud if full time bad been played, and I think Brooks made a mistake in suggesting that the match should end when it did. A lot of scoring can be. done in ten minutes if luck only favours the attacking side, and Warrington were getting much more of the attack at this stage than before. In the first half they made a sorry show, With wind and rain in their faces, and Widnes were easily top-dogs. Their forwards beat Warrington badly with dashing footwork, and quite held their own on the change of ends. Still, Warrington had chances and they came so near scoring on several occasions that there was room for hopefulness if the match had gone on. As CO minutes were played the game stands a 8 a completed fixture.

Somehow the Warrington front rank men always come off second ,best at Widnes and yet the two packs are about equal in weight. Behind there was not much to chose considering the difference in the opportunities afforded each set of backs. Nicholas handled the ball well at the pack, but the centres were both slow. Brooks was much the better of the two wings, and always made headway when he got the ball. Jolley had a heavy afternoon's work and put tIP a plucky and resourceful defence which was worthy of all praise.

div.head: TO-DAY'S MATCHES.
div.p: TO-DAY'S MATCHES.

div.head: Warrington at Widnes.
div.p: Warrington at Widnes.

A Rain-Spoiled Match. Warrington had the worst day of the season for their visit to Widnes on Saturday. Heavy rain fell con- tinuously, and the ground was partially under water. Warrington played a.: selected, but Widnes were abort of Taylor, Noon and Higgins. Only about 1,000 spectators assembled. The teams were: Widnes—Jones; Laws, Daiuteth, Pennington, Swin- ton; Lally, O'Garra (J); Aspey (G), Aspey (S), Lloyd, Reid, O`Garra (H) and Cosgrove. Warrington—Jolley; Brookes, Tranter, Dickenson, Woodburn •, Nicholas, Rushton; Thomas (G), Thomas (R), Cox, Cheaters, Skelhorn and Fearnley. Referee, It Robinson, Bradford. Warrington started against both wind and rain, and were soon beaten back by the energetic home forwards Reid early broke away from centre and after a fine run sent the ball out to Cosgrove who scored a good try. Daintith failed at goal. On resumption, Rushton was hurt in tackling Reid and was carried off. A dribble by Woodburn quickly changed the venue. Jones saved , in grand fashion, and the game once more ruled in the home team's favour. Jones, later, missed an easy penalty shot, and then Jolley cleared grandly from Swinton. Nicholas made an impression with a smart run from the pack, but he was badly supported. Brookes was at fault when the Warrington backs were passing in promising fashion, for he knocked on badly. Laws picked up from the pack but he was cleverly tackled by Tranter. A moment later Lally was well held on the but finally, a movement in which OW'aGrarriurt°li line,Swinton and Pennington passed effectively, led to Swinton scoring behind the posts. Jones kicked a good goal. Widnes were holding their own, but were penalized when Pennington and Swinton were danger- ous. Thomas made useful ground, and at this stage Rushton returned. Good use of the touch line carried Warrington down the field, but Lally drove them back and Widnes attacked, Jolley fielded grandly, and a good exchange kick from Jones was responded to by Tranter, who marked finely. Nicholas, Dickenson and Tranter passed neatly, and Dickenson was well held by O'Garra when be looked dangerous. The Widnes forwards dribbled well, but Brookes saved. Warrington pressed and Rushton intercepted a pass from Swinton, but Dickenson was not allowed to go far. R Thomas made a bad offside mistake, and Warrington were successfully repulsed. Interval: Widnes, eight points; Warrington, nil. On resumption the ground was in an awful state, and rain still fell heavily. Brookes made a good opening and subsequent passing nearly ended in a score, Tranter being tackled on the line, Widnes were pulled up when going strongly, and from the free kick, Warrington got to the centre, where Nicholas and Dickenson passed finely, the former getting into Laws' way when near the line. Brookes made another effort to get through but his pass to Treater

came to naught, Dickenson being tackled in possession. Warrington now pressed strongly and Jones was forced to allow the hall to roll dead to save. O'Garra successfully checked Woodburn. and Jolley was cheered for a remarkably fine clearance from the Widnes forwards. R Thomas was responsible for a floe tackle of Laws and Brooks male a strong effort to breaN through, but Jones rolled him over in fine fashion. Laws ran well and looked a certain scorer y,rior to Tranter intercepting his pass. The Warrington player was well held by Jones a moment afterwards, and then Brookes was cleverly tackled. A had case of offside gave Warrington a chance and G Thomas scored a penalty goal. Ten minutes from time the referee abandoned the game owing to the continued miserable conditions. The score was : Widnes, eight points ; Warrington, two points. RUNCORN'S FINE WIN AT ST: HELENS.

This return game was responsible for the poorest gate of the season at Knowsley-road, torrential rain descending before and throughout the game. Early on St Helens forced matters, and Manchester dribbling away scored at the corner, but Turtill failed to improve 1 Following a burst by Pacibury, Watton picked up, and dropped a goal, and close on the interval Greenwood cleverly dropped a goal for Runcorn. In the second half the Cheshire men adapted themselves to the con- ditions more so than the • Saints," and from pretty passing Hughes crossed the line, for Richardson to goal. Play continued to favour !Runcorn, whose for- wards played a •great game in the mud. Richardson placed a goal from a penalty kick, and near the close Hughes again crossed, but Richardson failed. Result : Runcorn 3 goals and 2 tries (12), St Helens 1 goal and 1 try (5 points). Teams and officials : St. Helens—Turtill, back ; [Manchester, Greenwood Belshorne, and Woods, three-quarter backs ; A Kelly and Richardson, half backs ; 'Webb, Prescott, Mavitty, Butterfield, Wilcock, and Sballoross, forwards. 6 Runcorn—Shaw, back ; Hughes, Moores, Thornton, and Newell, three-quarter backs ; Stevenson and Wat ton, half backs; Massey, Peacock, Padbury, Donoghue, Prince and Richardson, forwards. Referee, T Walsh, Hunslet. Touch judges, J Jones, Wigan, and J Hannaford, St. Helens.

Attempts at combination were made by both'sides, but absolute failure attended every move- ment An individual effort by Dainteth (Warrington) looked likely to produce a score until Brennan stepped in and made dead. Carter, after running well, gave Clare a great chance to score, but the wing man failed to gather the greasy ball. Widnes now attacked and Wailing kicked a penalty goal. Half-time : Widnes, one goal (two points) ; Warrington, nil.—ln the second portion of the game the visitors showed superior tactics and Douglas (Widnes) ran over from the pack, but the kick failed. 'Mclntyre, Povey and Dainteth tried hard to break through the Widnes defence, but in vain. A change was made in the home side, Jordan exchanging places with Dalnteth, and Warrington made strenuous efforts to get on terms, but the defence held out and Widnes were deservedly winners by one goal one try (five paints) to Warrington nothing.

Rylands' lost the toss. Clifton kicked off, and considering the state of the ground the players handled the ball splendidly. Erma pack formed near the railway end, Morris passed out to Hennessey, who scored at the corner. RN,lands forwards still con- trolled the pack, and after all the backs had hnndled, Griffiths scored, Potter failing at goal. Griffiths shortly afterwards repented the feat. After 20 minutes' play four of the Clifton players left the field, which caused the game to be abandoned, Rylands leading by nine points to nil. The full-back play of Clifton was their one redeeming feature.

At 11-ea-tley in wretched weather. At the end Of 15 minutes' play Woodcock, with a nice shot, opened the score for Mobberley. Mobberley kept up the pressure, and Ogden, the home custodian, was penalized for bold- ing an opponent. Cragg, however, shot over the bar from the consequent penalty. Before the interval Shakeshaft, with a capital individual effort, ran clean through the home defence and placed the " Dockers " two goals to the good. Half-time : Mobberley, two goals ; Oughtrington Amateurs, nil.—The second half was more even and stubbornly contested. No further scoring took place until the last live minutes, when from a corner, the home team were rewarded, as follow- ing a struggle from the aforesaid corner in the goal- mouths Cragg put through his own goal. Owing to the inclement weather the game was not a success as far as hockey was concerned, , the ground towards the close of the game becoming a quagmire. The outstanding feature of the game was the grand display by Bloomer as centre forward. Although coot: only playing ten men the visitors were ',wally pressing, Swinton seldom crossing the half- way line in the first half. div.head: NEXT WEEK: FIFTH. OF NOVEMBER CELEBRATIONS.
div.p: NEXT WEEK: FIFTH. OF NOVEMBER CELEBRATIONS.

LATCHFORD. The First Eleven were not engaged last week. The Second Eleven are going great guns now and beat Brooklands 8-3, making up for the slating they received at Brooklands last February. Both teams played the three-back game and as is usual in this match there was a lot of good sporting hockey enjoyed by both teams despite the bad weather. The home team led 3-1 at half-time. Then followed some fine play by the visitors who scored three times, but Latchford came along again and scored five times before the finish. Brooklands bad hard lines on several occasions, especi- ally when their centre-forward (who played a fine game) hit the crossbar with a smashing shot. Bradshaw at centre-half touched his best form, and Eccles and Brubl at back did much useful work. Among the forwards Banks showed what a stick artist he is and shot five of 1 the goals. Minards also scored two goals. Laver of the right wing again did well, and scored one of the best goals of the match.

Thg First Eleven at West Kirby this afternoon is : Wright, goal ; Bruhl, Billington, backs; Gibbs, Wilkin- son, Isherwood, halves: Dale, Pearson, Banks, Jones, Starkey, forwards. Referee, Mr Cobb. Train from Central 1.50 p.m. The Second Eleven v West Kirby " A " at home is:— Three full-backs, Pecks, Dixon, Mull; Hobin,Bradshaw Banks; Diver, Fletcher, Hackney, 111inards, Colton. div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

IThe weather on Satu7day last seriously interfered with may outdoor games, but did not deter the enthusiasts of this sport who fought out some interest- ing fixtures in very heavy rain, as note some of the resulp :-At Radcliffe a pack of 60 ran twice over 3i miles trail, and at the end of the seven miles race, despite the fact that they were without J Horan, Bolton had won com- paratively easily, thus: Bolton: Lee 1, Bryant 2, Daly 7, Elsington 8, Chilton 11; 29 points. Radcliffe: Hogan 3, Greaves 4, J Hilton 10, T Hilton 12, Barton 14 ;43 points. Heywood : Schofield 5, Taylor 6, Mclntyre 9, Smith 15, Wood 16;31 points. At Sheffield, over 4 miles, a race between 16 Hallamehires and 9 I West Cheshires resulted.-Elallamshire : J Cooke 1, 8 , Revues 2, Len Chattaway 4, D Aldous 6, G Butcher 10, I Oldfleld 12 ; 35 points. West Cheshire : A Macmaster 3, J Preston 5, G Parkinson 7, A Montgomery 8, G Walker 9,1 Barnett 13 ; 45 points. At Lancaster, Sutton Harriers over a six miles course, proved too good for a combined team, result. Sutton : J Smart 1, WI Burrows 2, J Topping 3, D Brown 5, T Edwards 7, S Welding 8, 26 points. Lancaster S Chamberlain, Park, 4; T Parks, Primrose, 6 ; J Towers, Park, 9 ; W Redhead, Primrose, 12 ; J Gardner, Skerton, 13 ; A Gardner, Park, 14 ; 58 points; 26 ran and after the first two there was a gap of nearly 300 yards At Newcastle 155 runners represented 16 clubs in a run of the Northumberland and Durham Paper Chase League and a good race between the first five resulted: T Urwin, Blaydon, 1; J McCloskey, Cornett, 2; J W Breed, Durham,3 ; W Lee, Saltwell, 4; J Thompson, Heaton, 5. In a run over about 41 miles, Warrington A.O were captained by F Shadwell who, attended by a band of useful novices, followed A Gregson home after a very fast spin. Warrington A.O have arranged to decide their annual points competition in the following fixtures:- November 9th, Runcorn, at Runcorn; 160, Leigh and Bolton, atT,Leigh; 23rd, St Helens League, at Warrington; 30th, Salford Harriers, at Eleatley ; December 70, St I Helens League, at Runcorn ; January 4th, St Helens League, at Sutton; 11th, Runcorn. at Warrington. Novices are not being neglected as medals will be given to the first novice home in each of the NoveMber races and in addition a further chance will be afforded in the Novice Team Race ander the auspices of the West Lancashire C.C.A. to be held at Warrington on Decem- ber 14tb. The junior championship (Holder Fred Shadwell 1912 and 1911) is to be decided on the points principle in the West Lancashire and Northern junior championships at Lancaster on February Ist and Stock- ton on February 15th next and the result is very open as lowing to being in the count of the winning team of the last West Lancashire Junior, Shadwell will be ' proving his worth to the club by tackling Herbert Holbrook (Holder) in the senior championship of the club which is to be decided on the points gained in the open championships in which the club is represented. Briefly, the definition of a novice for club races is one who has neverwon a prize(Christmas handicaps excepted) For Cross Country Running and for the West Lancashire Novice Team Race the definition is one who has never won a prize for running at any distance; club prizes do not debar. Having regard to the report that a large number of sportsmen will be shooting in the vicinity of Moore this afternoon,members of Warrington A.O are requested to leave a clear field and meet at headquarters not later than three o'clock to take part in a run and learn full details of the sporting and social programmes which include a dance on December 6th.
' VICAR ADVOCATES THE "CAT" FOR PROCURERS.

Addressing the parish -C&iiC-I;l:Tr.anch of the Church of England Alen's Society on Sunday OD the white slave traffic, Vie Vicar of Lancaster said that the punish.nent provided for procurers in the bill should be much greater than mere imprisonment. As the " cat " was the means of stamping out garrotting, it ought to be used to put down the abominable and hideous trade in human flesh. The law as it at present existed was not strong enough. The bill must be restored to its original form, and they must trust the police force.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION. N. A. CENTRE.

Anglinglast week-end was almost out of the question and the fd‘v who ventured far from town were sorry for doing so. The water nearer home yielded far better results than those farther afield. Four gudgeon were marked up, and only for neglect on a member's part the number would have been five, and the one not regis- tered would have been first ;10z.Ildrms.was the heaviest and they ran cio.n to loz. 7drms—not at all a bad week-end for gudgeon. The other species were conspicuous by their absence, not a decent catch being heard of. The Long Barn affair was postponed, owing to the bad weather. We heard of one or two roach being taken during Sunday last, but none of any consequence. Norton seemed quite deserted, also the Gowy. There is every possibility of a new club form- ing to affiliate to the N.A.A. in Warrington and those desirous of joining please give their names to the Secretary. How LUEI rumour that the Northern Anglers had taken over the Gowy has got about we (the officials of the W.W.A.A.) fail to see, as we have not beard of it from the General Secretary, Mr Redford, of Bolton. There has certainly been something mentioned by our dele- gate, Mr J Potter, at the last Executive Council meet- ing that took place at Horwich, and the business that will arise from that will be published in the 'Examiner" in due course. But op to the time of writing the N.A.A. has not taken it over to our knowledge, and members may rest assured that they would not be kept in the dark for long if such a thing did happen. The set board has now registered its last fish for season 1912 and the competition has been open until the last day with the exception of the roach set which was recognised sea foregone conclusion after Mr. C. Ashton had weighed his catch from Castor near Yarmouth the biggest being Jib 12oz and the smallest well over llb Soz. These weights were considered winners directly they were put up. I think the lucky member who will capture the most specials is Mr. I'. Singleton and he has taken all his weighers from Norton. Next week will appear a full Bet of prize winners. A. S.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There are all sorts of" turns" except poor turns at the Hippodrome this week. Acrobatics and gymnas- tics are a strong line, and the performances of two separate troupe are full of interest. The Five Cliftons excel in muscular equilibrist tricks, and the work of the graceful Miss Clifton stands out by itself. She is exceptionally gifted by nature and performs feats which would usually be deemed impossible for the " weaker " sex. The great Lumars specialise in comedy acrobatics, and here again the lady is a not- able member of the company. She forms the living electric horizontal bar in the grand finale —a spectacle of uncommon brilliance. The Terry Twins are the top-liners of the week, and two brothers mere alike it would be impossible even to imagine. Their simi- larity of feature, expression, colouring and physique is positively ludicrous and the question " which of us is me ?" is puzzling in the extreme. Naturally the twins exploit the resemblance to the full, and their quaint notions frequently convulse the house. A comic boxing match between the two is screamingly funny and clinches the assertion that the Terrys are comedians as well as twins. Mr and Miss de Breen present a unique Japanese act which begins with some expert juggling and ends with a phenomen- ally clever exhibition of slaadowgraphy. Mr de Brunie hands must be almost as valuable as those of Paderewski. His finger-work produces the most bizarre effects on the screen, many of which, too, are irresistibly humorous. The Dick and Dorothy Trio combine harmomy and dancing in brilliant style. Their simultaneous footwork is am-ng the best of its kind seen at Warrington, and the end of a prolonged spell of dancing ensures the heartiest rounds of applause. Louis J Seymour is one of the most popular and breezy light comedians on the Macnaugh'ten circuit and his rollicking chorus songs go with rare gusto in the " gods." He is is a clean performer with a real sense of humour in song. Simple Smart doe* a lot of grotesque tumbling as "the acrobatic sportsman," and though his facial expression is overdone he raises many a laugh. Violet Romaine earns a good reception as a contralto vocalist, while the American civil war picture is one of the best thrown on the screen at the Friar's-gate house.

The recent speech of LORD ROBERTS' Lord ROBERTS was INDISCRETION. made 'a subject of questioning in the House of Commons on Tuesday. We do not think it possible that a better reply could .have been given to interrogatories in this subject than that of Sir EDWARD GREY. It was suggested in the first of the questions that Germany may have protested to the Foreign Office about Lord ROBERTS'S , speech. There has been no such pro- test said the FOREIGN SECRETARY, and he would deprecate any suggestion that either Government should make official representations to the other about unwise or provocative speeches made by persons who I are not in a position to control the policy of their respective Governments. That wise and straightforward reply seems to us to cvoer the whole ground. Lord ROBERTS speaks for himself. He has a clear right so to do. But it is a matter for regret that a man of his popularity and distinction should speak unwisely or provocatively about another great Power with which we are on terms of friendship.

There was a remark in the "Times" which seems to apply with great exactness to Lord ROBERTS'S case. It was this: "No Army will ever inscribe victories on its banners when its officers become politicians first and soldiers afterwards. Politics wrought the final undoing of the Turks as warriors." This is intended to apply to the Turks only, of course. It is not possible that the " Times " could have meant it for , wider applicat: But is actually a universal truth. The ancient proverb" Ne sutor ultra crepidam " was never more justified than in regard to the soldier and politics. The , soldier should stick to his soldiering. When he touches politics he is much more likely to be influenced by prepossessions than by knowledge of the political situation. There is nothing in any special form of human capacity which entitles its possessor to p ose as an authority on things in general. Mr. RUDYARD KIPLING is a very great and original writer, but the fame which he has won in that capacity does not entitle him to lecture our statesmen on this and that. He must prove his capacity for statesmanship before he can be accepted as an authority; and this he has quite failed to do. We sub- mit with all respect that Lord ROBERTS is exactly in the same position. He is a great soldier. It would be absurd to regard him on , that ground as a man who is capable of instructing Governments on questions which involve the peace of the world. Among the things said by Lord ROBERTS in the speech which has been most in question was this : " Germany strikes when Germany's hour has struck." As a European ?ower, as a Continental Power, we do not exist for war. Our Army as a belligerent factor in European politics is almost a neglig- ible quantity. Well, we are willing to sub- mit this to the ordinary judgment of the average man. Our military organisation, which is immensely better than it was when Lord ROBERTS was at the Horse Guards, is intended for our own special purposes, and not for Continental wars. It is the organ- isation suited to an Island Empire, the argest in the world. It could be broken to pieces, no doubt, if we forgot that we were an island, and if we threw ourselves into Con- tinental conflicts. But all British policy is built up on the advantages of our insular situation. It has always been directed, since FITT at least, to keeping us out of Continental complication. Is Lord ROBERTS quite the man—we are not questioning any of his great qualities as a soldier—to lead us into the adoption of a national policy based on the supposition that we are no longer surrounded by" the inviolate sea."
Seeing that a party THE MUNICIPAL political fight had to be, ELECTIONS. the Liberals have full

cause for rejoicing at yesterday's results of the municipal polling. Great victories have been secured, with the gain of a seat in St. John's and Whitecross Ward. In the one Mr. J. Shaw has at last turned the tables on Councillor Steel, and in the other, the popular chairman of the Liberal Party has secured a notable personal triumph, as well as bringing back 'Whitecross to its old allegiance. Against these great successes there is only one loss to deplore, and that is in Fairfield ward where Mr. Jarman made a plucky fight in a short time. The results in Orford, St. Austin's, and Bewsey all present encouraging features for Progressives, and there is reason to congratulate Mr. Wynne Jones on having halved the big majority of Councillor Wilson in Latchford. Tory domination in the town has received an unmistakeable set-back.
The Criminal Law THE WHITE Amendment Bill made
SLAVE BILL. good progress in the

House- o-f Commons yesterday. Mr. McKenna, on behalf of the Government, accepted an amendment to the debatable Clause 1, which will give the police as a whole power to make the arrest of a suspected person, and the amendment was agreed to. Mr. F. Handel Booth, M.P., pur- sued his opposition to the bitter end, but his amendment to omit clause 1 from the Bill did not even find a seconder. This is an indication how much public opinion has advanced of late—in the House and out of it—in favour of the Bill being made both stringent and effective. The prospects are increasingly bright for this belated measure of protection for the girl-life of the country, and the highest hopes may now be entertained of its reaching the Statute Book without further mutilation. It is pleasant to think that 11 Warrington had some small share in this great moral forward movement.
There is still a good SANATORIUM deal of confusion in the BENEFIT. minds of the public as

to the exact nature of "Sanatorium Benefit" under the Insurance Act. Light will be thrown on some of its more important aspects at the Conference which is about to take place under the auspice S of the Warrington Guild of Help. The public bodies specially concerned have been invited to confer with Guild workers. The subject is to be opened up by Mrs. Haslam, of Bolton, who has been untiring in her public service,indeed she comes of a family held in high honour for their civic leadership. Both her father and her brother have in their time occupied the post of chief magistrate in Bolton. Mrs. Haslam has only recently given up her seat on the Board of Guardians. In the Guild of Help she is one of the District Heads. She has made a special study of the administrative side of dealing with consumption and in the early summer gave an admirable paper on the subject at the Guild of Help Annual Conference at Croydon.

There has been a grow- " GENTLEMANLY " ing tendency amongst RUDENESS. the "Gentlemanly Party" to think that they have a perfect right to waive all the courtesies and decencies in their attitude to the Government. Mr Bonar Law has told a gathering of Tory Nonconformists that the present Government is only comparable to Robespierre's Reign of Terror. Courage under the existing" Reign of Terror," many mem- bers of the Opposition seem to think, can only be shown by rudeness. Of course, Mr Bonar Law's reference to the French Revolu- tion is only a poor joke on the "guillotine" a closure by compartments to which the Tory Party has not the slightest objection when in power, and the necessity for which can only be removed, not by revolution, but by devolution. But the Speaker has made the "Gentlemanly Party" realise that rudeness is not a form of humour which the House of Commons can tolerate. On one and the same day, Sir C Kinloch-Cook was reminded from the Chair that he could not expect a reply from the Government if his question was so " uncivil," and Mr Pretyman, a Tory ex- Minister, was told that when he taxed Mr Lloyd George with 'falsehood," he at once put himself out of court.

Councillor William BOOTS AND SHOES. Evans, J.P., the Presi- -AN INTERESTING dent of the Newport COMPARISON. (Mon.) Boot Trades Association, who has just returned from his third visit to the United States, gives, in the " Shoe and Leather Record " for October 18th, some impressions of the American boot and shoe industry.—Councillor Evans says :—" I have no desire to say anything on Free Trade and Protection, but still it is h remarkable fact that the American public have to pay through the nose as a result of their tariffs. I will give this as one instance. I was in Wanamaker's store in New York, and saw some shoes marked "reduced from ten dollars to six during sale." It was a well-known English-branded line made in Northampton. I am selling the very same article in my shops to-day at 215.; but they told me at Wanamaker's that their usual price for them was £2, and that they had no difficulty in getting the price. The further inland you get, the higher the prices. I purchased a cheap pair of boots at a sale, and paid 12s. 6d. for them. I have sold thousands of similar pairs in Newport for 10s. 6d. I naturally made enquires as to the higher prices, and learnt that Americans had to pay duty on all boots imported, as well as higher rent, rates, taxes, &c. I made exten- sive enquiries about the tariff question, awl gathered that while the average American was in favour of a low tariff, the general opinion was that the present tariffs were far too high, and were burden- some. It suited the big monopolies, but not the rank and file of the people." ,In an editorial comment on Councillor ' Evans's report, the "Shoe and Leather Record" says, "When an American boot manufacturer visits this country he finds , nothing so startling as the prices at which boots are marked in our retail shops. The boot generally sold to the public in this country at half-a-guinea is, he admits, fully as good as the American shoe retailed at a dollar more money." The figures relating to our foreign trade in boots apd shoes are instructive. Since 1903 (the beginning of the Tariff Reform agitation) our imports of leather boots and shoes have fallen from £881,066 to X 627,248 in 1911. Our exports in the same period increased from £1,845,380 to £3,354,691. Evidently boots and shoes must be included in the list of" going "industries.

div.p: Captain Crosfield's suggestion that there should be bowling facilities for children as Well as adults is worth more than passing note. The game is healthful, stimulating and inexpensive and there is no earthly reason why it should be confined to adults. The provision of the necessary accommoda- tion for young bowlers might tax the resources of our municipalities, but they could hardly engage in a better enterprise. They would be creating healthier open spaces—as well as recreative opportunity all the time !

We are glad to see that Col. Bromley Davenport has protested against the disparaging references to the Territorial Force made by Lord Roberts in his Man- chester speech. His Lordship had the temerity to say that "the Territorial Force Was now an acknowledged failure." Col. 'Bromley Davenport, who is a more reliable authority on the Territorials than Lord Roberts, says that the force has achieved "a ' remarkable success," and deplores the con- spiracy of National Service Leaguers to ' belittle the force and so bring about 'compulsory service. This feature of the propaganda is becoming increasingly apparent, and calls into question that very patriotism the League claims such a monopoly of.

A new and horrible advertising dodge Comes from Germany (says the" Manchester Guardian.") Some of the larger and more Prosperous dealers in various classes of goods send out one of their delivery carts at the busiest time of the day, with directions to the driver to remain outside the shop of a small dealer in the same kind of goods for an . .

our or two. Thus, a cart emblazoned with the name and trade of Herr Meyer, the big dealer in boots, is stationed outside the boot shop of the more modest Herr Schmidt. Naturally the passers-by who notice the phenomenon jump to the conclusion that Schmidt gets the boots he sells from Meyer; they sagely resolve to go to the fountain- head and not to let a middleman swindle Them out of extra pfennigs. But if Herr Schmidt is a man and not a worm there will soon be "wigs on the green." * *

- Mr. G. K. Fortescu*e, Keeper of Printed tooks at the British Museum, whose death is reported this week, was not unnaturally Proud of the great institution with which he had been so long and honourably associated. It is," he declared, "one of the most interesting and one of th, most cosmopolitan rooms to be found in the world. It now has a daily average of over 700 readers, of every nation, east and west, all of whom are work- ing at one literary pursuit or another— Writing books, correcting proofs, or collect- ing information for other people. One can hardly name an author of any great distinc- tion throughout Europe who at one time or another has not used the reading-room. It is full of memories of such .writers as Lord IVlacauley, Mr. Lecky, Mr. Samuel Rawson Gardiner, and a hundred others of equal fame and ncte during the last century."

The first entertainment of the season was given on llonday last consisting of songs and recitations by the rnembers of the above Band of Hope, assisted by the friends from Friars Green who gave a dialogue entitled "The Pawnbroker." Recitations were given bY Misses Amy and Doris Littlewood, which were received with loud apnlaune. and Mr E Littlewood gave a short address. The chair was occupied by Mr J tirmston. After a grand evening's entertainment a vote of thanks was passed to the friend 4 from Friars green. Mr E Littlewood, Misses Amy Littlewood and Doris Littlewood, which was heartily carried. The meeting concluded by singing the Doxology. 'The White Slave Traffic. The Arrangements Committee for the Town' lieeting on the White Slave Traffic (petition met a the Town Hall on Tuesday morning. The Rev G C triggs was voted to the chair and the secretary's Import was submitted by Rev W Cooper. From every Point of view the meeting was reported to have been a Success. The attendance name up to expectations, the tpeakers had dealt with their subjects with consum- Mate skill and good taste, and the results were sure 10 be of a far-reaching character. A statement of the finances was presented which shewed that the income was sufficient to meet the expenditure. The committee Warmly thanked the secretary for the services he had sO willingly rendered. After a discussion as to Whether the committee should be dissolved, it was decided that it would be preferable to remain as at Present. Warrington Shakespeare Society. , A meeting was held at the old Academy on Thurs- day, October 24th, at which a paper on "A Winter's Tale " was read by the Rev. LJ T Darwall. Mr. tarwall said the play was derived from a novel by It. Greene which was very popular. Shakespeare 4ept closely to the incidents of the first part, but introduced additional characters e.g. Autolycus. The Play belongs to the fourth period and reflects the Peacefulness of Shakespeare's later life, in contrast to to the sterner plays of the previous period. The key- !lute of the final scene is reconciliation. The inform- power in the play is the character of Flermione. he jealousy of Leontes is most unreasonable and 140 es not arouse the sympathy of the audience. There a double plot but a harmony of interest. Perdita subordinate to Elermione, but the p.ictive is perfect, the rural life of the second part Is i te finest in ")hakespeare ; no doubt it reflects the lie about his own estate in Warwickshire. A second paper was ''ead by Mr Landon, who commented on some of the views expre.sed in the previous paper and discussed laPecially the character of Paulina. A discussion °flowed thh in which Mr Dalby and Mr Perris took part. T e proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to readers of tile papers. Warrington Philomathic Society. The first ordinary meeting of this society for the current season was held at the Old Academy,when 'the President (Mr James Ball) read a paper on 4‘ Labour Unrest: Cause and Remedy," to a good "vttendance of members. Mr Ball referred to the atriuus disputes which had been so marked a feature 1911 and 1912 and considered that the causes were _Pious, viz. :—Distrust of spirit in which governing saes administered, the signs of surplus wealth as ii'vtdenced by the spectacle of pleasure referred to by G Wells, the practical stationariness in wages, Jo the fall in real wages owing to increased "t of a% livin Mr Ball took the years 1000 to 1910 a 1:"4. general basis and showed that during this period of living had increased about 15 per cent, and tat wages had remained stationary. At the same :6 the total national wealth had increased °lltiously as evidenced by Income Tax returns, t 55th duties, Sm. A minimum standard of life had aZbe conceded to all workers and a wage in accord- With such standard had to be the first charge on heY industry. Mr Ball pleaded for a better spirit to Orrn by the governing classes and in the mean- !s compulsory arbritation and wage boards should instituted, based on our Colonial experience in these. 11,Pects• An interesting discussion ensued in which tv„sPrB W B Ferahaw, A H Rathbone, N Nield, J "tBh, Dr Mellor and T E Knowles took part.

illar—rin—gien- Ragged School. "The condition and needs of poor children, with applied remedies" was the subject of a limelight lecture given at the Warrington Ragged School and Mission, Bank-street, on Monday evening, by Mr John P Barrow (organising secretary of the National Federation of Christian workers among poor children.) Mrs Dodds (president of the mission), presided over a large attendance and said she was pleased to do all she could for the benefit of the poor children. Their teachers were engaged in a good work and in that she gave them every encouragement. The lecture was a very instructive one and the pictures from London Manchester and Liverpool showing the conditions of the children there, gave an added interest to the subject. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mrs Dodds, the Lecturer and Mr Frank Owen for manipulating the lantern.

Sir Edward Carson Coming to Warrington. A meeting of the Executive Council of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Conservative Working Men's Federation was held on Saturday at the Manchester Conservative Club. Alderman -A Bennett (Warring- ton) presided.—The Secretary (Mr F W Deacon) announced that, since their last meeting, in accordance with their revolution to hold a great demonstration against Home -Rule at Warrington, Sir Edward Carson, KC , M.P., had been communicated with, and had consented to address the same on Saturday, November 30th, 191.2, The gathering would be held under the auspices of the Lancashire and Cheshire Conservative Working Men's Federation. Already the following gentlemen had signified their intention to be present : Mr Harold Smith, M.P.' Lord Minlmer, M P., Mr E G Craig, M.P., Col. John Rutherford' M.P., Mr .Righy Swift, MP., Hr Gershon 8 ewart, M.P., Mr Biglaud, M.P., and Colonel Alan Sykes, M.P. . _

St. Clement's Men's Club. The annual general meeting of the above was held in the club room on Thursday. Mr H C Rhoden (vice- president) presided in the absence of the president, Rev T Vickers, who was away on a missionary engagement. A very fair amount of business was done and ended very satisfactorily. The treasurer, Mr C Gandy, presented the balance sheet and was highly commended for the satisfactory result. The officers for the ensuing yesr were elected : President, Rev T Vickers ; vice-president, Ii C Rhoden ; secretary, II Broadhurst ; treasurer, C Gaudy; auditor, J Aikenhead • committee, Messrs Houghton, A Berry, J Macdonald, W Guest, It Slevin, A Beswick and W Warburton. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the officers for the past year for services rendered. The Chairman gave a kind welcome to all male mem- bers of Clement's Mission who have attained the age of 21 to join as soon as pos•ible. During the evening the Chairman presented Mr H Broadhurst with a cue and case on behalf of the members for services rendered as secretary for four years. A vote ( f thanks to the Chairman for presiding concluded a very pleasant meeting.
