At the anniversary dinner of the Loyal Viaduct " Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Man- chester Unity) held at the Wellington Hotel. Earles- town, on Saturday. P.P.G.M. I'. n. Steel,of Warrington, was presented with a solid silver Cigar case.— P.P.G.M. Thomas Tunstall, the oldest member of the lodge, in making the presentation, said the members, of whom there were over 000, desired in a small way to show their appreciation of many kindnesses Coun- cillor Steel had shown to them and to working men generally. He had attended their annual dinner for the past ten years, and had taken a real interest in the welfare of the lodge. Councillor Steel, some few years ago, presented them with a silver cup fcr annual competition in bowling which had been the means of bringing the members together each sear for a game of bowls, and had thus helped to create a good and friendly feeling in the lodge. (Applause.) The case which had been artistically chased bore the following inscription : " 1.0.0. F., MU. Presented by the members of the 'Viaduct' Lcdge to P.P.G.M. T. S. Steel. October, 1912."

Presentation to Alderman John Evans. On Twesday afternoon Alderman John Evans was the recipient of a handsome silver rose bowl in recog- nition of his twenty-one years' work as president of the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers' Association, and Mrs Evans was presented with a gold bangle watch. Alderman John Evans is the olderA licensed victualler in Warrington, and has been a member of the association for about forty years. He became licensee of the Bull's Head Hotel in 1811, and he and his family have lived in the house for four generations. Mr Joseph Shillcock, vice-president, made the presentations, and speeches of appreciation were also made by Mr R Shacklady (bon treasurer), Mr E Lockett (secretary), Mr G Finah and Mr J W Plinston. Mr Lockett said Alderman Evans had served his native town faithfully and well, and yet, because he was connected with a particular calling, he was debarred from receiving those honours to which he was justly and rightly entitled. It was a standing disgrace to those in authority that they refrained from adding the name of Mr Evans to the magisterial list. When a Royal Commission sat on the question of the election of justices of the peace one of the cases men- tioned as an illustration o- public services rendered, but not properly recognized, was that of their Presi- dent. He trusted that before long that state of things would be remedied. (Applause.) Alderman Evans briefly returned thanks. _ .

The Warrington Field Club. The first meeting of the winter session was held in the Museum Lecture Room on Saturday -last. Mr A J Jolley, J P., presided, and there we+ a fair attendance of members. This being the usual Emomological evening, the exhibits and records from the various researchers were chiefly of an E atom dogical character. Messrs W Muunfield, Womersley, and Dunlop exhibited numerous interasting specimens of local lepidoptera. Messrs Greening, A J Jolley, C Madeley and others then entered into a discussion of the records, during which Mr Greening reported the finding of a gannet on Helsby Marsh, a black-tailed gooclwit on the shore at Hale, and a piir of kingfishers at the Latchford tram terminus. Mr H Wolrnersley then read" Short notes on the scent scales of butterflies." He described and illustrated the peculiar plumed scent scales by drawings and microscopical slides. That they are evidently intended for some special pur- pose was apparent, and the lecturer contended that the fact that these scales are only to be found on the top side of the wings of the miles was evidence far toe conclusion that their use was of a special character. He concluded by describing the specific scale from the Pierene butterflies, a discussion then followed, Messrs. Greening, Madeley and others tiking part.
FOR MODERN FIREPLACES and Cooking Ranges com- bining economy with simplicity try .1. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge at.. Warrington.—Advt. A Warringtonlan's Death in Canada. -

Many Warringtonian's will regret tq hear of the death which has occurred in Canada of Mr. Thomas Knox, eldest son of Mr and Mrs Thomas Knox, of 12, Beresford-street, Manchester-road, Warrington. Mr Knox, who was 34 years of age, left Warrington for Toronto, Canada, in June 1911. News was received by cablegram that on October 25th he was killed instantaneously by electricity. The funeral took place at Toronto on October 28th, the chief mourner being his brother Mr Edwin Knox (late with Mr g Mounfield). Mr Knox has had a varied and adventurous career. He served ten years in the Royal Navy: seven of which be spent in China. The first commission there was for a period of four ' and a half years. AA the elaip H.M.S. Edgar was returning to England it encountered a I dreadful gale in the Bay of Biscay and lost two of her funnels. Great difficulty was experienced in reaching England and tugs were sent to her assistance from Plymouth. After Mr. Knox had been in England a year he was again drafted to China, and took part in the war between England and the Chinese Boxers in 1900. He was with the party which captured Pekin and received the war modal fcr his services. In 1902, I while serving on H.M.S. Woodlark in the Yang-tee River, China, a seaman fell overboard, Mr Knox, though conscious of the grave personal danger occasioned by the treacherous rapids, plunged overboard in full uniform and succeeded in saving the man's life. For this gallant act he received the Royal Humane Society's c niificate and was highly commended by the captain and officers of his ship. Shortly after his return to England he purchased his discharge from the Navy, but remained until he left England in the Royal Naval Reserve. He came to live in his native town and was for eight years foreman of Messrs Richard Evans and Company's coal-yard, earning the esteem mid respect of all who knew him.

For twenty-one years she was closely associated with Holy Trinity Church and since taking up her residence at Latchford she had also interested herself in the work at Christ Church. During her husband's Mayoralty she was of invaluable assistance to him in the dis- charge of the citifies of that high office, and the grace and tact with which she officiated at civic and social functions called forth many expressions of apprecia- tion. Much sympathy has been expressed with Alderman Forshaw and family (one son and two daughters) in their bereavement. The funeral will take place in the Hill Cliffe grave- yard this (Saturday) afternoon. The cortege will leave Ivy Mount at 1.30 and a service will be held in Holy Trinity Church at 2 o'clock.

div.p: DEATH OF MRS. FORSHAW. An Ex-Mayoress.

It is with deep regret that we announce the death of Mrs. Forshaw, skife of Alderman W. J. Forshaw, Ivy Mount, Litchford, who passed away on Wednes- day, alter five months' illness. Mrs. Forshaw, who was the Mayoress of Warrington in the years 1909 and 1910, had gained a high plare in the estimation of the tow m4peopie generally and enjoyed the affection- ate regard of tho,e who knew her intimately. She was the daughter of the late Mr William Barlow, an old Warringtonian, and was married to Alderman Forshaw over hirty-one years ago. It may truthfully be said of her that she never tired of good works and her services were alwat..s ungrudgiogly given to charitable and religious institutions, including Intl: mary, the Children's Camp, the Old Folk's Treat, and Fart ry-yard Mission. div.head: LEVERSON CASE ACCUSED DISCHARGED.
div.p: THE LEVERSON CASE ACCUSED DISCHARGED.

The final stages in the proceedings consequent upon the alleged victimisation of local tradesmen was reached on Wednesday when, at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions Julia Leverson (61) described as a dress- maker, was charged on three counts with stealing a quantity of goods the property of Messrs W Hodgkin- son, Limited, Warrington. Mr W Scott Barrett presided over a full bench justices and after a lengthy hearing the prisoner was found "not guilty." Mr Madden (instructed by Mr A Browne Warring- ton) prosecuted, and the prisoner was defended by Mr E C Burgis (instructed by Mr T S Steel, War- rington). It appeared that the prisoner first made her appear- ance in Warrington in April last. She became acquainted with Messrs Hodgkinson through an advertisement for a dressmaker. Sits was not engaged, and subsequently she asked Mr A Hodgkin - son if she might open an account with the firm. References were asked for, and in reply prisoner said she had a nephew who 50.8 a solicitor at Winchester House, London, where twenty-three clerks were employed; that she was the aunt of the famous actress, Miss Julia Neilson ; and that she was a relative and a great friend of the late Sir George Lewis.

Mr. Hodgkinson at first declined to open an account and the prisoner commenced an establishment in Museum-street, Warrington. She then began to trade with Messrs. liodgkinson, spending between £lOO and £l5O on goods. Counsel suggested that this was done solely for the purpose of gaining credit and confidence. She applied for goods, and these were supplied on approval. The understanding was that if the goods were not approved the prisoner should return them, and if accepted she was immediately to pay over the cash. She was supplied with a number of articles, and almost immediately afterwards she sold them to different people for considerably less than their value. The amount of the goods so disposed of was between .-F,36 and £lO. Witnesses were called to prove having purchased goods from the defendant. • For the defence, Mr Burgis contended that there had been no evidence of larceny. The testimony was that the goods were sold on approval, and invoices to that effect were given. The goods, he submitted, were voluntarily parted with, so as to enable the prisoner to dispose of them if she could. She might have obtained the property—though counsel did not for a moment admit it—by fraud, but having obtained the goods there could be no such thing as larceny in the case. If there was no taking of the property without the prosecutor's consent there could be no -theft. He contended that there was no case to go to the jury. The magist rates retired to consider the legal point raised, and on returning into Court, the Chairm an said : " After very careful consideration the magls- trates have decided that there is no case to be submitted to the jury." 1 The ~jury thereupon returned a verdict of " Not guilty,

div.p: DEATH OF MISS FRANCES CORM.

-- Many of our readers will deeply regret to hear of the death of Miss Frances Jean Corney, second daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Corney, Craig Gowan, Lower Walton, trho passed away on Tuesday. Miss Corney, who was in her twenty-fourth year, was trained for the teaching profession at Warrington Training College, and was appointed a mistress at the Thewlis-street Infants' echool in August, 1910. She discharged her duties with a diligence and sympathy whio commended itself to the authorities and endeared her to the children. Owing to the failure of her health, Miss Corney was compelled last November to relinquish the work to which she was so much devoted, and since then she had gradually declined. Like her parents she was do-ely attached to Wycliffe Congregational Church. Her father is the respected headmaster of Wycliffe day schools.—The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery yesterday afternoon. A short service was conducted at Craig Gowan by Rev. John Yonge who also oMciatel at the graveside. Canon Morlt y Stevenson (principal of the Warrington Training College) pronounctd the Benediction. The mourners included : V Alfred Corney (father), Mr Arthur Corney (brother), Miss Ferriman (superin- tendent of the Training College), Misses Porritt, , Mrs P T Winskill, Mrs J W Jeffrey ; Messrs William Besaick, Edward Wallington and E S Garland (representing the deacons of Wycliffe C mgregational Church), Mr E S A Robson (principal of the Secondary school), Mr Edward Watlington ('mailmaster of Aryl/Iv-street schools), Mr 8 W Jeffery (senior assistant master at Wycliffe school), Messrs J W Bouchier, J W Scott, George Wallington, T F Wallington, P. Crampton and NV T Eccles. Floral tributes were received from the following : " Father, mother, sister and brothers," Mr and Mrs Martin and family, Mr and Mrs Edgley and family, " Aunts and uncle at Bury," " Teachers at Thewlis- street school," Mr and Mrs Edward Wallintzton and family, Mrs Gray and Mr J W Scott, Mr and Mrs England and family, Mr and Mrs Bouchier and family, Mr and Mrs Armitage, Mr and Mrs Garland, Mr and Mrs Winskill, Mr and Mrs Robson, Mr and Mrs S Nv Jeffrey, Mr and Mrs H Haviour, Mrs Thomas and Gwen, Mrs and the Misses Porritt, " Mabel and Percy Crampton," "Annie, Dora aid Kitty," " Annie and Elsie,"" Nellie." div.head: , WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: , WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
Annual Sale of Work.

The church workers in the parish of St. Elphin are making a great effort by their annual sale of work, held this week in the Fair field Schools, to raise funds far the buildiug of a new vestry and to support many of the organizations connected with the church, including Church Institute, St. Clement's Mission and St. Gen-ge's Mission. Tlaursdayg's opening ceremony was performed by the Hon. Mrs. Harburd (grand- daughter of the late Lord Winmarleigh) who was accompanied by her husband Colonel Harbord. The Rector (Canon Willis) presided and amongst those present were tbe Revs A J Bratt, J M Buckmaster, E E Carleton, J H Garnett, Messrs J E Seeker and H Beresford Melville. Stalls, tastefully arranged and heavily laden, were in charge of the following ladies : Rectory Working Party : Mesdames Craik,Bottomley, Scott, Knott, Bill, Lees, Antwiss, flampsun and Miss Lee.
Mrs Willis Stall : MesdArnes Willis and Fowler and Mis 3 Shaw.
Institute Stall : Mrs S Taylor, Miss Dykes, and ladies ot the Institute. Sr Clement's Stall : Mesdames Hall, Houghton, Sanders, Grey, Blease, Has and Boater.

St GeOrgec Mission Stall : Mesdames Harbourne, Barnett, Buckler Misses Sumner and Bowles. Refreshment Buckler, : The Misses E White, M Brookes, D and M Harding, A Isherwood, and A Taylor. Flower Stall : Mrs Hopkins, Misses Lees, Gorst,and Lucy Isherwood. Girls' Friendly Society : Mrs Atkin, the M White, Mesdames Collin, Locker and Lunt. The RECTOR. in explaining the objects of the sale, stid for some time past they had been attempting to en targe the vestry on the south side of the chancel, which was very small and very inadequate for its pur- poses. At the beginning of August Mr. Isbervvood, the people's warden, came forward with the suggestion that it would be better for them if they built on entirely new vestry. The idea commended it•elf to him as it would leave the small vestry on the other side free for the use of the clergy. The enlargement would give th‘m a much larger room on the north side, with direct access from the main entrance to the churchyard. The matter was brought before the officers of the church who were unanimous in its favour. Owing to various el rcu nistancesthe scheme had been delayed and they were unable to proceed until last Tuesday, when the tenders were received, and the work which was to begin imme- diately was given to Mr. Robert Collin, one of their own officers. The old faculty granted to carry out an alteration would not be of any use;they feared it would be necessary to obtain a new one as the work could not be o unmenced without the faculty. The next court would De held on the 20th November when the application would he considered. They had obtained permission to commence the work on the understanding that the old fabric was not to be disturbed until the new faculty was granted. In conclusion the Rector said that during the 25 years he had been in charge of the parish the sum of £20,000 had been given to various Objects in the parish and he wished to thank all donors for their generosity and liberality. In additions to that sum, sites to the value of £5,000 had been given to them by Sir Gilbert Greenall and Colonel Robert Ireland B ackburne and he desired to express his deep indebtedness to those gentlemen for their kindness. Mrs Eimteonn, in epening the sale, expressed pleasure at receiving a kind invitation to come to Warrington and help them forward in their efforts. Alcmg with her husband, she had long wished to visit Warrington and that invitation came most opportunely: She did not think she had ever lived in Warrington but she had heard a grett deal about the town from her grandfather. In a large parish like theirs, there were always increasing needs and she , expressed the hope that the profits of the sale would 'alas show an increase. (Applaube). I On the proposition of the Rev A J BRATT (senior curate) seconded by Mr R T HARDING, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs Harbord. Celonel HARBORD, on behalf of, his wife, returned thanks and said he could fully corroborate what his wife had said about their wish to visit Warrington. He appreciated their welcome and he asked them to accept his sincere thanks. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. Yesterday's opening ceremony was performed by Mrs Lyon, of Appleton Hall, in the absence of the , Hon. Mrs. Willis. There was a fair attendance and the 'Rector announced that the sum received on the previous day was £l2O and that included a cheque from Lady Greenall for £25. (Applause.) He was sorry Mrs Willis, his neice, was unable to be with- them. (Hear, hear.) She had been hoping most earnestly to be present,but she had sent him a telegram stating that her grand,uother was dead and that she would be at the funeral on Friday, and so would be unable to fulfil her enagement at t'..e sale. She bad sent a cheque for £lO. (Applause.) Mrs Lyon had con- sented to perform the opening ceremony and he was sure no one could be more accept- able in /llrs Willis's place. In conclusion, the Rector dealt with another object of the sale. the extension of St Clement's Mission. They bad two flourishing missions, St George's Mission had been built for .£2,000 and in 1897 St Clements was built (or a similar amount. Another mission would be necessary before very long an excellent site having been given by Colonel Ireland Blacliburne. He had given them 10 years in which to turn round and two years had now past. When the alterations were made to the Church they would start on the building of the new mission. Mrs LvoN dealt with the excellent and noble objects for which that sale was held annually. She thought that no doubt in some way one would be glad if the necessary funds could be raised without such hard work as was occasioned by sales of work. On the other hand however she thought they would miss the cherry gatheringswhich they enjoyed in the preparation of the goods they offered for sale. She would very much like to press home, that seeing that the church assisted the souls of adults and children it was unwise to starve her. (Applause). Mr EDWARD ISHERWOOD (people's warden) proposed S vote of thanks to the opener and said Mrs Lyon was a lady, well known 'and highly esteemed by all of them. Having emphasised the need for a large amount of money to defray the cost of the vestry, he said in con- clusion that it did not often occur that parishioners were asked to contribute to An addition to a church like the Parish Church, arid be was sure all of them would do their utmost to assist in that noble work. (Applause). Mr SAMUEL TAYL3R seconded and said they would there might raise £3OO through the sale. Although Mrs Lyon and her husband were not in the district, whatever h might be that required support, they were the Pe9Ple,to give it. (Hear, bear). The resolution was heartily carried. The proceeds up to last night amounted to £2OO. •

div.head: MR. J. P. JOHNSON'S GREAT WARRINGTON CONGER f.
div.p: MR. J. P. JOHNSON'S GREAT WARRINGTON CONGER f.
A Rare Musical Treat.

- - - --- A remarkable concert party has been booked to appear at Warrington. Miss Alys Bateman, the most popular and gifted of English sopranos, is bringing Mr. Stuart Edwards to Parr Hall, Warrington, on November 14th. Mr. Stuart Edwards is a baritone of extraordinary culture, and possesses a splendidly strong and rich voice,which he uses with intense dramatic feeling. He will sing "Non pin Andrei," one of Mozart's most exquisite arias, and" All mine alone." Mr. Harold Wilde is hardly less widely know as England's gifted tenor, whose sweet and ringing voice is of wonderful range and perfect intonation. His song "I hear you calling me" produces a thrilling effect with its resonant call. His audience can rely on a rich treat. Miss Alys Bateman promises the lovely Bach-Gounod Ave Maria, with the violin obligate, her rendering of which is pronounced by well known critics to be superior to every other, and in which she certainly has no living rival. She will also sing the great" Aria " and duet, the " Miserere " from " II Trovatore " with Harold Wilde, which creates an immense impression and enthusiasm and is alone worth coming 20 miles to hear. The instrumentalists are no less famous, including the most famous violinist. Johannes Wolff, and the ever welcome, brilliant Parlovitz, who is so frequently com- pared with Paderewski, and has won laurels the world over. Miss Gertrude Wood, of Chester, will also take part and recite some of her popular pieces.' Last, but not least, the inimitably clpver Nellie Ganthony, whose sketches at the piano are delightfully witty and refined will complete this really wonderful galaxy of talent brought to Warrington by the famous entrepreneur Mr 3. P. Johnson, of Kendal. Mr. R. H. Pearson, of Warrington, has charge of the local arrangements and a great success is predicted at the Parr Hall, on Thursday, November 14th.

div.head: "NINEPENCE FOR FOURPENCE"
div.p: "NINEPENCE FOR FOURPENCE"

Mr. P. M. Oliver and the Material View of Polities. Mr P M Oliver was the lecturer on Sunday afternoon at the New Islington Hall, Ancoats. His subjeot was "Ninepence for fourpence, the modern tendency in politics." Mr Oliver found the first example of this tendency in the Insurance Act, which, itself a measure enshrin- ing the principles of co-operation and belf-sacrifice. was suffering from poor advooacy. The advocacy, which was merely an arithmetical calculation of benefits to be received by the individual, against his own 1 particular expenditure, was spoiling the ideal which lay behind the Act. Tariff " Reform " was another example. Beginning by being the material form of an Imperial ideal, it was becoming an argument about 'more work and higher wages," and in that form its essential ideal was undermined. Socialism, too, which deomuded a clean break with present civilisation, was particularising into a concern about drains and wages. The cause of this tendency, he took to be the pressure upon politicians of a population which was mainly occupied with the fact of poverty. That tendency I would go on but it was very desirable that it should be influenced by a realisation of ultimate ideals in all , classes of society.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND CONSCRIPTION.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND CONSCRIPTION.

Sir,— I have read the letter in your issue of Satur- day last under the beading "Mr. Crosfield and Con- scription " with much concern, on account of the attempt made to bring the question of national defence into the arena of party politics. This is sad indeed. The National Service League is not a party organisa- tion. It is inspired by our greatest soldier Lord Roberts, and contains in its ranks men and women of all shades of political opinion. Here in Warrington some of the keenest workers of tbe League are ardent Radicals while others are the bluest of Tories. Surely the question of the Army and Navy ought to be approached from a better spirit than that of one party trying to get a paltry advimage of another within the same nation.

The proper spirit I should ssy would be,—what is the best way of making or National position abso- lutely secure, in fact so secure that any attack on us in the present < r somewhat distant future, would so obviously be a failure that no nation would try it, and we should thereby maintain the peace which is so necessary for our prosperity. I pity a nation which leaves preparation for war till six months after war has broken out.— Ycurs F. AYLMER FROST. Orappenhall Hall, near Warrington. October 29th, 1912.

div.head: "CHURCHMEN AND CHRISTIANS GENERALLY."
div.p: "CHURCHMEN AND CHRISTIANS GENERALLY."

Sir.—On two occasions comment has been made in your columns on the above phrase; your critic affect- ing to find it ambiguous and implying a severance in meaning between "churchmen" and "Christians." I submit that the phrase is quite clear, and is not ambiguous; and further that it not only does not imply the suggested severance, but on the contrary it actually links the specific and the general together as one body. The expression is the same as "Churchmen and Christians in general." Would the phras‘ " Editors and journalists generally" be ambiguous and imply that Editors are not journalists? Your contributor has overlooked the word "generally."—Yours truly, _
H. J. WESTBROOK. Stockton Heath, 18th October, 191 t).

'While apologising to Mr Westbrook for the delay in publishing his letter, we hasten to add that we did nct overlook the word " generally.' Our suggestion, made quite jocularly, was that the phrase in question seemed to imply that." Church- men" were a superior kind of Christian. Mr Westbrook's conjunction of " Editors and journalists generally " emphasises our little point. Editors are a superior kind of journalist !—En. Ex.

div.head: AN OLD JOURNALIST AND WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
div.p: AN OLD JOURNALIST AND WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.

Sir, —Old Journalist is airing his Anti-Suffrage opinion again. Women are not revolutionising Town Councils by coming forward as candidates. Therefore they don't want to vote. The Anti-Suffrage position seems be (I am open to corre(tion) : Women have not time to vote ; it would take them away from the home, once in five years. They ought to have time to be Councillors. Well, so be it. But, I should like to ask Old Journalist two questions. 1. Does he know that married women (outside London) are not eligible as Town Councillors ? Can he tell me how many Town Councillors would be left, in _Warringtou if married men were excluded?
2. If, a; he suggests, women will not use the vote when they have it, why deny it them? You don't forbid chickens to swim.
We have heard much lately in Warrington about the White Slave Traffic. The following facts may give Old Journalist food for reflection :

In every state in America where woman vote, except Califoinia, where it has only lately been granted; in every state of Australia, except one; in New Zealand and every other place where women have the vote, the age of protection for girls has been raised to 18 at least. In Wyoming where women have voted longest it has been raised to 21. We heard last week in Warrington that the pro- moters of our White Slave Traffic Bill were warned that the Bill would not have a chance to go through Parliament if there were a clause inserted to raise the age of protection to 18 in England. Women are the natural guardians of the race. Till they vote,the interests of posterity are not likely to be properly safe-guarded. The protection of women means the protection of the future race. No question is so distinctly Imperial.—Yours &c. L. F. WARING. County Hotel, Pontypridd. October 30th 1912.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S C.L B. Annual Inspection.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S C.L B. Annual Inspection.

At the Drill Hall on Thursday evening, the thii cr annual inspection of the above Company took place in the pfesence of a large gathering. Colonel Appleton accompanied by Captain Cotton, was the inspecting officer. The signalling, amtulance, bugling and gymnastic displays were very smartly executed and reflected great credit upon each individual section. In the course of a few remarks Colonel Al'eLETt»i said he was pleased with all that he had seen, and congratulated the officers on the increase of the strength of the company without any decrease in efficiency. He also took the opportunity of presenting to the Company the Battalion challenge shield, given by the Hon. Colonel of the Battalirn (Colonel Buckton), which was awarded on a triple contest, viz., running, swimming and general efficiency. Captain Corrox next spoke on the importance of being able to use a rifle. He said they were not desirous of shooting, but some day they might be com- pelled to, and the better their shooting the sooner the dirty work would be done. The Rev W BRACEBAMP heartily thanked the officers and members and also the audience lot their interest in and sympathy with the movement. Captain Con'ox distributed the prizes and certifi- cates as follows :—The "John Gore Ashton Cup" given for efficiency, Colour-Sergeant Woodbridge; first class bars, Privates Ashton and Appleton; first class medals, Lance-Corporal Geary, Buglers J Gibson and Beacham and Privates Holloway and Dobson; second c'ass bar, Bugler Unsworth ; second class medals, Privates Sutcliffe and Palin ; good conduct stripe, Private Spencer; cyclist badges, Sergeant Pinsen, Privates Ashton and Appleton; ambulance certificates, second class, Lance-Corporal Geary, first class, Sergeant Gee, Corporal Renshaw, Privates Dobson, Holloway, Sutzliffe, Shaw and Spencer.

Alleged Shortage of Magistrates. In the House of Common 3, on Tuesday, Viscount Wolmer asked the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lan- caster whether his attention had been called to the shortage of magistrates at Warrington County Division Petty Sessions, and whether it was intended 1 to appoint any more magistrates for that Bench in the 'near future. Mr Hobhouse, in a printed reply, says: There are 23 magistrates for the County Palatine of Lancaster upon the rota for 'Warrington Petty Sessional Division. Appointments to the County Bench are usually made on the nomination of the Lord- Lieutenant, who has not intimated to me that any necessity exists for the appointment of more magistrates.

div.head: WARRINGTON CASES AT THE SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON CASES AT THE SESSIONS.

At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, \a Warrington youth named Samuel Marsh (17), who was shown to be of a roving disposition, was sentenced to three years under the Borstal system for stealing a bicy6le. George Jameson (56), a fitter, pleaded guilty to breaking into the counting house of Hugh Fairhurst Greenhough at Warington. There was a list of previous convictions against the prisoner, who was now sent to hard labour for two years. 'kir Bates Thompson (instructed by the Town Clerk of Warrington) prosecuted.
SUICIDAL MANIA.-THREE YEARS UNDER THE BORSTAL SYSTEM.

- --- -- At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, Rebecca Aspinall (19), of no occupation, pleaded guilty to attempting suicide at Warrington, by drinking a -quantity of benzine. Mr. Bates Thompson explained that the girl was seen in Victoria Park, Warrington. to drink something from a small bottle. She was taken to the Infirmary, where she was medically attended to. Chief Inspector Williamson said the girl had been a great source of trouble to ber parents, and had twice previously attempted to commit suicide. The prisoner, in a written statement, asked to be sent away for a time in order that she might redeem bar character.—She was sentenced to three years under the Borstal system.

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr J W Hayward (in the chair) Aide-man Smethurst and Mr W T Williams. DRINK AND BAD COMPANIONS.—ENEAbeth Pritchard 2, Poachers-lane, was charted on remand with stealing during the past five months, ten fowls value 30s. the property of Joseph Walker, New Farm, Poachers-lane, Latchford.—The Chief Constable said that the prisoner had been before the Court on Saturday on a charge of stealing one fowl, but since then inquiries had been made and it was found that the woman had taken ten. Mr Walker had been in the occupation of the farm since • February and between then and Saturday last he had missed over 20 fowls. It appeared that the prisoner had been in the habit of enticing the fowls into her kitchen by giving them food. She then bad them killed and sold some,and the others she had herself.—Prisoner who appeared to be about 50 years of age, attributed her downfall to bad companions and drink. The fowls bad some to her door day after day.—A fine of 40s. was imposed or in default one month's imprisonment. AFTER MANY YEARS.—William Rowlands, I, Stanley- street, was charged on remand with stealing on the 25th October six pairs of socks value 3s. 3d. the property of Annie Houghton, from the pawnshop, 28 and 30, Mersey-street —From the statement of the Chief Constable it would appear that about 4.30 on the day in question George Buckby, employed at the pawnshop, saw the prisoner loitering about in a suspicous manner. He saw him take the socks, and when charged the prisoner said" I am not going to say any- thing."—Prisoner said he had been a bad character four years ago and he bad been trying to do the best be could to keep in the straight path.—Rowlaods was sent to prison for one month with hard labour. THURSDAY.—Before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair), Mr W Roberts, Dr Naden sad Mr A J Jolley. THEFT OF WElGHTS.—Blizabeth Lavin, 24, Portland- street, was charged with stealing on the 25th October, two weights value Is Gd, the property of George Broad- hurst. fruiterer, 56, Brick-street. —The Chief Constable stated that the previous Friday morning Mr Broadhurst had been away and on his return, from information received be communicated with the police, complaining of two weights having been stolen. Detective Summers interviewed the prisoner,' and when asked about her movements that morning she said "I have not been to Mr Broadborst's shop this morning." She tried to evade the officer, but Summers found out that she bad sold the weights for a few coppers. The prisoner bad been drinking for some time previous to the day of the offence.—Prisoner was sent to prison for three months. DRUNK IN CEARGE.—For having been drunk in charge of two horses and a lurry in Sankey-street George Thomas James, 3. Leonard-street, Stockton Heath was fined lOs and costs. P.O Nicholls proved the case and stated that the defendant ran into a hand cart and knocked some drawers off it.—Prisoner said his horse shied. THE MOTOR NUISANCE.—Ernest Little,67, Lawrence-

, road, Liverpool, was summoned for driving a motor car at a speed dangerous to the public having regard to all the circumstances of the case, in Sankey-atreet on the "25th October.—lnspector Stuart stated that the defen- dant was driving a large motor car coming from the direction of Bank Quay Bridge. When he got in the narrow portion of Sankey-street be was driving at about 15 or 16 miles an hour. A few minutes later the defendant returned at a similar speed through a lot of traffic. The defendant had raid be was not driving at a dangerous speed and returned again through the traffic at about 12 or 13 miles per hour. Prisoner said the rpeedometer only registered 12 miles per hour. The Chief Constable dealt at some length with the great danger occasioned by motors driving through the narrow portion of Sankey-street at any great speed. They tore along the " bottle-neck " at a wicked speed. Several complaints had been made. Defendant was lined 40s and costs.

div.head: MAGISTRATES WITNESS WONDERFUL ZAM-BUK CURES.
div.p: MAGISTRATES WITNESS WONDERFUL ZAM-BUK CURES.
Two Children's Bad Heads.
LIE GRATEFUL MOTHER'S STORY.

The Shrewsbury Magistrates had before them Mrs. Allport, wife of Mr George Allpowt, of 20, Coal Wbarfe Square. Shrewsbury, for the non-attendance of her two children at school. Mrs Allport said that her children were suffering -very badly from eczema on the bead, but that if she were allowed to persevere with Zam-Buk she was sure tttey would soon be cured. The Magistrates, impressed by the good mother's story, bought her a further supply of Zam-Buk, and a fortnight later when the case came on at the Court again Mrs Allport appeared and testified that, thanks to Zam-Buk, her children were now quite better and attending school again. The Bench cheerfully dismissed the case. Interviewed by a reporter outside the Court, Mrs. Allport said : My two boys Thomas (aged 13) and Willie (aged 12) bad this eczema trouble for four years. "A thick coating of scurf first came at the hair roots, and when the boys scratched it off the scalp was left quite raw. Then a scab grew, as hard as this table top. If I touched it with the comb blood flowed. "Our children attetd St Chad's Soh, ols, but they were away as long as six months at a time. For four years both boys were treated at Salop Infirmary. "My daughter came home one day with a partly used box of Zatn-Bult, which a lady had given her. I tried the balm on Thomas. with surprising effect. "When I appeared in the Shrewsbury Police Court and told the Magistrates what Zam-Buk had done for my boys, they very kindly bought me a further supply of the balm, and advised me to persevere with it. I went home and set to work at once to get my boys better " Wam-Buk, besides soothing the irritation, worked through the hard crust of scurfy scabs. The disease was killed, and both boys shed the thick coating from their heads. Their scalps were cleansed and sweetened and the hair grew again in a wonderful way. "When I appeared again at the Police Court I was able to tell the Magistrates that both Thomas and Willie were back at school, certified as cured by the Medical Officer. I can't tell you how thankful I am to Zam-Buk for ridding the children of the awful disease. Mrs. Allport, to confirm her statement, showed tha reporter a card of admission she used for her children's treatment at the Hospital, and the reporter `himself interviewed the Presiding Magistrate, who, as further proof, handed him his own signed state- ment, confirming what the Bench had done and their belief in the great benefit Zam-Buk bad been to Mrs. Allport's children. This striking cure by Zam-Buk points the moral to all rnbthers who at any time may have their children affected by skin or scalp trodble. Get a is. 11d. or 23. 9d. box of Zam-Buk from the chemist at once and keep it handy in the cupboard. Where there is a large family the 2s. 9d. box will be found the more economical because it contains nearly four times the quantity that is in the smaller size.

COMMERCIAL FAlLURFS.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette." the number of commercial failures published in Great Britain and Ireland during the four weeks ending Saturday, October 26th, was 588. The number in the corresponding four weeks of last year was 637, showing a decrease of 109, being a net -decrease in 1912, of 415.

div.head: ENGLAND A PARADISE.
div.p: ENGLAND A PARADISE.
WHAT MIGHT BE, IF MUNICIPALITIES USED THEIR POWERS.
Rev. H. Dunn!co's Speech at Latchford.

The Rev HERBERT DENNICO, of Kensington Baptist Church, Liverpool (formerly of (iolborne-street Baptist Church, Warrington), addressed a meeting in support of the candidature of Nir E Wynne Jones in Latchford Ward, on Tuesday evening. He said that when he was ' in Warrington he did something to break down the combined forces of Toryism and breweryism. Although since that time the electors had fallen from grace, he hoped they would soon recover themselves and that Warrington would stand once more among the pro- gressive and enlightened towns of the Kingdom. (Applause.) Men came and went, political parties came into being and ceased to be, but the cause of progress and the principles of righteousness were eternal. He was present that night to support the great progressive movement which had for its object the emancipation of humanity, the securing to every man, woman and child the opportunity of living the best possible life. He rejoiced that Mr Wynne Jones was giving an important place in his crusade to the enlightenment of the children to securing for them a decent education and everything that was essential for the making of clean, efficient, intelligent and able-bodied citizens. They must not for a single moment become doubtful or hesitant if their education rate happened to rise, for education was one of the most economical forms of expenditure and would mean, in the long run, a decrease of the poor rate and the cost of prisons. In addition to education and medical inspection, they wanted school clinics to pro- vide those things which the doctors recommended and, if necessary, they must feed those children who were unable, through various circumstances, to get nourish- ment. It was an insane, nonsensical, suicidal policy to spend thowands upon thousands of pounds every year in trying to cram children who were unable to profit by education because they were under-fed, when a halfpenny or a penny additional rate would eauip them to make the best use of that costly educa- tion. If Mr Wynne Jones became a member of the Education Committee, he (the speaker) hoped he would fight strenuously to secure equality of opportunity for the poorest lad, along with the richeet. (Applause.) To-day there was a serious handicap on the poor man's child. The law did not permit a teacher in a secondary school to have control of more than 30 children, but in the primary rchool one teacher could have charge of sixty children. Moreover, in the secondary school every teacher was compelled to be fully .qualified, but 15 per cent, of the teachers in the primary schools were absolutely unqualified for the positions they held to-day. It might be said : "There are scholarships for the poor lad, to enable him to get into the higher brrnches of education." Yes, but the poor man's child was handicapped there,because the rich man was able to provide a private tutor and thus obtain an advantage for his child in the examination room. Mr Dunnico next touched upon the housing problem. How came it, be asked, that in Scotland-road, Liver- pool, infants died to the number of 300 and 365 per 1,000 of those born, while in Port Sunlight the per- centage fell as low as 49 to 51 ? The explanation was the vile and abominable conditions in which the people in the first-named district had to live. It was estimated that the average value of every life, from the age of 15 to 65,was something like £l5O. Yet every year 55,000 people died in this country alone of consumption, and 56 per cent, of those were between the ages of 22 and 45. Consumption was often the direct and inevitable outcome of poverty, and every year in the death of those people we were losing about £8,000,000. The powers vested in mw•icipalities were enormous. If the Houses of Parliament could be closed to-morrow and kept closed for ten years, and if the municipalities would make the fullest use of the powers at their dis- posal, this land could become a

VERITABLE PARADISE OF OOD, A Tory always stood for retrogession.He was a man who capitulated to the past, vtho simply stood still and let the great stream of progress flow on or did his best, in his own puny way, to stop it. He (the speaker) never had any mercy on a Tory. Be was born with an intense and inherent hatred of Toryism, and whenever he came into conflict with a Tory, he loved to fight him. He remembered somebody accusing him, when he was in Warrington, of being very bitter against Toryism, and so he was. Torvirm was always the enemy and opponent of mankind, especially of the lower classes. The seething diFcontent and unrest of the present day, continued Mr Dunnico, did not make him despondent, but gave him hope and inspiration. It was but the brooding of the mighty Spirit of God over the troubled waters of humanity and out of chaos would come order, out of confusion would come beauty, out of death, life. Why were men crying out for a larger life and opportunity? It was because they were beginning to think. The world was becoming increasingly intelligent and men were refusing to accept their political creeds, just as they were refusing to accept their theological creeds, ready-made and second-band. Notwithstanding all our power over nature,our inventive and mechanical skill, our improved means of communication and our marvellous wealth, we found a comparatively few living and even rotting in luxury, while millions existed on the verge of starva- tion. Politics without ideals were worthless. They heard a great deal of talk about patriotism. Because a man waved a Union Jack, called himself a Tory and sang" Rule Britannia," half drunk, be thought be was a patriot. When he (the speaker) heard some men talk- ing about patriotism—Mr F E Smith, his member— (laughter)—for instance—be often thought Dr Johnson was not very far wrong wben he said "Patriotism Is often the last refuge of scoundrels." The true patriot was the man who blushed every time he saw a ragged, hungry child in the streets, who wiped away a real tear of sorrow when he heard of women who were compelled to eke out an existence by immoral means, and who felt a pang in his heart when he saw industrial warriors going down to paupers' graves. Those were the things to get excited about and to work for. He WEiS no party politician; be was sometimes sick to death of party politics as we knew them to•day. He would not not lift his little finger to help a political party as such. It was because he believed that, politics. rightly understood, were the practical application of the teachings of Christ to every day life, that. he was driven to stand there, by the logic of the Gospel he preached. (Applause.)

div.head: LANCASHIRE TERRITORIALS. – The King's Visit Next Year.
div.p: LANCASHIRE TERRITORIALS. - The King's Visit Next Year.

The visit of the King and Queen to Lancashire next year will enable the military authorities to give some idea of the success that has attended their efforts to raise, maintain, and equip the two Lancashire Territorial Divisions. King Edward and Queen Alexandria came to Lancashire in July, 1908, and presented colours to the troops entitled to carry them fheir MajPsties were the guests of Lord and Lady Derby at Knowsley, and as the Royal visit extended over two days, the King arranged to review the two divisions separately, the West Lancashires in Knowsley Park and the East Lancashires in Worsley Park.

_ The visit of King George and Queen Mary will not be confined to Liverpool and Manchester Their present intention is to visit some of the more important centres of industry in the county. A tour of this charactei will not allow of a divisional review either in Liverpool or Manchester. But arrangements are being made to approach the King and Queen and to invite their approval of a programme which will specially concern all the Territorial units in the towns through which their Majesties will pass. Lord Derby, Major General Sir Henry Mackinnon, general officer commanding-in-chief, Western Command; Major General Lindsay, general officer commanding the West Lancashire Division Territorial Force ; and Major General C W Park, general officer commanding the East Lancashire Division Territorial Force, have each considered this question of bringing the Lanca- shire troops of the second line army prominently before the King and Queen during their Lancashire tour.

div.head: PAVLOVA AT LIVERPOOL NENT WEEK.
div.p: PAVLOVA AT LIVERPOOL NENT WEEK.

There is some sorcery in the dancing of Pavlova ; for she has stolen the heart of Europe. To give an account of her triumph is to tell a romance. She has cotne from the land of snow and revolution to fascinate the world with the poetry of motion. It is a revelation to see her dance in " Giselle' " her favourite ballet, which was put on for her at Covent Garden. The piece gives rare opportunities to the actress as well as to the dancer, and Pavlora's histrionic talents are as wonderful as her technique. She sways her audience. In the " Passing of the Swan," danced to the tender music of Saint-Saens. she touches one to the depths with the tragedy of her conception of the music. In "Le Papillon " she is gaiety incarnate. The frenzied whirl of Glazounov,s Bacchanal, as danced by her and M. Novikoff is a revelation of the spirit of ancient Greece. The truth is that Pavlova has the spark of genius which differentiaties the great artist from the capable performer. There has been no such dancer since the time of Taglioni, who danced for our fore- fathers. And in real life Mme. Pavlova is the simplest, least affected person in the world. She dresses quietly and is never happier than when in the country, away from the life of the theatre. Madame Pavlova pays a return visit to the Liverpool Shakespeare Theatre next week.

div.head: REL/G/011
div.p: REL/G/011

The Bishop and His Salary. During a discussion on Church finance at the Liver- dool Diocesan Conference on Tuesday, Mr J Burgess (Liverpool) urged that greater efforts should be made towards increasing the salaries of poor clergy. He said they generally asked for and expected a married clergy but they did not provide for a married clergy. They could not expect or have married clergy with the pittance provided for ministers in many of the benefices in the country. Nobody wanted men to enter the ministry for what they could get out of it, but they at least desired that they should have enough to live on comfortably. He did not believe in bishops having from £4,000 to £15,000 a year and parish priests less than £l5O or £2OO. Neither in the Diocese of Liverpool or anywhere else would they ever make an effective appeal to the laity until the episcopal incomes had been reduced. A few years ago one of the best bishops in the country, whose stipend was several thousands a year, said that he only got about £3OO a year for himself, because he bad to keep up three palaces, stables, coachmen, liveried men, and all the rest of it. (Laughter). "If you want the Church of England to be really the ( hurch of the people," declared Mr Burgess, " the first thing you have to do is to reform the scandal of the inadequacy of payment to the clergy." The Bishop : Speaking for myself, I am perfectly willing, if the diocese desire it, to give up ray house and £3.00J a year end live on a very much smaller scale (" No, no.") But you must not ask a bishop to fill a position which requires £4,000 a year and then complain that he is too well paid. I can only say for myself that I was never so poor as I am to-day.

div.head: Baptist Missionary Meeting.
div.p: Baptist Missionary Meeting.

Under the auspices of the Warrington and District Baptist Union a united missionary tea and public meet- ing took place at Latchford Baptist Church on Thursday evening. Over 100 sat down to tea in the schoolroom between six and seven o'clock and the meeting was afterwards held in the chapel. The Rev 3 S Chedhurn presided and was supported by the Revs H Ogden and G Curtis. The princiral speakers were the Rev F Harmon of China, and the Rev RD Derby, of Leigh, formerly a missionary on the Congo who gave an excellent address on their work. The choir rendered the anthems "0 Worship the Lord "and "0, taste and see." The meet- ing was a great success in every way.

div.head: St. Clement's Men's Club.
div.p: St. Clement's Men's Club.

This successful club hns just held its annual meeting. Mr H C Rhoden presided in the unavoidable absence of the President (the Rev T Vickers.) The balance-sheet was passed as read, and the treasurer was thanked for the excellent manner in which he hid presented the accounts for the year. The following officers were elected for the ensuing year :—President, the Rev Vickers ; vice-president, Mr H C Bbcden ; secretary Mr H Broadhurst ; treasurer, Mr C Gandy ; auditor, Mr J Aikenhead ; committee, Messrs H Houghton, A Berry, H Slevin, H Macdonald, W Guest, A Beswick and NV 'Warburton.

Wycliffe P.S A. Society. There was a fair attendance on Sunday.presided over by Mr William Beswick. The Rev H Ogden gave the address upon " Nurse the child and I will pay thee thy wages." He said that now, as at all times, the influencer of the child's life was the mother ; the child looked up to its mother as its supreme guide and counsellor. The mother's influence was not only for the child's good but to the national advantage. As a famous Cardinal said, " Give me the child and I am satisfied." The child's mind well trained, brought forth good results in the days to come. Mr C Cotton read the lesson and the Chairman led the prayer. Mr Payton presided at the organ. Three new members received a hearty welcome.

div.head: Call to Congregational Minister.
div.p: Call to Congregational Minister.

The Rev Alfred A Lee, of Seaforth Congreeati,znal Church (who has frequently preached at Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington), has received a hearty and united invitation to the pastorate of the Macfadyen Memorial Church, Manchester. Mr Lee has been over three years at Seafortb, and previously was at Emmanuel Church, Bootle, for five years with the Rev Thomas Dunlop. He has been secretary of the Liverpool and District Congregational Council for some years, and his removal, should he decide to go, will he keenly felt throughout the Congregational churches of the district. Mr Lee Is asked to follow the
-- Rev Sidney Berry, M.A., who recently succeeded Dr Jowett at Carr's-lane, Birmingham.

div.head: Wycliffe Congregational Church.
div.p: Wycliffe Congregational Church.

Mr. F. Chaim.- ra Rogers, M.A.,8.D., senior student oj Yorkshire United College, was the preacher at the morning service in Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday. In an illuminating address to the children he explained the text : "The Word was made flesh.,' The ',object of the sermon was Christ's forgiveness of Peter (John xxi. 16). The incident, he said, contained the whole meaning snd significance of the doctrine of Divine forgiveness. If he could put the whole meaning of Christianity into one sentence he would say that Christ came to restore the broken relationship between God and man. Uutil that restoration took place they could not know the real meaning of life. To admit that this life was given to us simply that we might strive and toll in order to support life was to admit that we were only animals, tor that was mere animal existence. That was only one side of our life, and could never satisfy the soul's deepest needs. It was necessary to have intimate relationship with God. The Rev Stanley Rogers, 8.A., of Bootle, father of the preacher at the morning service, occupied the pulpit in the evening. The subject of his discourse was "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in par- ticular " (I. Cor. 12c 27v). The text set before them, be said, was the true ideal of the Christian church. They needed to be continually adjusting their spiritual com- passes. The forces of evil were quite as potent and even more subtle, than in the past. They saw mani- festations of it in the covert attacks of secularists and of the voluptuous and self indulgent men of to-day. He suggested that the church was suffering from the timorous uncertainty of the utterances of the men who should be leaders and active in its support. If there was one quality which marked the early Christian church it Wafi its enthusiasm. It had a holy ideal which was that the church was the body of Christ. Be pleaded for every member to be an enthusiastic worker in the church and strive for that unity which Christ prayed for. The Rev. D. Burford Hook, D.D. of London, secre- tary of the Colonial Missionary Society is to preach morning and evening to-morrow (Sunday), and op the following Monday be will deliver a lecture, illustrated by limelight views, entitled" From the Cape to the Zambesi."

On Sunday evening the Rev. Wm. Reid delivered the first of a series of sermons on the life of St. Paul, taking his text from Acts VII. (the account of the martyrdom of Stephen setting forth that those stoning him laid their clothes at a young man's feet, whose narde was Saul.) In Stephen' day, said Mr. Reid, he (the preacher) believed deacon was just another name for " minister," and the duties of Stephen were not defined by his office, but by his own abilities. Stephen stood for something beyond doctrines and dogmas ; be was for something and someone he saw in his vision. uhrist was a person to him, not a mere name or theory. Prejudice raged against him because he witnessed for Christ and for the great union between God and man. The very glory that suffused the face of Stephen, Paul only looked upon as the work of Satan, and yet 30 years later he too gave up his life for the Nazarene, so wondrously did God work in human souls. It bad been said if there had been no Stephen there would have been DO Paul. There was no progress or advance unless they devoted their lives to the objects they were pursuing. Truth might be stricken to the earth, but she wduld rise again, for the eternal words of God were hers.

div.head: New Church Lectures.
div.p: New Church Lectures.

The last of the series of New Church lectures was delivered in the Masonic Hall on Tuesday evening last. The subject of the lecture was " The Problem of Sin" and the lecturer the Rev J Howarth, of Bolton. After referring to the importance of the subject and the many difficulties that surround it, it was pointed out that in its consideration one or two premises must be conceded viz., either that man is a subject of pre- destination, ordered by degrees of the Divine will, and therefore not responsible for any act of omission or commission, or be is endowed with a freedom of will and of choice by the exercise of which he becomes responsible for the choice he makes. In the first instance men are not responsible for the con ditions that prevail, and.in any ease it would be futile for them to attempt to free themselves from the destiny preordained on their behalf, and all the tenets and teachings of Sacred Scripture would be of no avail. On the other hand granting man freedom of choice in the exercise of which he may choose the good, the holy, the pure, he may come more and more into the image and likeness of his Creator, even to the fulfilment of the Lord's behest " Be ye perfect as your Father in the heavens is perfect." We prefer to accept this latter because it is the teaching of the Divine Word. Here comes in the most important division of our subject, for we are now prepared to ask how has in come into the world, which has been so disastrous in its consequences ? Let 119 s,y at once that it certainly is not the working of the Divine Providence. It is not the Lord's doing. Our God is a God of love and it is beyond the corn- prehension of man to understand how Divine Love could design evil which is so degrading to the human character. The cause of the existence of sin in the world must be sought for in another direction. The faculties of freedom of thought and choice may find many channels for their exercise either in the con- firmation of the good and pure or in the selection of the unholy and impure. This is the point from which to examine the cause of evil and sin. Another point of great importance with the subject is the question as to what sin is. Sin in the true meaning of the term is the violation of the known laws of God had the nature of all sin is according to the violation of these laws. This truth is involved in all the admonitions of both the Old and the New Testament Scriptures. We are faced with the fact that all the responsibility of sin rests with the human race. Sin comes of the abuse of our freedom and the prostitution of the powers given us by God, and what was intended for our uplitting becomes the means of our downfall. A useful discussion followed the lecture.

div.head: " Religion and the Individual."
div.p: " Religion and the Individual."

Continuing his course of sermons on "Religion and Democracy " at Cairo-street Chapel, the Rev. Dr. Stanley Mellor took for his subject on Sunday evening when there was again a crowded congregation, " Religion and the Inoividual." He said that if they looked round over the ranks of those who to-day pro- fessed religion, who said that they were religious, they could hardly help noticing that there were many, very many, for whom religion, the religion they professed, was little more than an accidental addition to life, a something casually tacked on, a fringe, an ornament, which in no sense affected their life or their thought as a whole. If what they called their religion were taken away from them, they would scarcely miss it; indeed they might find it a relief to he without it— their Sundays would be less occupied and there would be fewer calls upon their purse. In their individual lives those people did not seem to be in the least degree affected by their religion ' • for all the actual power it bad over them, they might as well not have it at all. It made no difference to their outlook on existence, to their ideas about daily life, to their attitude towards the world. And yet, surely, if religion was genuine and real at all, it should make a difference in all those and countless other ways. Religion, for many, seemed to have become sadly separated from the rest of life, and the strange thing was that people should be content to leave religion in that separation. So far indeed had the separation gone, that there seemed to be actually abroad in the world a notion that religion was at its best when it was as far removed from actual life as possible, that, rightly to flourish, it must be kept literally unspotted by the world. The preacher maintained that religion, if it be genuine, most affect the individual through and through. No man could really become alive to religion, possessed of it and by it, and remain what he was. To prove that true, they ' had but to glance at the essential character of religion. What was true and genuine religion? Was it thd recitation of a creed? Assuredly not. Was it the ' repetition of long prayers and the listening to burden- some sermons? Assuredly not. Was it the support of a sect and the upholding of a denomination? God forbid! Was it the belief in some particular dogma, or doctrine, or article? Most surely no. Genuine religion was faith and vision and aspiration. It WdEl faith in the Divine significance of life •, it was vision of that order of being in which truth and beauty and the good, and fellowship and communion in these, were triumphant to the vanquishing of falseness, ugliness, and wrong; it was aspiration after the achievement of the ideal. This faith and vision and aspiration were peculiarly personal things, things that a man felt and knew in his innermost heart, things that he possessed inwardly, not as accidental but as essential elements of his life. Religion was never a cold and calculating thing, a matter simply of the reason and 1 the logical understanding; there was in it, on the contrary, a deep and passionate quality which made a man burn as with fire and glow with an intense heat. Religion was a kind of sacred enthusiasm for the good and beautiful, an impassioned ardour for joy and happi- ness, which, when once it. had occupied a man's heart, would give him no rest. It suffused his whole being, overwhelmed him ; like the ocean, once it bad found entrance to the soul, it poured in, wave breaking un wave, each wave rushing upon its predecessor till at length the last barrier gave way and the whole man was, as it were, flooded, swept down, consumed. "Religion's all or nothing " cried Browning- " Stuff of the very stuff ; life of life and self of self." There was in it soiLething, perhaps, extravagant, something excessive ; it was indeed a passion, no little thing hut a great, the gisatest in life, a stormy tide that rushed in on finite existence, shaking a man to his foundations, an angel with a flaming sword destroying the littleness and the meanness of life. It was a glory and a radiance which permitted a man to behold nothing but the ideal. At its coming, self interest dropped vanquished,selfishnesscotvered stricken to the dust, meanness, smallness of spirit, littleness of aspiration vanished. The preacher next developed his argument that religion should permeate every detail of existence and pointed out that it could never be served or realized by withdrawal from the world. A man told him once that he could not afford to let religion enter into his business ; but that did not prove that religion was a thing that ought not to have a place in business. All it proved was firstly. that the man who made the remark was, in existing circumstances, relatively honest and secondly that there most be something radically wrong with the business and the conditions of business into which religion might not enter. Another man told him that religion bad no place in politics; but that VINO no proof that religion and politics had really nothing to do with each other ; it was, on the contrary, only a severe con- demnation of existing politics. If our politics were devoid of religion, the sooner we get rid of them the better. It might sound extravagant, but it was never- theless utterly true, to say that unless our legislators and politicians, municipal and national alike, were sincerely concerned with the things of religion, justice, mercy and truth, to the exclusion of all else, they had better abandon the business. The picture which our social existence presented to the eye of genuine religion was awful in the extreme, horrible and shameful to the last degree. And religion, by the very necessity of the case, believed pasionately that it might all be different, believed that human nature was capable of making it all different, if only the opportunity were given. The man who professed at one and the same time to be both religious and contented with things as they are was simply making a mockery of himself and of religion.

Rev. Father Day on Divorce. 1. Polygamy by Instalments."

The Red Father Henry Day,S.J., of the Church of the Holy Name, Manchester, preached a striking sermon on' Divorce " at Our Lady's Cburch, Latchford, on Sunday evening. He said that Martin Luther over 300 years ago uttered his famous dictum "Marriage is a worldly thing " and that rtere utterance of the founvler of Protestantism had made history. More and more as years had gone by, public opinion had tended to recognize the right of the State to legislate in the matter of marriage,so that at the present time legislation was entering into the whole province of marriage. The State undertook to make laws regarding the contract of marriage, to give dispensations and to sever the bonds which united men and women in matrimony. In our country divorce was a part of the legal system. In 1910 a Commission was appointed to study and decide upon certain issues which had long been under agita- tion. It was now quite evident that both Majority and Minority Reports of the Commission recommended an equality of the sexes in regard to the law of divorce, and this would mean that it would no longer be incum- bent upon a wife to prove more against her husband than a husband must prove against an unfaithful wife in order to secure a divorce. This principle was an open contradiction of the common sense of mankind in every age. Misconduct as regards man and woman, the preacher said, was the same sin but the consequences in both cases were widely dissimilar, and this fact, could not be ignored when they came to give a valuation of sin from the moral as well as the social standpoint. The woman who committed misconduct, continued Father Day, might introduce into her husband's house- hold progeny which was not his own' and which be was fraudulently induced to and legally compelled to support. To ignore this circumstance was criminal folly, and if this recommendation of the Commission were acted on an intolerable social injustice would be the result. Father Day, alluding to the second recom- mendation of the Commission, as foreshadowed by the forecasts in the Press, said it meant that divorce should be more readily obtained by the poor, and this sugges- tion was more in the nature of cruelty than in justice. Christian teaching and eugenic science both declared that it, was not divorce but marriage that was at the heart of the social question. Divorce was in reality simply a pagan and reactionary institution. It was a I return to a lower civilization than we were supposed to have at the present day. It was the sin of successive polygamy or polygamy on the instalment plan. It could not possibly be the basis of social advancement in a Christian country. Referring to the connection of the Archbishop of York with the Commission, Father Day said it was deplorable to find such a highly placed dignitary of the State Church associated with such pagan principles. Discussing the Christian law of marriage, Father Day said it was not simply a civil contract but a sacred act confirmed I and sanctioned by the authority of Almighty God. "Those whom God bath joined together, let no man put asunder." Marriage cv•,s not a natural but a super-natural function. Once marriage was a natural function, but Christ came and raised and elevated that contract, making it super-natural. The State was powerless before the Christian Church, and the Church could say to the State," Hands off. You have no right here. lam the representative of God in this matter. I stand in the place of Christ. I have the defence of this institution, which is a heavenly thing—a Sacrament instituted by Christ, the Saviour of the world." Christian men and women,trying to live up to the Christian ideal, merged their lives together to sink their individual merits, ambitior,s and pleasures, and sacrificed them- selves for the children. In view of that end the Church said divorce was utterly intolerable, and could not be allowed—intolerable because it necessarily sacrificed the children. Divorce in itself was a doctrine of despair, and to talk about the freedom of the individual was a contradiction of marriage. It was an outrage against nature, a crime against society, and a sun against Almighty God. Where the family was strong, society was strong. Weaken marriage and they weakened the family and the State. div.head: DEFENCE OF TERRITORIALS.
div.p: DEFENCE OF TERRITORIALS.
Cheshire Critic of Lord Roberts.

Colonel Bromley Davenport, presiding at a meeting of the Cheshire Territorial Association on Tuesday, protested against references to the Territorial Force which Lord Roberts had made in a recent speech at Manchester. He said it was a poor compliment to the Territorial Force throughout the Urtited Kingdom, who had been wen king throughout four years, and had shown good results. It was also a poor com- pliment to those distinguished officers who bad been appointed as instructors and trainers of the Territorial Forces at the end of it all to say that the Territorial Force was an acknow- ledged failure. If they wanted to make failure they only hal to shout "Failure," while if they wanted to make success they had to shout " Success." At the same time Lord Roberts had been carried away by his enthusiasm for compulsory service. Compulsory service was an unfortunate necessity for European nations whose boundaries were an imaginary line almost. For us, surrounded by the sea, and having the advantage of the protection of the sea, it was not absolutely necessary to compel people to service. But when Lord Roberts asserted as proof of the necessity , for compulsory service that the Territorial Force way an acknowledged failure, then he was riding his hubby a little tot hard, and was guilty of injustice to tens of thousands of people, and guilty of that exaggeration which was no less grotesque than the statements of other extremists who said the efficiency of the Territorial Force was equal to that of the Regulars. He (the Chairman) denied that the Territorial Force was a failure. It was a remarkable success—that had been achieved in the face of many difficulties and many diseouragements. It was hardly too much to say that in certain quarters there had been a kind of conspiracy against the Territorial Force in order to tiling about the only alternative, which was compulsory. service. The Territorial Force had been damned with faint praise. The spitit of patriotism was not dead, only patriotism was a plant which could not thrive in an atmosphere of discouragement.

div.head: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
THE MEANING OF STEPMOTHER.

You have all heard the phrase Step- mother, but 1 wonder how many boys and girls know the meaning of the word step, when used in this way. Perhaps most people if asked to explain it would say that it meant a woman who had " stepped " into the place of the true mother. But that is not the correct interpretation. The word step is really the Anglo-Saxon " steop," and its true meaning appears to have been "orphaned." It was first used in the form step-child, which meant orphaned-child, and step-son and step-daughter described those left without a parent. As time went on the meaning beame obscure and " step-mother " came to be used of one who took the place of mother to orphan children. Of course it is incorrect to speak of step-father and step- mother since it is the little folks who are the " steops " or orphans, but if we understand it as meaning "mother of orphans" perhaps it will be all right. We need a word to describe the relationship, and perhaps this is as good as any.

" lIELP ONE ANOTHER." " Help one another," the snowflakes said, As they cuddled down in their fleecy bed ; " One of us here would not ke felt, One of us hero would quickly melt; But I'll help you, and you help me, And then what a big white drift we'll see! " " Help one another," the maple spray - Said to its fellow leaves one day; " The sun would wither me here alone, Long enough ere the day is gone ; But I'll help you and you help me, And then what a splendid shade there'll be !" "Help one another," the dewdrop cried, Seeing another drop close to its side; " This warm south breeze would dry me away; And I should be gone ere noon to-day; But I'll help you, and you help me, And we'll make a brook and run to the sea." "Help one another," agrain of sand j Said to another grain ust at hand; "The wind may carry me over the sea, And then, 0 ! what will become of me? But come, my brother, give me your hand; We'll build a mountain, and there we'll stand." And so the snowflakes grew to drifts, The grains of sand to mountains, The leaves became a pleasant shade, And dewdrops fed the fountains. THIS WEEK'S STORY. DREAMLAND.

INJUSTICES TO NONCONFORMISTS.
MR. RUNCIMAN AND GOVERNMENT ANXIETY TO REMOVE THEM.

Speaking at Thornhill Lees, Dewsbury, on Saturday Mr W Runciman, the President of the Board of Agri- culture, said the Government were also anxious that religious liberty and equality should be established in this country. He must remind them that there still existed in England with our educational machinery gross injustices to the Nonconformists. They had attempted to remedy some by adminibtrative action. but they had not succeeded in getting their Education Bills through, and were it not for the Parliament Act he did not think they ever would have succeeded. The Parliament Act cleared the way for the establishment of religious equality just as it cleared the way for self- governmert in Ireland. (Hear, hear.)

Upon the death of Dr. Taylor the position of Divinity Tutor was offered to Dr. Aikin. His acceptance left vacant the classical tutor- ship and to this post the Trustees invited the teacher who was destined to become most famous of them all, Joseph Priestley.

div.head: ADVENT OF JOSEPH PRIESTLEY.
div.p: THE ADVENT OF JOSEPH PRIESTLEY.

11 The invitation reached him in the summerl lof 1761 and in September of that year he removed from Nantwich to Warrington. Mr. Priestley was in the prime of young manhood and had already revealed the fine qualities which were to make him world- famous. Born at Field Head near Leeds on March 13th, 1743 he had been sent to the Daventry .Academy and placed under the tutorship of Dr. Ashworth. His training finished he accepted a pastorate in Needham in Suffolk from whence after three years of ministry he had removed to Nantwich. Upon the financial side the prospects of the Academy were anything but bright when this distinguished young scholar decided to share its fortunes, but the undaunted secre- tary travelled to London in quest of new subscribers, and after journeying to several other towns as well was able to make the future look much more hopeful.

div.head: NW ACADEMY.
div.p: THE NW ACADEMY.

It was probably the success of these efforts that made it possible for the Trustees to give to the Academy a more spacious home,and to undertake the responsibility of commodious premises erected in Academy-Place.. Five years had been spent in the building at Bridge Foot. In 1762, the year after Priestley's arrival, the new building was opened and the Academy entered upon its most fruitful and happy years.

The character of the buildings erected for the Academy and its tutors reveal the confi- dence which its friends felt for its future. Two of the houses still stand, one on each side of Academy Street, their style and quality preserving for us a knowledge of the parts that have vanished. Academy Street, as it came to be called in honour of the Institution, then led into a quiet square, the Academy proper facing the visitor as he entered. Though not an impos- ing building it was commodious and substan- tial, and its facade and bell turret gave the touch of distinction which such a building deserved. The students' quarters occupied the west side of the Square and stood until the making of Holt Street in 1898.

With Pr-iestly and Aikin as its guiding spirits—both of them in the hey-day of their youth and charm—this little Square became a hive of intellectual activity. Dr. Priestley drew upon happy memories when he wrote in later years "The tutors in my time lived in most perfect harmony. We drank tea together every Saturday, and our conversa- tion was equally instructive and pleasing. I often thought it not a little extraordinary that four persons, who had no previous knowledge of each other, should have been brought to unite in conducting such a scheme as this."
