Dr. Priestley's sojourn in Warrington, though it can hardly be called a memorable period in his career, brought several events of which he makes happy mention in his memoirs. During the second year of his residence he married " a daughter of Mr. Isaac Wilkinson, an ironmaster near Wreiham " with whose family he had become acquainted in consequence of having the youngest son in his school. To her unselfishness he delighted to pay the highest tribute and he records that at Warrington their daughter Sarah was born. There came to him also at Warrington the honour of a doctor's degree, an event which he records with characteristic modesty." After tho publication of my Chart of Biography' Dr. Percival, then a student at Edinburgh, procured for me the title of Doctor of Laws from that University."

A distinct epoch in his intellectual career alsd opened to him during thqse years. His experiments in electricity had brought him into touch with Dr. Franklin, and it was upon the recommendation of that interesting scholar that Priestley came into touch with the Royal Society. Letters from Franklin came regularly to Academy Place, and Priestley's "History of Electricity" passed in manuscript portions back to Dr. Franklin to receive criticism and comment.

As' successor to Dr. Priestley the unhappy choice was mide of Mr. (afterwards Dr.) John Reinhold Forster, a German naturalist and scholar, who undertook Tutorship in Natural History, Latin, Greek and Modern Languages. He proved himself during a short stay quite incapable of the economies that were necessary in the Academy and his irritable temper placed him very much out of harmony with his collegues. He afterwards accompanied Captain Cook upon his second voyage (an honour that had been offered and partly accepted by Dr. Priestley himself) and upon his return became a Professor at Halle. THE DEATH OF MR. SEDDON.

The year 1770 brought a further calamity to the Academy in the loss, by death, of Mr. Seddon. The end came with tragic sudden- ness. Seized with apoplexy when on horse- back he lingered but a few hours.Mr Seddon's removal was a severe blow to the Academy. His persistent labours had brought it into being and his continued labours had formed from the first hour the pillar upon which it had rested. As secretary he had given unremitting care and during the closing years of his life,as "Rector Academile " he had been the guide and adviser of the tutors and the inspiring genius of the scholars. Few men have shown to the world how powerful and precious a thing is the grace of perseverance, and there are few memorials of patience more remarkable than the Warrington Academy.

div.head: ACADEMY SOCIETY.
div.p: ACADEMY SOCIETY.

A scribe with an ear for interesting things could have left us a valuable little book gathered from the echoes of those Saturday tea parties and one dare not guess whether the small talk or the big talk would have been most prized. Priestley's keen intellect was already at work upon theories that were to work revolutions in the world of science, and doctrinal discussions that were to leave a lasting mark upon religious thought were already taking place in the precincts of the Academy. But he would have been a scribe of uncommon genius who could have forseen how very big indeed the big talk of the parties was to prove. Of the small talk let Miss Anna Letitia Aikin, herself one of the sparkling ones, give us materials for guessing. She wrote to Miss Belshaw : "We have a knot of lassies just after your own heart, as merry blithe and gay as you would wish them, and very smart and clever—two of them are the Miss Rigbys. We have a West Indian family too that I think you would like, a young couple who seem intended by nature for nothing but mirth, frolic and gaiety." Miss Aikin was blossoming into a famous poet, and her brother, John Aiken, into a scholarly physician interested in a hundred things besides medical science. Mrs. Seddon was a lady of fortune, and Mrs Priestley on the good-will of all who met her. A stimulating atmosphere indeed it must have been in which Miss Aikin was reared and one that could hardly fail to stir the genius she possessed. Upon a fashion for versifying that sprung up in the Academy " set " there is a happy passage in a letter of Miss Lucy Aikin. "Both bouts rimes' and vers de societe 'were in fashion with the set. One copy of verses' a very eloquent one, puzzled all guessers a long time ; at length it was traced to Dr Priestley's self. "Somebody was bold enough to talk or getting up private theatricals. This was a dreadful business 1 All the wise and grave, the whole tutorhood, cried out, it must not be The students, the Rigbys, and, I must add, my aunt, took the prohibition very sulkily, and my aunt's Ode to Wisdom was the result."

div.head: DISTINGUISHED VISITORS.
div.p: DISTINGUISHED VISITORS.

_ These intellectuals were supremely happy among themselves. They had a world of their own and needed to seek little from the outer world..: It was rather the outer world that came to Warrington. Pennant the Naturalist, Currie the biographer Of Burns, Roscoe of Liverpool found pleasure in War- rington Society, and to John Howard, at a later stage, it was a home of help as well as of sympathy and delight. Miss Lucy Aikin's comment, to quote that estimable lady again, impresses one as perfectly true and beautiful. "I have often thought with envy of that society. Neither Oxford nor Cambridge could boast of brighter names in literature or science than several of these dissenting tutors—humbly content to live in an obscure

div.head: OF THE ACADEMY.
div.p: OF THE ACADEMY.

town and on a scanty pittance, to cultivate in themselves and communicate to a rising generation those mental acquirements and moral habits which are their own exceeding great reward. They and theirs lived together like one large family, and in the facility of their intercourse they found large com- pensation for its deficiency in luxury and splendour."

Happy and useful as were these days they did not bring real prosperity to the Academy. Straightened from the beginning in finance, the dispute with Dr. Taylor proved an incurable wound. Dr. Priestley puts the matter quite plainly: "The Academy did not flourish. There had been an unhappy difference between Dr. Taylor and the trustees in consequence of which all his friends, who were numerous, were our 'enemies; and too many of the subscribers, being probably weary of the subscription, were willing to lay hold of any pretence for dropping it, and of justifying their conduct afterwards."

Lack of funds made it quite impossible for the Academy to offer sufficient salaries to its:tutors and Miss Aikin is obliged to say "The alma mater of Warrington was ever a niggardly recompense of the distinguished abilities and virtues which were enlisted in her services."

Dr. Priestley received £lOO a year and his house, and finding the income insufficient and there being no prospect of better days he felt abliged to resign his post. After six years residence in Warrington he left Academy Place in September 1767 and took up the .vork of a pastorate in Leeds.

div.head: FREE TRADE TRIUMPHANT.
div.p: FREE TRADE TRIUMPHANT.

In pleading for a return to Protection, Tariff Reformers habitually ignore the slow progress made in international trade by competing European countries generally, and as evidence of the benefits of Protection cite the one and only European country, viz., Germany, whose progress can in any way be compared with our own. Even were it possible to prove that the expansion of German trade was greater and more healthy than our own, and further was the result of Protection, it would still be necessary to supply reasons why in all the other Protected countries progress was so slow. Putting aside the above consideration, let us examine the facts and figures relating to German and English trade during recent years. Taking the years 1903 and 1910, the period in which the Tariff Reform agitation has been before the country, we find German exports as a whole have increased rapidly. When, however, we divide the exports of both countries into the three divisions of manufactured goods, raw materials and food stuffs, &c., we find the progress mad 6 by this country is much more healthy than that of Germany. That is taking it on the ground usually adopted by Tariff Reformers and accepted generally by Free Traders, that the more manufactured goods sent abroad,,and the less manufactured goods imported, the healthier may be consideted the national trade. During the period in question our exports of manufactured goods have increased £109,000,000 against German £83,000,000. While on the other hand our imports of manufactured goods have only increased £13,000,000 against the German £29,000,000, leaving us to the good £26,000,000 on exports and £16,000,000 on imports. Mr. E. Enever Todd, M.A., has, in connection with the Free Trade Union, recently published a series of charts, which we are kindly allowed to reproduce. Next week we will illustrate in this way the change in the character of German exports and show that since the introduction of the New German Tariff in 1906 the proportion of manufactures in Germany's Exports has fallen, and that of the Raw Material and Food Stuffs has risen. This is very significant because the purpose of all increased duties is designed to have exactly the opposite effect, namely, to increase the proportion of exports of Manufactured Goods and to lessen the proportion of exports of Raw Materials and Foodstuffs. A MOTOR TRAGEDY.
WARRINGTON TRAVELLER FINED AND LICENCE SUSPENDED.

At the Blackpool Police Court on Monday, Thomas Cumin, commercial traveller, of Thurston, Latchford Without, near Warrington, was summoned for driving a motor car at a speed dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case. Mr .1 W P Loftos, Deputy Town Clerk, prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr C J Jackson (instructed by Mr Bernard Knit) defended. Mr Loftos stated that about 1050 on the night of July 25th, the defendant was driving a two-seater motor car, with two lady passengers, along the promenade. lie passed the North Pier, travelling in a southerly direction, and his speed along Central Beach was from 16 to 20 miles an hour. Generally speaking, the car proceeded down the middle of the carriage way, and when he arrived opposite the entrance to the Palace Theatre, the defendant seemed to have started swerving to the right and then back again to the centre of the road. Ile continued at the same speed up to the north side of Victoria-street. Here a young woman, named Ethel Atkinson, with two companions, was endeavouring to cross the carriage-drive from the footpath opposite the Tower Cafe, in a south-westerly direction. They had got about half-way across when they heard a hooter, and saw the defendant's car. Ethtl Atkinson separated from her friends, who stepped back, and continued running in a south-westerly direc- tion to get away from the car. The defendant, who was very close to her at the time, swerved to his right with the intention of trying to pass her. Unfortunately, the car caugh. her, knocked her down, ran over her, and killed her. The car stopped a few yards further on, with the two front wheels resting on the island foot- path. When the defendant swerved he seemed to have put on his brake, but it was too late, and owing to the dangerous speed at which be was travelling, he was unable to pull up, and the sad fatality was the result. At that particular time of the evening it was the busiest time of the day for that portion of the promenade. The conduct of the defendant in driving at that speed seemed without any excuse at all. When be passed the North Pier he ought to have seen a motor warning signal, " Drive slowly," on the edge of the island footpath, and he must have noticed the crowd pouring out of the Palace and Tower. He seemed to have thought that so long as be blew his horn he was entitled to go on at that speed. Having regard to the reriousneas of the affair, the Chief Con- stable had no alternative but to bring it before the Bench, and his instructions were if the care was proved, to ask the magistrates not only to fine the defendant,but to suspend his licence and see that he should not obtain another for such a period as they thought fit. Ilubert Beswick, assistant treasurer at the Tower, gave corroborative evidence. That part of the promenade was very busy at the time, and, in his opinion, the driver could have parsed the people on the east side of the road.

Witness, further questioned, said that if the man bad swerved the other way he might have run into the deceased's companions. Lie, however, did not think the case would have been brought to court but for the accident.

Robert Lioney, a pugilist, said he saw the car zig- zagging opposite the Palace, and the driver seemed to have lost control. The car was travelling at from 16 to 20 miles an hour, and there was danger to other people besides the deceased. itness admitted to Mr Jackson that he did not notice the people crossing the promenade until after the accident occurred. _

Joseph Johnson, cabdriver, said the car was going at any speed up to 20 miles en hour. Mr Jackson, for the defence, appealed to the Bench not to be prejudiced by the accident itself. lie con- tended that the girl lost her head, and did what many other people did, put down her head and rushed into danger. The defendant, he argued, took every pre- caution to avoid knocking her down. Be would not put the defendant in the box, or call any witnesses. 1 The magistrates retired, and on returning into Court, 1 Alderman Fish said they bad decided to convict, and would like to know the defendant's record. _

The Chief Constable stated that in May, 1906, for obstruction with a motor car, Outwin was fined 40s. and costs ; in February, 1908, for driving a car in a manner dangerous to the public, 20s. and costs; in September, 1908, for a similar Offence, £5 and costs ;

in October 1908, failing to produce license, 10s. and Costs; April, 1910, driving motor car at speed exceeding 20 miles an hour, .£5 and costs ; April, 1910, driving to danger of the public, £lO, including costs; and in October, 1911, for recklessly driving motor oar, 40s. and costs.

Mr Jackson pointed out flat defendant was travelling over 11,000 miles a sear on accom t or his business. Alderman Fish said the Bench imposed a Bite of RIO and costs, In default two months, and defendant's licence would be suspended fer two years.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
THE CELESTIALS.

On Thursday evening our Baptist friends met at the Latchford Church in the interests of their great Missionary Society, and had specially under considera- tion the claims of China. It is as rare for me to com- ment upon such an incident as it is for the public at large to greatly c ,ncern themselves about foreign missions in general. On the whole the Church even at home is somewhat lax and indifferent in relation to such work. Yet it is incontrovertible that the Church's interest in her stations and agents abroad is a fair and reliable test of her spiritual vitality and fidelity. On Thursday, as intimated, one of these self-sacrificing representatives told the story of his society's enterprise in China, and, of course, barrated some highly interesting personal experiences. We laugh st John Chinaman's habits and customs ; it seldom occurs to us that he may well think many of our ordinary everyday ways absurdly peculiar. Be would not tell us so, neither would he betray amusement or surprise, for he is by nature studiously polite. Again, we ridicule the Chibese fear of dragons and evil spirits and weird notions of many things; still, some very foolish super- stitions linger in our very midst. However, my object for the moment is mainly to acknowledge the good influence exercised and the excellent work consis- tently wrought in the dark places of the earth by such men as the one who has this week so forcefully appealed to local congregations on behalf of the Baptist Mission Society. The world is steadily shrinking under the civilb.ing influences of the ever-increasing means of inter-communication ; trade and commerce and travel are doing much to inform and bring the nations into more intimate and desirable relations; but the missionary must have the credit of the pioneer and the pilot, and those who either actually deride or are cold and indifferent s ) far as he is concerned are pardonable only in so far as ignorance may be an excuse for so mistaken an attitude. THE MAYORAL PURSE.

At the last meeting of the Warrington Town Council for the year, speakers to the customary vote of courtesy to the Mayor remarked upon the way in which one or other is everlastingly tugging at his Worship's purse-strings In Warrington, as in many boroughs, it has somehow come to be assumed that the holder for the time being of the highest office with 'which it is possible for the burgesses to honour a fellow-cir zen must be prepared in return to "shell out "at the call of all and sundry. I happened once to be stationed in a district when a charter of incor- poration was obtained. The first Mayor was a wealthy man who was prepared to do things handsomely all round, and after three years of banquets and other costly enteitainments, he was succeeded for a similar period by another rich person who was equally ready to treat folk on a lavish scale. The third member of the Council who was called to the p %Rion said be would so proceed that it would be thereafter possible for the poorest of his fellow-mem- bers to occupy it. There were no more big dinners and fashionable receptions. We bad a thoroughly capable and altogether excellent Mayor, but, beyond opening a bazaar now and then, he atanded no outside functions of a character calculated to make undue demands upon his ptivate purse. Such has been the rule in that borough ever since. When Sir Ryland Adkins, M.P. for the Middleton Division—a Liberal fort wh'ch is to he attacked by the Tories under the leadership of Mr B S Townroe—was first invited to represent that constitu- ency, he had a distinct understanding on this very point, accepting with the stipulation that he should not be expected either to attend or to contribute to anything that was outside the mope of his political duties. The conditions have been strictly and honour- ably observed, and the member is decidedly the most popular of his line there. CAUTION AS TO GUNS.

The sad accident whereby Mr. Arthur Peacock was so seriously injured at Barmouth, as reported in these columns a week ago, suggests the reproduction of a few words of warning which I once penned in view of the grouse season. One would hardly expect any experienced gunner to need anything of the kind, but the tyro may be reminded of the piincipal rules to he observed. Should he have occasion to lay aside his gun for a while, he should invariably first draw the cartridges ; even if, when near a wall, he happens to I relax his hold upon it, for a few moments only, he should be careful to place it in the angle of the wall, and not simply to rear the weapon against it—an unfortunately too prevalent habit, but always attended by risk. True, the danger is not nearly so serious as it was in the old days of percussion caps, and so on; in the steady evaution of the gun, the parts which used with good reason to cause anxiety have been eliminated or very anpreciably modified; all the same, it requires careful handling, and in this important particular the beainner should cultivate the habit of carrying his gun so as to ensure the absolute safety of himself and all about him. Even when these precautions have been observed, the responsibilities of the man with the gun are by no means at an end. That is plain from what has happened to the unfortunate Mr. Peacock.

"BUSHELS OF CATS." The American story as to these, quoted by: "Uncle Caleb" in last Saturday's "Examiner," reminded me of a very similar instance that came under my own notice when I lived in Yorkshire. An enterprising Yankee firm of dealers in rolled oats went so far with their advertising projects as to desecrate the local landscape in hideous and scandalous fashion. One particularly aggravating and inexcusable example consisted of an inscription on an eminent landmark in tremendous whitewash characters exhorting the beholders to " Eat-- oats." So far as this awful monstrosity was concerned " beholder " and "community "were synonymous terms, for there was no getting away from the wonderful and horrible thing without leaving the district. Soon, however, some bold and resourceful joker stole up under cover of the darkness, armed with a bucket of tar and a big brush, and blotted out enough of the first letter in "oats " to make it read " cats." Killed by ridicule, the hated thing was promptly interred, and there was no resurrection. DANCING. In an article in the " Pall Mall Magazine," a while ago Mr. Theodore Kosloff argued that, bringing as it does every muscle into play, dancing conduces enor- mously to health. Long, long before that, Charming wrote :—" This exercise is among the most healthful. The body as well as the mind feels its most gladdenning influence. No amusement seems more to have a foundation in our nature. The animation of youth overflows spontaneously in harmonious movements The true idea of dancing entitles it to favour. Its end is to realise perfect grace in motion, and who does not know that a tense of the graceful is one of the higher faculties of our nature ?" As Jack Bunsby says, the healing of these observations lies in the application. The moral is that the reader should turn to tho front page of this paper, pick out the advertisements respecting forthcoming balls, and read, mark, learn, and inwardlf digest the same. LITTLE SLIPS.

- --- The. 'subject of printers' errors cropped up in the " Children's Corner ' a week afro. It is a fruitful ' theme, and one might continue it until further orders. ' Some time ago, in a paragraph in this column, I referred to "the ancient command to be fruitful and multiply "—or intended so to do, but my hand-writing being far from good, the compositor re:dered it "to be faithful and multiply." Feeling that my own defect had caused my fellow-worker to stumble, I thought it well at the time to "lay low and say nuffin." Af'er all, it was a mere bagatelle compared with the achievements of certain contemporaries that might be mentioned. I have already had occasion to refer to Middleton as a constituency upon which a Warrington Tory who is ambitious to enter Parliament has set covetous eyes, and not very long before that gentleman's advent a local paper produced the follow- ing gem :—" In the afternoon a service was held in the church, when a sermon was delivered by the Rev C Brown, DI)., president of the National Council. Ile took as his text the words, 'I suggested Appolos water and God gave the increase '(first epistle of St. Paul to the Corinthians, iii, 0)." I am glad to think that there is nobody on the " Examiner" staff who can come within miles of that. The one who failed to recognise ray Old Testament quotation might perhaps like to look this up in the New.

FARMERS AS INSURANCE RESISTERS. Two prominent Berkshire farmers, Mr George Adams, of Fernbam, and Mr George Baylis, president of the Berkshire Resisters' League, were convicted at Faring don on Tuesday for refusing to stamp the cards of their workmen. Mr Adams was fined £lO on one case, and other penalties were deferred for a fortnight. Mr Baylis was convicted, but the penalties were deferred.
The Examiner, Saturday, November 2, 1912.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Buckingham Palace.— Buckingham Palace, the London residence of the Sovereign, is never thrown open to the public for inspection, in the same way as the state rooms of Windsor Castle. All that the general public see of it, is the facade, which is really the back of the building, cverlooking St. James's Park. The garden front, presenting a fine example of Georgian architec- ture, is screened by the eater sive grounds, which extend to over fifty acres, but n glimpse of it may be obtained from the top of omnibuses, passing down Grosvenor- place, when tle foliage is off the trees. When Q ien Victoria first went to reside there in 1837, the Palace had cost the country nearly a million of money and since then , Parliament has voted large sums for its improvement. At oce time the Marble Arch, since romoved to Hyde Park, formed the main entrance. The somewhat dinzy aspect which the Palace presents to the world, is sadly out of harmony as a background to the magnificent Victoria Memorial, and it is next sesr to be givens new facade, of classical design, in portland stone. Sir Aston Webb's plans for this purpose have not escaped criticism, but the scheme of improvement will at least give the Palace a more stately and imposing appearance, Women's First Calling.—The Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress of London, recently received at the Mansion House, a party of French engineers on a visit to this country, to study our methods of sanitary work, and among them was a French woman, who is a certifi- cated plumber, glazier and satitary engineer. Then we are told, that women have been employed in America as conductors of tramcars, railway guards, and also as policewomen. Daniel Defoe declared that women were In every way capable of the same accomplishments as men, but it Is only now—two hundred years later, that they are beginning to prove it. Whilst however, women are every where distinguishing themselves in professional commercial and industrial pursuits, Lady Esher thinks thlt they should all become practical cooks. She is greatly interested in voluntary ambulance corps work, for which a knowledge of plain cooking is a very important qualification. With this object mainly in view, she has organised a series of practical cooking classes, at the Polytechnic Annexe in London. It, of course, requires more than a few lessons, even of a practical kind, before a duchess or a countess can expect to become a " good plain cook," but even a little knowledge of this kind is very useful, especially to those who undertake helpful social work among the poor.

Ifoop-Trundling.—lt is not very long since the medical profession was warmly recommending skipping —especially to the middle-aged and " livery." So many skips before breakfast, so many before lunch, and so many before dinner. This craze did not last long, the remedy in many instances being found worse than the disease. Now, hoop•trundling is set forth as one of the healthiest among exercises, but alas this cannot be indulged In so privately as the skipping idea. It would require considerable courage and nerve in the " middle-aged and livery," to be seen trundling a hoop along the public road or even round and round an ordirary everyday garden, and the majority of seekers after childish exercises will probably after all, prefer the once much-boomed "skip "or even battledoor and shuttlecock.

New Watches.—Once upon a time, the watch of five- shilling-piece dimension was the usual thing. Then slowly, but surely, it grew smaller and smaller, until vanishing point was very nearly reached—and the tiny watch was no longer a novelty. Then came the filbert- shaped watch, with the narrow dial, like a plaque, and the numerals marked in groups, instead of at the properly regulated intervals—which meant learning to tell the time in a new way. Now, ready for Christmas —and elastic purses—comes the " bunch of ribbons watch," which looks like a ribbon bow, the narrow strands being composed of coloured gems,and diamonds. Ile Coat of Gems.—The price of pearls and diamonds is still rising, and at the present time ti-ey cost nearly twice as much again as they did a decade ago. This state of affairs has caused coloured gems to come very much to the fore, but here again a considerable rise in price is reported. Still the imperounious need not des- pair for more and more desirable good ornaments con- tain imitation gems, while bead ornaments are the last word in all that is charming and artistic. It is little short of marvellous what n delightful effect may be gained by a necklace of beads matching Of blending with a simple toilette.

The Price of Ermine.—Ermine is very much used for trimmings of all sorts, hats, dresses, muffs, begs, Stc., and the smallest pieces may be joined in string and used. Many families have all kinds of things in the way of dress stored away and forgotten. It is quite worth while to search among these for odd pieces of ermine. They may have changed colour, but several applications of magnesia will bleach them effectually. In comparison with other costly furs, ermine is less expensive this winter than some four or five years ago ; it is said that the big houses overstocked for the coronation, hence the lower price. It is a charming fur when new, but it soon spoils in a big town. This year the tails are not placed at intervals on the fur, but are used to form a fringe or stole, necklet or muff.

The Ever-Popular Blouse.—Fashions come and fashions go, but the blouse remains. Every season we hear that its day is done, that it is doomed, that it is dead, but it turns out that it is more popular than ever. The present season has proved no exception to this rule, and dressmakers are devoting more time and atten- tion to this garment than ever before. The basqued blouse of the past summer is still very much worn, with a slight difference, viz., the hasques are somewhat longer. Very often the basquo is attached to the skirt, although it appears to be a part of the blouse itself. A sash hides the division quite effectively. Even with a coat and skirt,the choice of a blouse is most important, for it his to he relied upon to give individuality and distinction to the tailored suit. The Return of Covert Coating.—Next spring is some way off, or seems so now, therefore it is rather early to predict with certainty that a particular material or style will be popular. But it is quite safe to say that covert coating will have a vogue in the coming year. It always loos smart and neat, and no cloth wears better; in this respect even serge cannot beat it, there- fore its return to favour is a matter for congratulation to those desiring durable materials. Shoes for Day and Evening Wear.—There can be no doubt that the temptingly pretty shoes to be seen in all the good shops have had much to do with the continued popularity of the short skirt. In form, style,and decora- tion, there is endless variety and modish women have different shoes for each toilette. Some outdoor shoes have varnished toes,and uppers of suede or soft doeskin with two straps across the instep—and these button at the side. Others are entirely of varnished leather, or of suede. Coloured kid shoes in red, brown, grey,green, or navy, are also much worn. Evening shoes are of the loveliest brocade, adorned with jewelled buckles, set on finely pleated tulle, lace, or satin, in the shape of a rosette. Many buckles ars valuable, and are priced at as much as forty or fifty pounds, for they are studded with brilliants. These rosettes, instead of being placed as hitherto in front of the slipper, are fastened at the side. Old-fashioned buckles are very frequently I by the fortunate folks who own them for theinty shoes. used dainty

div.head: LANCASHIRE AND GERMANY.
div.p: LANCASHIRE AND GERMANY.
A Great Task.

Addressing the four or five hundred Lancashire men assembled in the Hotel Cecil on Monday night for the annual smoking concert of the London Lancastrian Society, Sir Thomas Barclay made a notable appeal for better relations with Germany. " Reference," he said, "has been made to my con- neetion with the bringing about the Entente with France. But I can tell you this; there would have been no Entente with France to-day but for Lancashire. It was in Lancashire that the movement really began ; it was there that the first response came to the over - tures from Paris." The explanation was that the people of Lancashire thought independently ;they had a manly way of coupling thought with action. They thcught it right that there should be friendship with France, and as a consequence friendship resulted. There is another great piece of work for Lanca- shire now," Sir Thomas Barclay continued. "We believe that our French friendship is eternal, that we shall never go back to the days of the French scare. There was a time, not bug past, when the French menace was made the fashionable bogey.' Even in 1889 there was an attempt to work up a French invasion scare. The same people are now at work engineering a German scare. We know something of the Germans in Lancashire, and particularly in Man- che.ter. We know that there are no better business men, and when they settle among us we have no better citizens. Lancashire thus has a 'peat task, and lam sure that she will perform it as she did before." (Cheers).

div.head: FIRST AID TO THE INJURED.
div.p: FIRST AID TO THE INJURED.
COMPETITION FOR THE CROSFIELD
AMBULANCE SHIELD.

"First aid to the injured." The phrase represents such a commonplace of every day life that we hardly realize what we owe to the St. John Ambulance Brigade for ensuring the efficiency of this important humanitarian work. Warrington has long been worthily identified with the movement and Messrs Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., have done a great deal to stimulate the interest and enthusiasm of the brigade members by presenting a challenge shield for competition among the various corps in the North-Western District, which is the strongest in the whole of the Brigade. The annual contest for this trophy took place in Messrs Crosfield's assembly room on Saturday afternoon, when ton teams were subjected to viva voce and practical tests by Dr Pooloy. the district chief surgeon, and Assistant Commissioner Garnett, of Burnley, respec- tively. After an exceptionally keen competition, llonNich succeeded in winning the shield for the third year in succession, by a single point. Crompton, who have been awarded the shield on four occasions, were placed second,and Warrington secured the third position Only two points sepsrated first. and third. The scores were :—Horwich, 169 points ; Cromptor, 168 points ; Warrington, 167 points. Other teams which competed were :—Burnley, 156; Nelson, 152; Stockport, 115; Tyldesley, 107 ; Stalybridge, 102; Whitfield, 96 ; and Prestwich, 85.

Excellent arrangements for the competition had been made by Superintendent Hose,of the Crestleld Division, assisted by First Officer Cawley. Among others present were Colonel Trimble (deputy commissioner of the dis- trict), Mr A E Spann (the Secretary to the Head- quarters Division) and First Officer Williams

Councillor H ROBERTS distributed the prizes and said it was a source of pride that out of 20,000 members of the Brigade in the United Kingdom, the North Western district comprised considerably over 4,000 and out of the total number of ambulance men present at the Royal Review some months ago that district sent two men to every one from any other district in the kingdom. What appealed to him in connection with that association was the fact that they stood for a keener recognition of the personal responsibility of the individual to his fellows in matters of social service. The principle underlying the formation of that Brigade and its prime motive was a magnificent one. He wished them in their noble work God speed, prosperity and success. They were, he hoped, all men of humanitarian senti- ments and patriots. The sentiment that had brought that association into existence appealed in another direction. They were all patriots, but what was the good of a patriot who could not shoot? He thought, without in any sense or degree subscribing to the alarmist speech of the revered head of his clan in Manchester, or anywhere else, that it was their duty, if they were men of patriotic sentiments to be pre- pared at any time or undei any circumstances to give a good account of themselves, and do what they ought to do as trained men. (Applause). Colonel TRIMBLE voiced the thanks of the brigade to Messrs Crosfield for their continued generosity. He bad always appreciated the work of the National Service League and agreed with the remarks of Coun- cillor Roberts. The men of the Ambulance Brigade had set the nation a very high example indeed. The help given by the Brigade to the country was demonstrated in the South African War. Ile had received several applications from men who wished to go out to the Balkans as ambulance men. Up to now the Order of St John had not decided to send men out, but the Red Cross Society were doing 53, and men who wished to go out should apply to him for leave of abserce. (Applause.) First Officer CAWLEY seconded the vote of thanks to the Arm.
Councillor ROBERTS replied. A vote of thanks was accorded to Colonel rrimble on the proposition of Superintendent ROSE, seconded by Sergeant NEWNS.

div.head: APPEAL TO LIBERAL CHURCEINIEN.
div.p: APPEAL TO LIBERAL CHURCEINIEN.

Alderman P. W. lia flan, M.P. for Leigh, opening a Liberal bazaar at Golborne on Saturday, said the agita- tion against Welsh Disestablishment was absolutely polit;cil in its character. Those who desired to continue the present State connection were purely members of the Conservative party Alio were interested in main- taining their opposition t,) the Liberal party. An appeal w‘s being made to Liberal Churchmen to desert their party. He asked Liberal Churchmen to consider that the Liberal Churchmen in Wales, who knew the conditions best, were an unbroken force behind the Liberal Government on that question. He challenged any of their opponents to point to any Welsh Church- man of distinction who had detached himself from tbe Liberal party upon that question.

div.head: RED CROSS SOCIETY.
div.p: RED CROSS SOCIETY.
Inspection at Grappenhall.

The first annual inspection of the Local Voluntary Aid Detachment (Cheshire 22, as registered at the War Office), took place last week at Grappenhall Hall, by permission of Mr and Mrs Frost. The billiard room was arranged as a temporary hospital, and the necessary appliances were prepareed by Mrs Frost and Nurse Callender. The inspecting officer was Major Grech, who expressed his satisfaction with the efficiency or the members of the detachment ; with their answers to his interesting and searching questions ; and with the way in which they bandaged the small boys, who were there to represent the wounded in time of war. Dr Bower, of Stretton, who is the commandant, tied who has devoted endless time and energy to the train" ing of his detachment of women, was present with e large number of members, including Mrs Aylmer Frost, quartermaster, and Nurse Callender, - lady superintew dent. The members looked very smart in their white aprons with the red cross, rnd their neat white ners. Major Sidebotham, county director, was also present at the inspection. The detachment has been drawn from the DaresburY Division of the Cheshire Branch of the 13.11.C.5. Were has been going on in this division two or three years to qualify women, by passing both first-aid and nursing examinations, to form a voluntary aid detachment. Much interest has been shown in the townships of, Grappenhall, Latchfovd and Stretton, and it is hopen that Stockton Heath and Dareslawy will follow suit /37 holding classes in first-aid end nursing. The Red Croon Society is a county organisation, and its object is .te fill in the gaps left by the St John Ambulance Assocto" tioo, the excellence of which it thoroughly appreciates, but in no way to work in opposition. The two ar°, parallel societies, the only difference being that the Hen Cross detachments are under the War Office and .are trained for home nursing only, in case of invamoni though they are free to volunteer for foreign service, as is seen by the departure of several men's detach' meets for the war in the B liken States. Mrs Aylmer Frost was the first to organise the Daresbury Division and to be its vie-president, under the Duchess of Westminster. Miss Sylvia Broadbent has accepted this position on Mrs Frost's resignation, and Miss Mabel Fairclough is hon. secretary. The Division is divided into townships with a lady oe township leader and a committee. Nursing classes are now being held in Latchford, and invalid cooker/ classes have just been concluded in Grappenhall. .14 course of first-aid lectures will probably be held la Stockton Heath during the winter.

div.head: GIFTS TO SIR GILBERT AND LADY GREENALL.
div.p: GIFTS TO SIR GILBERT AND LADY GREENALL.
Appreciation of the Belvoir Hunt.

Sir Gibert Greene'', Bart., who severed his oonnee' tion with the Belvoir Hunt at the end of last seasoo. after being Mester for Hi years, was on Saturday, Grantham, the recipient of his portrait in oils by NU' Oswald Birley. The portrait had been subscribed for by members and followers of the Hunt, as a mark of appreciation of the excellent sport he had invariably shown. Lady Greenall received a diamond bracelet, and Ben Capel, who acted as huntsman during Sir Gilbert's mastership, was presented with a cheque for £BOl. .

The Duke of Rutland, the owner of the Beivoir Hounds, in making the presentations, said Sir Gilbert had succeeded in winbing the full confidence of ell Ocoee connected with the Hunt, and he had been able to keep the pack up to that high level which it was under- stood throughout the world to have reached. Neither the Duke's late father nor he had had the faintest feel; iug of uncertainty in respect of matters whizh passe' between Sir Gilbert and themselves, and throughout those long years there bad been a feeling of ccoficlenc? and knowledge that everything was going right. gir Gilbert had proved himself to be a true friend „t;1 fartutrs and occupiers of land, and Lady Greene"; voice lad always been taised to aid and assist them en prevent damage to crops. Sir Gilbert Greenall, in returning thanks said i ' t 1181 been a great gratification to him to know that he ?s: been able to keep up and maintain the very lugl standard of the Belvoir Hounds not.only in the but on the flag. That had been almost entirely due tv the hard work put in and excellent judgment used by 13IS huntsman, Cape!. Lady Greenall also returned thanks, and Cape,t is expressing his thanks, said that to be the huntsman t's the Belvoir was the proudest place a huntsman con fill.

LIDERAT. MEETING.—OPENING of' THE SESSION.— The Lymm Liberal Association opened their winter session with a public meeting in the Congregational schoolroom on Thursday night. Mr 3D B Smith was in the chair and in his addreEs he eulogised the National Insurance Act and spoke of the weakening opposition towards it. Speaking about the present feeling that is being shown in the country's relation to Germany, he condemned Lord Robert's speech in which his Lordship spoke of war as being inevitable, and he (Mr Smith) said that it was his belief that legislation could best bring about a better feeling between the two nations and he pleaded for support on such grounds. The speaker for the evening was Mr 'l' Worthington,of Wigan, who said that be supported Mr Smith's remarks re Germany. He said that though Liberals were feeling pleased with the success of their Government they in Lyrnm must not forget that the Parliamentary repre- sentative for this Division was of contrary views to their own and they should strive to have their opinions represented in the House of Parliament. He then gave a resume of the work of the party since they came into power in 1006. He first mentioned the great success of the Liberals in reducing the National Debt, and expressed his hope that it would ultimately be lessened to nil. He next refered to the advance in the free feeding of poor school children. His third point dealt with the Old Age Pensions the ridicule that the Tories had made of it and their desire to have it made so that people could only buy it on the principles of an annuity ; and then proved what a great blessing the Act had been by citing several cases of its beneficial operation that he had personally come in contact with. Poverty and the efforts of the Government to diminish it," came next and he showed that poverty often came from 1, sickness and 2, unemployment. With regard to unemployment, the Liberal party had made a big advance towards its abolition by forming and working the Labour Exchanges, so that if there was no work in one town to be found for a man on their list, efforts were made to get him work in some town near by, and he gave a good example on the point. As for sickness' the National Insurance Act will become a means of endowment to many. The sanatoria benefits were of inestimable value themselves. He said that out of the 75,000 consumptive persons who died in one year it was believed that by proper treatment 7 out of 8 could be cured, and it was his

prayer that this healing might quickly come to pass He gave the example of what tnis treatment would mean to Manchester and said that be had heard that it will ultimately save the ratepayers £40,00C per year. He also demonstrated the improvement that the maternity benefits will bring about. "This is what the Liberal Government have done so far and what are they going to do now ?" The highest gift you can give to a country is a good constitution, and that is what they are trying to do for Ireland." He spoke at length on the bubject and showed how that Irishmen had to emigrate to free countries because their own country, though so fertile, was denied them. If this was the case under existing conditions, then let us try Home Rule and see if that would not improve matters. He quoted the value of Home Rule as shown by that of the Routh African Government. "England, we are often told by our Tory friends, is going to the dogs." "Is that so "No ?" He then referred to the flourishing conditions that now exist in the coal mining, cotton and woollen manufacturing industries. He declared that the fact of our being able to grant loaus to Argentine and China proved that our finances were in a good condition. • Another great thing their party had on their pro- gramme was Disestablishment of the Church.in Wales." He dwelt on the value of Disestablishment and men-
tioned the fact that Disestablishment had not killed the Irish Church but had on the other .hand strengthened . . . .

it. Electoral Reforms, and especially in relation to plural voting were promised them by their party. The land question was also to come up for treat- ment by this Government. He said that we ought to be prouder of belonging to a party that had done so much good work and he desired that full confidence should still be placed with them. (Applluse). Mr. G. L. Welford in proposing a vote of thanks declared himself (amid applause) to he an earnest supporter of the Home Rule, Disestablistonent, Scotch Veto, and Land Measures, and he hoped that the Government would continue their work fearlessly. Mr. R. Barker seconded the resolution and it was carried with acclamation. Mr. Worthington responded and a vote of thanks to the Chairman was also passed.

div.p: PADGATE.

WESLEY GUlLD.—There was a good attendance at the weekly meeting of the Guild on Monday evening. The Rev E Morgan presided. The Rev A M Mitchell, of Buttonwood, gave a very interesting address on 'Alcohol and Eugenics." The annual visit of the redoubtable vicar has become quite an event in the Guild Syllabus, and a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded him on the proposition of Mr Newton seconded by Mr Birchen.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONARY SOCIETY.— In connection with the above society, the Peaketh branch held their annual meeting on Tuesday evening in the Chapel. The meeting was presided over by Mr J G Withinshaw, supported by the Revs J Gunnell and H sliddlewood. The speaker for the occasion was the Rev J Edwin Reeves,of the Foreign Missionary Society. He told an interesting story of his Missionary work in British Bechuanaland amongst the Swazi Tribes and said how much they were in need of more workers, especially medioal Missionaries. The Rev J Gunnell save—as is usual in anything he undertakes—a roost interesting report in connection with the local branch. The report for 1911 was the 95th annual report of the Auxiliary Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society for the Liverpool District for 1911 from all souices is £9,503 8s 10d, a decease of £l7l is 11d. But taking into consideration the extra £l9B Is fid collected at the Synod in 1910 and the Newtown contribution of £3O us Id, now credited to the first North Wales District there was an increase of £57 4s 10d Contributions from Penketh : Collections, £lB 4594 ; subscriptions, etc., £l7 us 103 ; Christmas offerings, £1 3i sd; total, £67 decrease on 1910, £8 15s 7d ; but the women's auxiliary banded in £7 83 3d and so reduced this deficiency making the grand total for Penketh £74 Bs. 3d. Special reference was made by Mr Gunnell to the work and interest that the late Mrs Garnett took in Foreign Missions and mentioned the fact that 50 years ago when he first came into the Warrington Circuit that Mrs Garnett was one of the subscribers then and was also one in the report this year. The Chairman in his remarks made special referencl to the work the late Mrs Garnett had done for those on the foreign field. Rev H Middlewood also took part in the service. Miss Mary Watson presided at the organ. Special hymns were sung and the collections amounted to over £l3 an increase on last year. Miss Parker, Penketh Lodge, is the kcal secretary.

div.head: PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: PARISH COUNCIL.
In connection with the above a special meeting was held on Tuesday last in the Council schools, Stocks-lane to further consider the attempted closing of
THE FOOTPATH AT FIDLER'S FERRY.

The meeting was poorly attended, only 3 out of 7 being present. Mr R Routledge presided, and there were also present Messrs William Davies, James, Wood- ward and Mr E Foster (clerk). The Chairman said the matter in question was one of great importance to the neighoourhood and he hoped they would be able to find out what further steps they could take. Mr Woodward emphasised the importance of the footpath in question and suggested that if the Council let Captain M Hughes close this one be would perhaps close others after wards. He said he had received information to thoeffeot that they as a Parish Council, could only refer it to the District Council. Mr Woodward moved the following resolution to be forwarded to the District Council. That the Clerk send the correspondence between himself and Captain Michael Hughes relating to the closing of the footpath at Fidler's Ferry with the request that they take the necessary action to protect the interests of the public and to express the Parish Council's strong disapproval of the closing of this right of way." Mr Davies seconded and the motion was carried.

ALTERATION TO STATION ROAD. Mr DAVIES proposed the following resolution that C onsidering then. is now proceeding a rearrange- ment of the fencing along the east side of the road. this Council seek the opportunity of approach- ing the landowner and the London and North- Western Railway Co. with a view of making a much needed improvement by rounding off the very dangerous corner opposite Mr Ditchfield's two cottages. —Mr Woodward seconded.—The Chairman in support- ing it said he was very pleased Mr Davies had pointed this out. They should not miss this opportunity of having it attended to.—Carried.

div.p: MR. AND MRS. A. H. CROSF/ELD AND A GROUP OF OFFICIALS.

feeling sure that the work of the mission was worthy of the acceptance of the neighbourhood—Applause— £3oo had been mentioned as a desirable sum to aim at and he hoped they would be able to raise that amount. Mr Tilling paid a tribute to the self-sacrificing labours of the ladies who bad diposed of coupons for goods to the amount of £llO, the management of this enterprize necessitating at least 8,000 visits to the homes of the contributors. (Applause). Mr A H CROSFI EL D, who had a hearty reception, said he had perused the annual report which was splendidly encouraging reading all through. Going back to the initiation of the work of the mission, in the days referred to by Mr. Joseph Monks, be often recalled what his father used frequently to say—that never in his life had he spent money in any way that had given him as much real pleasure and satisfaction as the money devoted to the mission at Bank Quay. (Applause.) The seedEOWLI in those days had fallen on very good ground and bad borne fruit, thanks to the faithful, earnest and noble work, so unostent.tiously carried out, with a sincere desire for the good of their fellow men and women, by those who were responsible for the „maintenance of the mission. He could assure them that none felt more whole- hearted gratification at the magnificent progress of the work, ever since it was founded, than Mrs Crosfield of Colwyn Bay—(applause)—and the labours of 'Which the Workingmen's Mission was the centre shodld excite the deepest admiration of all well-wishers of the district. He was convinced that the democratic chrteacter of the control and management (upon which stress was laid in the annual report) and the very human character of the services had been important elements in the prosperity of the mission and that the humanity of the Christian Gospel preached there was another leading reason for its success. He was particularly impressed by a passage in the report which called attention to the declaration of a great statesman: "It is the duty of every Church, of whatever creed or denomination, to bring to bear the searchlight of truth upon the cesspools of vice, misery, poverty and wretchedness which are so common in our laud, and to keep the searchlight upon the evils until no statesman, of whatever party, will be able to overlook the great clamouring that will arise from the evils to be swept from our midst." (Applause.) Know- ing bow much the Workingmen's Mission was doing in that direction, and how steadily it was striving for social amelioration, it afforded his wife and himself the deepest pleasure to do any little thing they could to contribute to the successful realization of their present object, and their satisfaction was increased by the knowledge that they were being of some assistance to Mrs. Crostield, of Colwyn Bay, who had the welfare of the mission so closely at heart. (Applause). Mrs A H FIELD, who was also cordially greeted, said she felt very proud to be there and to act as deputy for ens who stood so high in the esteem and affection of all present and, in fact, of everybody in Warrington. Although she could never hope adequately to replace Mrs Crostleld, she bad still le-s hope of doing so that day, because she was animated by sentiments which were quite unworthy and which she vas sure none of them had ever felt wicked enough to entertain. (Laughter.) She was afraid she had been breaking the Tenth Corumandment—(laughter)-T;for when she looked round the stalls and saw so many articles of clothing she , could not help wishing that some of them might find their way to relieve the tragic suffering which was going on in the Balkans and clothe some of the poor little children and refugees who were flocking into the towns. Most of her hearers would doubtless have been following the war with anxioua interest—(besr, bear)—and they would have read of the horrors which had been perpetrated daily. To her the conflict was of special interest, not merely because of the national reeling which she had, but especially because it was a struggle of Christianity and humanity against the most fanatical kind of oppre-

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

SANKEY CITORAL SOCIETY.—On Friday of last week the above society had an interesting whist drive and dance at the Sankey Sunday School, when there were over HO present. The dancing commenced at 8 p.m. and continued till 130 a.m. Games of whist taking place in the meantime in one of the smaller rooms. The following were whiners of the whist drive :—Ladies : Mrs R Foster, Mrs J Ray ; consolation, Miss Jones. Gents : Messrs T Ray, S Tunstall ; consolation, Percy Fair., The Bros Ray were in charge of the musical part of the evening's programme and gave every satisfaction. MOORE. WEISLEY GUILD.—A pleasant evening was spent on Weduesday last in the schoolroom on the occasion of the opening social of the session. The programme consisted of a short musical entertainment which was opened by a pianoforte solo by Miss Basnett, songs by Miss Ethel Done, Miss Ruth Tanner and Miss Alice Millington and recitations by Miss Dutton and Miss Ruth Tanner. The competition caused much enthusiasm and amusement. The musical guessing competition.was won by Miss Tanner, and the gentleman's button stitching competition by Mr Horace Wilkinson. The committee were very energetic in trying to make the social a success,qight refreslaments were provided during the interval. New games were introduced which proved a great success. The proceedings were ably presided over by Ito Rev. 11. Middlewood.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

A YOUNG INCORRIGIBLE. At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, Harry Walters (20), collier, pleaded guilty to stealing half a sovereign in Widnes in September. Mr. Singleton informed the court that the prisoner after being five years in a reformatory had subsequently been convicted, And sentenced under the Borstal system. Apparently nothing could be done to reform him. Prisoner was sentenced to Biz months' bard labour.

WIDNES GAS CRITICS. At, the Widnes Town Council, held on Tuesday, Alderman Smith, on the highway minutes, suggested that all workmen in the employ of the Corporation should have the week's holiday in place of the annual excursion.

The matter was referred for further consideration. The recent outcry about the quality of gas again caused much discursioh. Alderman Smith championed the committee, and said the had been was quite up to standard, but the engineer ad been hampered with a large accumulation of napthalene in the pipes. Councillor Miller said the lighting in varione parts of the town was bad, and some of tbe lights he had personally inspected were like glowworms on a pedestal. They were told that the world possessed seven great wonders. Widnes contributed an eighth in the cheapest gas on earth, and he wondered as the ninth how the people had Mood its poor quality so long. Alderman Smith, in reply, said the gas was efficient and up to the proper standard. They suffered as other towns from the presence of napthalene. lie was sorry that the undertaking, which was a prosperous one, and one which was the envy of others, should receive so many rebuffs from t heir own peopie. The engineer had kept strict watch over the matter, which had cropped up in a severe form.

FUNERAL OF MR. J. MAY, ST. HELENS. The service was conducted by the Rev T E Barron-Renton. I.lr SY Hatton (Chairman of the Com- mittee of Management of the Royal Liver Society) was present.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL EFFORT AT THE WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL EFFORT AT THE WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.
Mrs. A. H. Crosfield and the War In the Balkans.

Beautified by an artistic scheme of floral decora- tions, the schoolroom at the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, is at present the scene of an exceptionally attractive bazaar. Each stall has its distinctive flower and the general effect produced by the array of rosos, clematis, chrysanthemums, daffodil's and many other choice blooms—remarkably good imitations of nature's handiwork—is harmonious and pleasibg to the eye. The ever-expanding work of the mission' has made another addition to the accommodation absolutely necessary, and it is hoped by the bazaar to raise £3OO for the extension of the chapel which is unfortunately crowded at the Sunday evening services. The members of tbe congregation have taken up the project with great enthusiam and the large attendance at the opening ceremony on Thursday angured well for a complete relization of their ambition. The stalls were in charge of a baud of willing workers, under the direction of No fpllowing : Congregation and Society Class : Mrs John Hassel (treasurer), Mrs Brimelow (secretary). Women's Bible Class: Mrs T "raylor (treasurer), Mrs Barratt (secretary). Young Ladies' Bible Class: Miss Tanner (treasuter), Miss Dobbins (secretary). Sunday Schools : Mies Ethel Dale (treasurer), Mrs George Dale (secretary). Men's Bible Class : Mr Bsn (treasurer), Mr Thompson (semetaryj. Young Men's Bible Class : Mr H Yoden (treasurer), Mr Arthur Webb (secretary). Christian Endeavour society : Mrs Peter (Meaty') (secretary and treasurer). Refreshment Stall : Mrs David Hill.
Flower Stall : Miss Oakley (secretary) end Mr F Atkinson (treasurer). The treasurer of the bazaar is Mr Thomas Taylor and the secretary Mr A Tilling.
OPENING CEREMONY. MRS. A. H. CROSFIELD AND THE WAR IN THE BALKANS.

The bazaar was opened on Thursday afternoon by Mrs A it Crosfield. Mr A fi Crosfield presided and amongst others present were : Miss Croslield, Miss Le Thicke, Mrs Ziba Armitage, Messrs T Dale, N Hough, A Tilling, T Ashley, and P Peacock. it was announced that Mrs John Crosfield, of Colwyn Bay, was unable to accept an invitation to open the bazaar, as she was on a visit to Ireland. She wished the effort every success. Another letter of regret for non-attendance was received from Mr Joseph Monks, a former president of the mission, who recalled the great interest which its founder (the late Mr John Crostield) took in it up to the time of his death.

„ • Air 111.1.1NG explained that in the annual report on the work of the mission, presented last Christmas, reference was made to , the growth of the °Lurch and school and to the need for increased accommodation. Mrs Crosfleld of Colwyn Bay had relieved the congestion, as far as the Sunoay School was concerned, by the provision of a beautiful hall. The chapel however, was still over- crowded on Sundays and the object of the bazaar was to enable them to enlarge that building. He appealed in confidence for the generous support of their friends,

• WESLEYAN CHURCll.—Anniversary services were held on Sunday last, the preacher morning and evening being Rev Thomas Miller of Liverpool, whose discourses were greatly appreciated by large congregations. In the afternoon a musical service was given, presided over by Mr F A Harris, at which several anthems were given by the choir, and solos were exceedingly well rendered by Miss May Isherwood, Mr William Booth and Mr Ernest Walker. FUNERAL OF MR. Ross BAILEY.—The funeral of the late Mr Ross Bailey, son of Mr and Mrs John Bailey, 11, Brackley-street, whose death under tragic circum- stances was recorded last week, took place in St Thomas's Churchyard on Saturday afternoon, amid many manifestations of regret and sympathy. The service was conducted by the Rev James Collins. The chief mourners were the father and mother, Mr Frank Bailey Miss Ida Bailey. Mr G Pimlott, Altrincham (uncle), Mrs G Hewitt, Runcorn (aunt), Mr and Mrs Ben Weir Culcheth (uncle and aunt), Mr George Bailey (uncle), Mr Frank Weir (uncle), Mr Joseph Bailey', Mr John Weir, Mrs Fred Weir, Stratton ; Miss Annie Hewitt, Altrincham ; Mr Sourbutt (representing the Altrincham butchers), Miss A Broomfield, Mr Jos Davenport, Mr E 13k1shaw, be members of the Young Men's Bible Class B and their leader, and many others. div.head: Yesterday's Opening.
div.p: Yesterday's Opening.

Yesterrlay afternoon the bazaar was re-opened by Mrs Henry Roberts, Mr .7 G Withinshaw presiding. Mr TILLING announced that h the sum raised the previous day amounted to £147 7s 4d, which exceeded their anticipations. (Applause), The CNA] RMAN expressed his admiration of the work of the mission and congratulated the members upon their splendid premises. It was most exhilarating and heartening to find a place of worship in Warrington that needed extending in order to accommodate the congregations. They at Bank Quay bad a splendid neighbourhood to work in and no-one need complain of lack of opportunity. They were pro- ceding on the right lines in enlarging their Sunday schools, for the hope of the Church lay more in the Sunday school than in any other direction. Sometimes they were apt to put the Sunday school in a secondary place—which was quite a mistake—but the money spent iu that work, was toe best spent. (Applause). Mrs ROBERTS, in opening the school, referred to her long and intimate acquaintance with the work of the mission stud said it was not surprising tbat in such a populous district, their premises required extending. She sincerely hoped their efforts would be crowned with success. She could appreciate the self-denial and labour which the bazaar had called forth. They heard a great deal nowadays about women taking a more forward place in the world's affairs. She did not know that she was one who desired that—certainly not for herself—but in the work of the Church women could always be useful. (Applause). .
Arbearti vote of thanks was passed to Mrs Roberts and the Chairman, on the proposition of Mr T DALE.

div.head: WARNING TO WOMEN,
div.p: WARNING TO WOMEN,

It is high time that a word of warning was spoken to women regarding a matter which at one time or another affects every one of them. There are no excep- tions, nor can there be, fur Nature does not dis- criminate. The rich and idle woman suffers with her sisters of the kitchen and the loom. Every woman, no matter what her station in life, is subject to the ailments of her sex. Time and time again the dull aching pain in the back and sides reminds her that she must pay the penalty of her sex. How heavy that penalty is, women are too only well aware, It is thew: women who are warned against trifling with these pains. They must not be hushed up and concealed. It is a woman's duty to herself and to her children to see to it that they are checked before they play havoc with the constitution. A Derbyshire lady, once an exceptionally great sufferer, writes : "I feel it my bounden duty to send a few lines. I suffered for many years and got no relief from any- thing. I at last took my husband's advice and pur- chased a bottle of Lydia E. Pinkham's Vegetable I Compound. After two doses I was surprised at the relief I had got, and now I can say that the pain I used to experience has entirely left me. I am perfectly convinced that I owe my relief to your wonderful Vegetab'e Compound." All chemists sell Lydia E. Pinkhana's Vegetable Compound at 2s. 9d. and 4s. div.head: PUBLISHED BY SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT
div.p: PUBLISHED BY SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT
HOW FOOD IS FAKED.
[COPYRIGHT.]

"Who buys land buys stones; who buys meat buys bones; who buys eggs buys shells; Who buys good ale buys nothing else." So ran the time-honoured posy on the Toby jugs of olden time, when you might, with ordi- nary precaution distinguish chalk from cheese, and the pit:dice of adulteration -was not yet elevated to the status of a fine art. We should count ourselves well-served to-day if we found nothing less desirable than the substances men- tioned thrown in with our weekly shopping. It is an ago of imitations and humbug, of paper- leather, jerry-built houses, and lying trade terms; an age when rags re-appear as new woollen cloth; when you scratch brass to find iron in the middle; and when authors •O aim oE their stale old novels under new titles; an age wherein the whole secret of success appears to be to sell something cheap and nasty at the price of what is -good and genuine. No wonder. that the purveyors of the 'nation's food have fallen. a prey to the spirit of such a time! The old-fashioned roan, -who "hikes to know

what he is eating" must know the.want, as the saying is, since it would surprise most people to be put face to face with the deleterious matter and worthlees bulk which is put cn'their tables under the name of food. GOOD (P) ALE. •

"Who buys good ale buys nothing else!" The "glorious beer" of the British workman could tell a story that would astonish honest John Barleycorn of old time not a little. The " xrreatliy hop" of the poet's lay has very little to do with the composition of the national drink; and to-day the chemically manufactUred article, with all its horrible possibilities of brown oil of vitriol, and other hitherto undis- covered frauds, is positively preferred to the wholesome and less heady brew that 'stashed down the roast beef of old England. The arsenic scare of a, few years ago only differed from a good many other similar perils in that the fraudulent deception was found out. It re- called to middle-aged people another alarm of arsenic 'poisoning; when more than a hundred children succumbed in Bradford to the effects of cheap sweets, prepared with arsenic treated glucose. . . _ .

- Calling at a large spirit-dealer's office the, other day, a gentleman happened to see a row of sample-bottles on the mantelshelf which spoke volumes as to the integrity of the liquor-trade. They n'were labelled grain-spirit; maize-spirit; potato-spirit: whiskey-flavouring, gin-flavouring, brandy-flavouring! It appears, then, that not only the outposts of Empire con- sume the Continental output of raw spirit. Tho Britigh workman, who likes his morning coffee "laced" receives a modicum of virulent potato- spirit in return for his extra penny. n THE MYSTERIF.S OF MILK.

But he who buys milk is in still worse plight than the beer drinker. True, we are at great pains to insure ourselves against the contami- nation from tuberculous cows, and have made regulations against too copious watering. Above the minimum of richness demanded, the Ntily. dealer never allows his milk to rise; any un- due creaminess is hastily corrected., if a cow ha.s calved, and raised the standard of a whole kit with her generous supply, the separator is there to do its work. Skim milk is then added to make up the bulk; and bring it down to the recognised poverty. After a night in the refri— gerator, yesterday's milk may be warmed to bloodrheat, and sold for new milk. Anather in- geniolus way of reserving the cream to take home at'the end of a round is to sell it from a dandy with a tap at the bottom; thus the consumer is served from the skim milk, the best part of the milk having risen to the top. But the greatest danger in the
-COlll-

mercial commodity which we call milk is the presence of boracie acid, that most harmful so-called preservative which finds its way into many' articles of diet, which will not keep indefinitely. In hot weather, it is next to impossible to get milk without it; and medi- cal men have repeatedly laid stress, on the opinion that it-is largely, responsible for the prevalence of gastritis and kindred ills. There are many creameries (save the mark) with fancy names, whose dairy work is done in the lowest neighbourhoods, and -who bottle thickened cream, highly preserved, for sale in the town shops. It is not cream, though the public ac- cepts it as such, as blandly as the child who, seeing a cow milked for the first time,, ex- claimed, "We don't have milk out of a dirty cow. We gets it from a nice, clean shop." Far some reason, perhaps because it is easily detected, butter.manages to lead a pretty honest life, with the exception of a goodly -weight of salt, and an enormous proportion of water. But the manufacture of a host of butter-substitutes affords scope for the use of a large quantity of waste offal fats, which are chemically-treated, from no matter what stage of putridity, to a metamorphosis into 'table delicacies of butter. ' CUD hue.

div.head: PRESERVATIVES AND SELF-PRESERVATION.
div.p: PRESERVATIVES AND SELF-PRESER- VATION.

In conjunction with meat, the action of pre- servatives is a positive menace to the commu- nity. It is bad enough to have last °year's sal- mon offered ,for sale after a season's retirement into cold storage. It is bad enough to be pre- sented with grouse on the glorious twelfth, which were shot at the close of last year's shooting, and have spent a close season in the refrigera- tor. It is bad enough to buy New Zealand bun- nies for English, but you may tell these by the squashed condition of the corpses; unless the dealer has found a way to plump them out again. But it is positively criminal to conceal the signs of tainted meat by washing the ex- posed surface with a solution of borax, as many butchers and fishmongers and a few misguided housekeepers do. The borax induces a fresh,. rosy tint, and the purchaser fondly imagines, and the dealer pretends, that the taint of which the green iridescence or yellow flabbiness was. Nature's-danger signal, is economically averted. I have seen this insanitary practice recom- mended in a cookery-book vaunted for ite hygienic principles. The borax does not avert the taint: meat which is once unfit for humSn food ought to be at once destroyed. The process of decay and putrescence may be arrested, and the appearance and smell concealed, and the taste, that most valuable guide, deceived; the borax may deodorise, but the harmful condi- tion ia as powerful as over. The germs de- posited by exposure to the air may indeed suc- cumb to heat, but the deadly ptomaine is- armour-clad against the powers of frying-pan- or oven. This and other preserving wrinkles* place the public very much at the mercy of un- scrupulous restaurant keepers and landladies,. who delight in serving up such petty economies. It is nauseating to think of the doubtful eggs,. and the nasty butter that go into the confec- tioner's cake mixture; Miss Olive Malvcry, who has gone to the heart of some disagreeable ques- tions, states that bad eggs are regularly used to glaze the tops of buns. The topic recalls a school treat, where one scholar repeatedly passed the slabs of cake pro- vided; and being pressed for a reason, bashfully explained: "I rayther wouldn't. I works where that comes from."

div.head: POTATO "JAM" AND ELDERLY SHRIMPS.
div.p: POTATO "JAM" AND ELDERLY SHRIMPS.

Large consignments of imported fruit-pulp which has fermented in the tins, are condemned regularly as unfit for food in our seaport towns; but what becomes of the pulp which passes the inspector before fermentation has set in? It goes to tholam factory, to be worked up, with. potatoes and fruit-flavouring, and the remains of jelly and raspberry vinegar, into "This Sew son's Whole Fruit Preserve." Rhubarb is the great standby of the jam manufacturer; as it has the happy knack of imbibing the flavour of anything that is put with it. The sausage is, of course, a mystery-bag. ov the face of it; c. dark horse indeed! But it is not generally known that oxide of iron is used lo give a fresh pink hue to the skins; and that the same solution restores a youthful freshnese and pinkness to an elderly shrimp, after a long absence from its native waters! Really with sand in our sugar, salt in our beer, sawdust in our coffee, cornflour in. OUT pepper, and fuller's earth in our flour, the won- der is that we can get a square meal at all, anS greater wonder that so many of us survive t 4 tell the tale.
