div.head: UP THE POLL-THE RIGHT MEN at the TOP.
div.p: UP THE POLL-THE RIGHT MEN at the TOP.
WHITECROSS WARD.
Peter Peacock (L), Samuel 0. Allen (C),
Majority 389
LATCHFORD WARD. W. J. Wilson (C),
E. Wynne Jones (L),
Majority 331
•TOWN HALL WARD.
W. H. J. Jenkins (C), P. Delaney (1),
Majority 136

Almost unprecedented activity was shown in the Warrington Municipal Elections which took place yesterday with the above results. it has of late years become the fashion to decry the apathy of the average elector towards matters municipal, but on this occasion, at any rate, his interest was awakened to a degree reminiscent of a Parlia- mentary struggle. There was a contest in each of the nine wards in the borough and in the majority of cases the issue was between the Conservative and Liberal parties. Several Independents were also in the field and such was the energy displayed that in very rare instances could the result be looked upon as a foregone conclusion for either side. In only one Ward—Howley—did the fight lack reality, for Mr. F. J. Owen, who stood in pro- test against the over-representation of " the trade" in the Council, contented himself with issuing an address and did not attempt to influence the electorate by canvassing or even by putting in an appearance in the ward on election day. A battle royal was waged in St. John's Ward where the Liberal and Conservative parties exerted themselves to the utmost of their power to secure the victory, Mr. James Shaw being generally regarded as a formidable opponent of Mr. T. S. Steel, the retiring representa- tive. The Tories were very fearful lest the representation of this typical workingclass ward should be wrested from them, and, in addition to flooding the ward with workers, held numerous meetings, the closing one being notable for the vehemence and bitterness with which the Liberal nominee was assailed. In the Town Hall Ward the situation presented unusual features and the poster warfare was keener than in any other part of the borough. The exceptional circumstances surrounding the withdrawal of Mr. William Issac led to that gentleman openly supporting Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, the Conservative member, notwith- standing the fact that the Conservatives had not scrupled to make capital at Mr. Isaac's expense by ridiculing the course of action which he had felt compelled to adopt. Mr. Jenkins also boasted the support of another prominent Liberal in the person of Mr. William Roberts. His opponent, Mr. Peter Delaney, came forward as the nominee of the insurance workers, who worked like Trojans on his behalf. In Bewsey Ward piquancy was lent to the contest by the fact that the candidates were uncle and nephew, in the persons of Mr. Samuel Gough (I.) and Mr. A. C. Binks (C.) In Whitecross, Latch- ford, Fairfield and Orford Wards the fights were political, although the introduc- tion of imperial politics came from the Conservative side, the Liberal candidates holding that party colour had rightly no bearing on Town Council work for which business experience and acquaint- ance with the needs of the wards should be the main qualifications. In St. Austin's Ward, two Independents were opposed, for although Mr T H Ashcroft is a Conservative in politics, he had not made use of the party organization to further his candida- ture. Mr Edmund Osborne had supporters and workers from all parties, for there was a consensus of opinion among those who take a broad view of municipal life that he would make an ideal representative. A round of the polling booths disclosed little in the way of incident. In St. John's Ward it was reported that a boy of nine had recorded a vote, his name having found its way on to the register, notwithstanding the zealousness with which the list is guarded by the powers that be. Some of the Liberals complained of the shortage of vehicles but each candidate had the aid of a large body of enthusiastic workers.

_ The Conservatives resorted to the time- honoured device of issuing a bill in the Liberal colours, the subject matter consist- ing of personalities about all who had had the temerity to oppose the Tory nominees. IN THE COUNTING ROOM.

Owing to the exceptionally large number of contests, two rooms at the lown Hall were required for counting purposes. The votes for six of the wards were counted in the Council Chamber and those for the remaining wards in the large committee room. All the candidates with the exception of Mr T S Steel and Mr F J Owen, were I present. The results having been declared the customary votes of thanks were passed to the presiding Aldermen and officials. Councillor Jenkins thanked his opponent for the kindly spirit in which the election had been fought. There had been nothing calculated in the slightest degree to annoy. Councillor Chrimes said his only regret was that his opponent had not had the courtesy to show his face at the polling booth. Alderman John Evans (presiding alderman for Howley Ward) also expressed the opinion that Mr. Owen might have shown his face and given some reason for putting the town to the cost of an election. -

Councillor Taylor said he had nothing whatever to reproach his opponent for in the way in which the election had been fought. He hoped some day Mr. Jarman would be returned to the Council, as he was worthy to fill the office.' Mr. Jarman said the fight had been clear and fair from beginning to end. Councillor H. Roberts (who deputised for Alderman IJames Evans) congratulated Councillor Taylor and condoled with his opponent. He considered that both candi- dates were exceptionally well qualified to serve the town in the Council.
iCILLOR PEAI

votes of 449. In Fairfield and Latchford Wards they had defeated two of the most pronounced Liberals in the town. In St. i. Austin's Ward he had no doubt the candi- date would have won had he come out n Conservative colours. He hoped he would reflect upon that in the future. Hear, hear.) Councillor Jenkins remarked that he was exceedingly tired but exceedingly cocky (laughter). They had had to combat a coalition of forces in the Town Hall Ward, but they had done it successfully. He had not- a word of reproach to utter. His opponents were perfectly justified in think- ing they could crush him" , but they had not done so. (Applause.) Councillor Wilson said that in the Latch- ford Ward they had, fought honest, straight, and clean. He had polled more than any candidate in the Ward had polled before, and that against a big Radical. (Applause.) It was something to be proud of. Councillor Chrimes humorously remarked that he did not know whether Ite had had a fight or not. If he had not, he had the. satisfaction of knowing that he had driven
LIBERAL ELECTION TRIUMPHS.
Great Victories in St. John's and Vk, hitecross.

div.head: SPEECHES AT THE CLUBS.
div.p: SPEECHES AT THE CLUBS.
AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
A DEJECTED CROWD.

At the Conservative Club a considerable period elapsed before any " jubilation " could be worked up on the declaration of the results. A more dejected crowd has probably not assembled within the precincts of the club for some time. Coming events may possibly be casting their shadows before. . .

Mr. Fulton Smith at last made a short speech in which he said they had nothing to be ashamed of. They were not in the least downhearted. They had been very much handicapped through causes over which they had no control. They had also to combat the usual tactics adopted by the other party. So they could congratulate themselves upon the successes they had gained. They had made their opponents sit up and spend a good deal of money—at least they hoped so. It might keep them quiet for a little time. fie hoped the successful Conservative can- didates would keep up the traditions of the Party in the Council and its reputation for being the Party of purity and honesty. (Applause.) Mr. E. A. White said they had perhaps not been as successful as some of them had hoped, but when they analysed the results they had certainly no cause to be down- hearted. They had polled a majority of

a strong opponent away. He thought his opponent 'ought to stand the cost of tho election. He had only been opposed be- cause he was a member of the " trade," but from what he knew of his opponents they did not put " it " in their shoes when they got "it " on the cheap. (Laughter and applause.) MR. E. WYNNE JONES AT THE JUNIOR _

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB.

Speaking at the Junior Liberal Club after the election, Mr. E. Wynne Jones said he had to-day offered his hand to Mr. Wilson, his opponent, but he refused to take it. He , personally, felt glad he had not done so because he did not wish to make either the acquaintance or the friendship of a party who would descend to such mean actions as they had shown themselves cap- able of to-day. (Hear, hear.) They had blown the disenfranchisement horn, played the Home Rule cornet and beaten the Insur- ance kettledrum. (Applause.) They had actually told him in some of the houses which he visited, that if he was elected it would take the living from the Vicar of St. James'. (Laughter.) He was going to contest the Ward again on the first opportu- nity, for he meant to be the representative of Latchford Ward. . (Loud and prolonged cheers.)

div.head: AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

Immediately after the declaration of the results Councillor James Shaw proceeded to the Liberal Club, where he was greeted with tumultuous cheers and the singing of " For he's a jolly good fellow." A short meeting of congratulation was presided over by Mr. William Clegg. Councillor Shaw said they had had " the third time of asking," and now there had been a marriage between James Shaw and St. John's Ward. (Cheers.) He was confident that their opponents would find it an extremely difficult task to break the partnership. (Cheers.) Nothing succeeded like success, and now that they had broken the ice and their forces had been inspirited by victory, he believed they could remove a second Tory representative from St. John's Ward (cheers) and possibly a third (cheers). They had beaten their opponents' best man (cheers). Having stormed the citadel, they were confident that they would eventually they St. John's Ward entirely for the progressive,* cause (cheers). Mr. George Walker said the victory in St. John's Ward was one of the finest ever achieved. It was the thin end of the wedge —(cheers). In the past the Liberal party had felt a little bit " down" about St. John's, but they had now given their opponents something to think about, and if they could maintain the present enthusi- asm they might do even greater things in the 'future (cheers). Mr. Walker ex- pressed regret at the loss of Fairfield Ward. ' In Mr. Jarman they had an exceptionally good candidate and no - one could have tought a cleaner fight (cheers). If all the ; candidates and public workers in Warring- ton possessed the same mental calibre and honesty of purpose as Mr. Jarman, there would soon be a reformation in the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. E. A. Sanders also added a few words of thanks to all who had worked so strenuousfy in St. John's Ward. COUNCILLOR PEACOCK IN WHITE-
CROSS WARD. Coun. Peacock motored to his committee room in Whitecross Ward, where he addressed a most enthusiastic gathering of workers.

He said that when they asked him to contest the Ward, it was the greatest honour bestowed on him since he entered public life, and the victory, despite his enforced absence assisting other Wards, afforded him the utmost personal gratification. He could not thank them too heartily for the way in which they had supported him. When they considered that they had gained three victories and only lost one seat—Fairfield Ward—he thought it augured well for the progressive cause in Warrington—(cheers) —and the results would be reflected, to their credit, in the Council. (Cheers.)

div.head: TOWN HALL WARD.
div.p: TOWN HALL WARD.

----- • Some confusion was caused in this ward by the nomination of three candidates, two of whom were understood to be of progressive views. Mr W H J Jenkins, the retiring representative, again stood in the Conservative interest and his return was challenged by Mr Peter Delaney, who was the nominee of the life assurance workers. Mr William Isaac was originally in the field as a Liberal candidate, but under circumstances explained in our last issue, he withdrew his name to avoid a three-cornered fight. The officials of the Liberal Association and ward committee deemed it necessary to issue an explana- tion to the electors, in which they stated "In the first instance the Liberal Ward Committee appointed a deputation to wait upon several gentle- men, but as it was understood the Insurance Coln- pauieS were considering a candidate in their interests, nothing of a definite nature was heard for about three weeks. During this time, however, Mr Delaney was seen, and told the Liberal representatives that they were at liberty to choose their own candidate, without considering the Insurance Companies. We waited upon Mr Isaac on Wednesday, October 16th, and he consented on Thursday night, October I;th, to contest the seat, and on the next day at noon Mr Delaney was informed we had a candidate. He replied there was a meeting of the Insurance agents that aftecnoon, and it would rest with that meeting as to whichwaardthtrheeey- would contest. Seeing that Mr Delaney was adopted for Town Hall Ward, the Liberal Association thought it best to advise Mr Isaac to withdraw, as cornered fight would be of no use." Mr Isaac issued a strongly•worded poster on his own account, but as in some quarters this was construed as a reflection on Insurance companies and workers, it was followed by a withdrawal in which Mr Isaac disclaimed any such intention. iThe Conservatives sought to turn the incident to their own advantage by asking the electors "not to be humbugged by Radical squabbles " but to " vote for Jenkins, one of the founders of the Children's Camp." Yesterday Mr Isaac announced that he intended to vote for Mr Jenkiaa and asked all electors to do the same. Mr Delaney had

the support of a large body of insurance workers who conducted a thorough canvass on his behalf. The Conservatives invited the electors to "stick to your old friend Jenkins " but Mr Delaney contended that his own business training and experience fitted him in a special degree to represent this ward. Reasons " Why you should vote for Delaney " included : Because he is pledged to protect the interests of the 25,000 insured persons under the National Insurance Act, and also the interests of the ratepayers ; because he is pledged to work for a reduction of high rates, which will mean more industries and more wages ; because be will al ays insist on the adoption of the fair wage clause in all Corporation contracts. Mr. W. Roberts Intervenes. On behalf of Mr. Jenkins, the following letter, printed in red, was circulated : •
Dear Mr. Jenkins, Re YOUR FIGHT IN TOWN HALL WARD.

I should like to say how much I hope for your success on Friday. Liberal as I am in politics, if I bad a vote for Town Hall, I should record it in your favour. Your services to our town and the many ways you have laboured for the less fortunate of our towns- prople make me feel that the electors will not allow your services to he lost to the Council. Should I be able to come round and help you on Friday I most certainly will.—Yours faithfully, NVII. ROBERTS.
19, Bridge-street. WHITECROSS WARD.

The result of the fight in this ward was regarded as a foregone col elusion —in fact it was only at the eleventh hour that Mr. Samuel 0 Allen came forward to oppose Mr Peter Peacock, the popular chairman of the Executive of the Liberal Asscciation. Although Mr Allen clainnd to he tied to no political party, it was understood that he bad the backing of the Con- servatiN,s Mr Peacock referred the electors to his experience of Com cil work and to his qualifications as a bw.inessman. He pronuis..l to adv, cate better wages for the workers and called upon the ratepayers to ',lump for Peac.ck and progress." Mr Allen appealed to woikingmea as 4.ne who believes in purity in municipal life," and also dubbed himself a " right good sport." FAIRFIELD WARD.

Altheugh Ir Samuel Taylor, tliP Conservative candidate, was prevented by illnPss from taking an active part in the fray, every effort was put forward by the Conservative org.nization to ensure his return, ands, me of the head.; of the party addre4sed a meet- ing en his behalf. Mr J Jarman, the Liberal nominee, was late in the 11-Id, but lie VA; ew himself into the fight IA ith chatacteriitic who's-hearted! ess and spoke at Feveral lice baa. Re mad,- a point of the land gut stion, aa it effects 1 wal tating, ad laid stress on his ousiness ability and.kn •wledge of financial matters.

div.head: COUNCILLOR OSBO:
div.p: COUNCILLOR OSBO:
ST. AUSTIN'S WARD.

Mr. Edmund Osborne, whose candidature as an Independent had influential support, conducted a very energetic campaign in this Ward where the retiring representative, Mr. T. H. Ashcroft, also fought on non-political lines. Mr. Osborne promised to treat municipal affairs on business lines, and he also strove to arouse the electors to a true realization of the importance of measures affecting the public health. As one means of abating the smoke nuisance he advo- cated the increased use of gas and, in order to make this pcseible, pledged himself to support a reduction of the cost to the consumer. He considered it unfair that the huge profits arising from the gas undertaking should be allocated to the relief of rates. Mr. Ashcroft did not hold any meetings, but relied upon a strenuous canvass of the Ward.

div.head: BEWSEY WARD.
div.p: BEWSEY WARD.

The retirement oI Councillor Toole left the Liberals without a candidate in this ward. The redoubtable Mr S Gough came forward as a non-trader and had as his Conservative opponent Mr A C Binks, a prominent worker in connection with All Saints' Mission. In his address Mr. Bloke pointed out that he is Chairman of the Bevvsey Ward Committee of the Civic Guild of Help, President of the Health of Oak Local Associa- tion Benefit Society, and a past president of the Engineers' Society and the Warrington Trades and Labour Council. Mr Gough re-iterated his opposition to " any member of a public body deriving profit in any way whatever by reason of such membership, whether done through public or private limited companies." He also made the startling statement that the introduction of a government audit for the Corporation accounts will save £5OO per year in cab fares.
COUNCILLOR SHAW.

div.head: LATCHFORD WARD.
div.p: LATCHFORD WARD.

Mr E Wvnne Jones made a gallant fight in this ward but liad to meet a very determined opposition from the Conservatives who again brought forward Mr W J Wilson, the retiring member. Unscrupulous use was made by the Conservatives of the poster issued by Mr William Isaac in the Town Hall Ward, but their attempt to excite prejudice against Mr Wynne Jones in this way received a check on Tuesday evening when Mr Isaac explained at a public meeting that the poster was intended for Town Hall Ward only and had been published in Latchford Ward against his wishes. The depths to which the Conservatives descended in their campaign were even more strikingly exemplified in their introdution of the White Slave Traffic as a count in the indictment against Mr Jones's political faith. Said a Mr Councillor Campbell, who spoke on Mr. Wilson's behalf : " They had had a meeting in Warrington about the White Slave Traffic. He attributed that traffic to the policy advocated by the party to which Councillor Wilson's opponent, belonged. They told them it was the duty of the people of the country to buy the cheapest labour possible, I and that was the doctrine which he (the speaker) I believed was responsible for the immorality which existed in the country." • Mr Wynne Jones took his stand as a convinced advo-

cab e of progressive administration and emphasised such great questions as housing and the public health. He made a strong point of inequalities of local rating and gave some striking kcal instances. At a meet- ing on Tuesday evening he said there was a business place in Latchford for which the occupier was paying £26 a year ground rent. The community had created that value of between £6OO and £7OO per acre, yet the landlord was able to extract the rent and get off soot free, as far as local rating was concerned. "They tried to sell the skating rink a short time ago" said Mr Jones "and no-one would look sideways at it. Why? Because there is a ground rent of £BO which , works out at something over £l,lOO an acre. Yet that land was let only a few yea's ago at about 5:3 an acre for agricultural purposes." Mr Wynne Jones main- tained that the people were entitled to a share of the values which they had created and said municipalities throughout the country should approach the Govern- ment on the question.

div.head: ST: JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: ST: JOHN'S WARD.

One of the most interesting fights of the series was witnessed in this ward, %here the Liberals had a strong candidate in Mr. James Shaw, who has twice previously contested the seat and come very near to victory. The Tories put forth stupendous efforts to keep the representation of the Ward in the hands of Mr. T. S. Steel, and meetings galore were held to advance his candidature. Mr. Shaw reliea upon his thorough acquaintance with the needs of the ward in which be has lived all his life. He also criticised the way in which his opponent had curled out the duties of the office, as evidenced by his recorded attendances at Council and committee meetings which, a handbill declared, were practically one half of the total possible for the past year. The Tories professed an anxious concern for the under-paid worker, and in this ward promises were made that Councillor Steel, if re-elected, would join with other Conservative members to establish a wage of 30s, per week.

div.head: ORFORD WARD.
div.p: ORFORD WARD.

Mr. Elijah Cunnington, who has done good service for the V ard in the past, was again the Liberal candi- date and gave pronainence in his programme to the provision of open spaces, healthy housing accommoda- tion, clean and well-lighted streets and open-air swimming baths lie also emphasised the necessity of a motor 'bus service in Orford ard, and promised to do all in his power to further that object. The Ele,q3 icity and Tramways Committee, he stated, have a scheme in hand to run a service from Cental Station, via Orford-lane, Orford-avenue, Gorsey-lane to Cemetery and hack. The Conservatives brought for- ward Mr. William Bradbury who gave the novel undattaking that if elected " he would ptzt his hand on the shoulders of the present representatives of the ward and s,y I have come here to try and intro- duce a little bit cf enthusiasm into the Council. Chamber, and it must be put into some practical logical form.' "

div.head: HOWLEY WARD.
div.p: HOWLEY WARD.

The Conservative cause in this ward was championed by an cif-licence holder in the person of Mr J Chrimes, the representative of the Friendly Societies on the Education Committee. As a protest against the con- tiauity of "the trade's " over-representation on the Council, Mr F J Owen stepped into the breach as an Independent candidate. He did not conduct an organized canvass but left it to the discretion of the electors t say " whether Howley Ward should be particularly selected for three licensees out of four representatives it, the Council." Mr. Owen promised that, if elected, he would always be on the alert to ''heck extravagant expenditure and would see to the lower paid workers having their full share for their work.

div.head: MR. ISAAC AND TOWN HALL WARD. An Explanation. --- TORIES' UNWARRANTABLE USE OF POSTER.
div.p: MR. ISAAC AND TOWN HALL WARD. An Explanation. --- TORIES' UNWARRANTABLE USE OF POSTER.

What Mr. E Wynne Jones rightly characterised as the " mean and contemptible trick" of the Tory party in making use of Mr. William Isaac's poster, addressed to the elf-ctors of the Town Hall Ward, to prejudice his cmdidature in Latchford Ward, was responsible for Mr. Isaac's appearance on Mr. Wynne Jones' plat- form on Tuesday evening. Mr. I.sAAc said that Mr. Jones had informed him that a poster which he had issued to the electors of Town Hall Ward was being used against him. That was contrary to his wishes and instructions. The poster was addressed to the electors of the Town Hall Ward and no other, and he had not the slightest intention that it should be used against Mr. Jones or any other insurance agent. simply as an insurance agent. When he consented to stand as a candidate for Town Hall Ward it was on the understanding that there was to be a straight fight, without the interven- tion of a third party. It appeared that for two or th-ee weeks Mr. Delaney had been asked by the Liberal Association to stand as a candidate. He kept them in a state of indecision and in the meantime he was parleying with an association of insurance agents. He might have given the Liberal Association an answer straight away that be could not stand as a Liberal candidate, but he kept them waiting and finally the association decided that they could not wait any longer. " Now, last Wednesday week," continued Mr Isaac, " I had no more idea than the man in the moon of putting up for any ward. I have refused several times to stand as a candidate. They said 'See, Mr Delaney has legged' us down. We are in an awkward fix. We haven't much time. Won't you come to our help this time?' I'm not pre- tending to give the exact words, but that's the pith of it. I thought the matter over, and I then consented. On the Friday night I heard for the first time that a third candidate was in the field. I found that he was a member of the Liberal executive, and had used his influence with several Liberals to vote for him and .work for him. When the association and myself found that out we came to the conclusion that it would be a useless contest, and I with- drew." Continuing, Alr Isaac said he was a Liberal of the Gladstonian school and he could not relish the action (la man who belonged to the asso- ciation of which he was a member, defying that association, setting up against them, and refusing to recognize their official candidate. He had nothing to say against Mr Delaney as a man. If he stood merely as a citizen he would not have had a word to say, but he came forward as the nominee of the insurance people, and that was not the position a man ought to I occupy when he asked; for the votes of the electors I generally. He ought to stand as a citizen to voice the needs of the people and to do their work and not to do the work merely or specially of an insurance organization. Mr Jones was standing as a citizen, and they could not have a better candidate. If he (Mr Isaac) had a vote in the ward be would give it to Mr Jones. The poster was placed on the walls of the Latchford Ward against his wishes. (Applause.)

div.head: TORIES AND BOWLING GREENS.
div.p: TORIES AND BOWLING GREENS.
Mr. Peacock and Personal Attacks.

"If ever there was a time in the history of Warring- ton when St John's Ward was neglected it is to-day" commented Mr Peter Peacock at a large and enthu- siastic meeting in support of the candidature of Mr James Shaw in the Brick-street Mission on Wednes- day evening. They had not a single real representa- tive in the Council Chamber for that great ward. In looking up the attendances at Council and Committee meetings during the last 12 months, he found that Mr. Steel should have attended 104 meetings, but be had only attended 58. He was a representative who claimed to have served the ward faithfully and well. (Laughter). He, however, was not the only unfaith- ful one. Councillor Lashford should have attended 124 and he had only attended 39. (Oh !) Councillor Dr McKee should have attended 163 meetings and he bad actually attended 57). They could however excuse him a little if he had been in attendance on patients. The total of attendances for those three great repre- sentatives was 0n1y.152. ("Shame ") After showing how the Liberal members had far outshone those quoted for attendances, Mr Peacock said the ward had been wilfully neglected. The other side were playing on the ignorance of the working class by bamboozling them with great signatures like those of Sir Gilbert Greenall and others of the party. Men were wanted in the Council to represent the working men and not the party. (Hear, hear.) The Tory party had attacked him in Whitecross Ward. They talked about purity in municipal affairs, suggesting there, was something impure about him. He could lay his life open from birth and they could not point to one black mark on his life. (Hear, hear). He stood up for the people. Continuing, Mr. Peacock said the Tory party ruled the Town Council. Various bowling greens passed by the Council years ago had never been made \Thy could they not have a bowling green iu Winwick- road ? The plans had been passed and the land was there, but the brewer's party or the Tory party—same.

Why should we have more when our party have supplied them, attached to our public houses? What was wanted in the Town Council was a body of working men to represent working men. (Applause.).

The bride, who is cyan known in the Warrington district, was for several years a , , teacher at the Parish Church Sunday schools. ger father is also highly esteemed in local military circles. having been stationed at Orford Barracks until early last year, when he received hi 9 commission and was appointed Quartermaster ( , to the 2nd south Lancashire Regiment.
